translations.text: The Ladder of virtues that leads up to heaven, spoken by Daniel, monk of Raithu, concerning this book, the enlightener of souls, which is called Climax, that is, Ladder. Those who wish to have their names written in the book of life in heaven, and who hasten to ascend toward the good things of heavenly blessedness, let this holy book show them a good pattern and teaching for their course. And those who read it will find an unerring guide, who leads all who follow him toward the kingdom of heaven and keeps them from stumbling on any of the stones that cause stumbling. It will become for them a ladder raised from earth to heaven, leading from earth to that holy one, which shows God standing upon its top. And it is like that ladder which Jacob, the trampler of the passions, once saw as he rested on the bed of ascetic struggle. Therefore I beseech you, brothers, let us too ascend, with faith and love, this spiritual ladder that leads up to heaven, whose first step teaches us well. On renunciation of this vain world. On hatred of the world and its affairs. On estrangement, in which it speaks also of empty dreams. On the martyrdom that comes about through obedience. On repentance, in which it speaks of the prison.

On the remembrance of death. On the mourning that cleanses sins. On freedom from anger. On the remembrance of wrongs. On evil-speaking. On silence. On lying. On despondency. On gluttony. On fornication. On love of money. On poverty. On hardness of heart. On singing in the assemblies. On vigilance. On cowardice. On vainglory. On pride, in which it speaks also of blasphemy. On gentleness and simplicity. On humility. On discernment and understanding. On stillness and withdrawal and the guarding of the mind. On prayer with a collected mind. On dispassion. On love and faith and hope. The God-clad father John strove well and gathered all the work of the monastic life into this book. And he made the number of these spiritual steps correspond to the years of the Lord's bodily age, for at thirty years of age the Lord Jesus Christ was baptized; and so this man has depicted for us a ladder of thirty ascents, and if we reach its top we shall be from then on

perfect and unfalling. But whoever has not yet been perfected on this Ladder is an infant, useless and untrustworthy for every testimony of the heart. And we have thought it necessary first to set down here briefly the life of this all-wise man, according to my ability and as far as I attain to knowledge, so that we may see his labors and not become unbelieving of his words.

The letter of the holy father John, abbot of Raithu, to the blessed John, abbot of Sinai. To one blessed in God, the equal of the angels, father of fathers and teacher of us all: the sinner John, abbot of Raithu. Rejoice in the Lord. We poor ones know your unwavering obedience, along with all your other virtues, and above all the way the talent God gave you keeps growing and multiplying. For this reason we write to your holiness, following the word of Scripture that says: "Ask your father, and he will tell you; and your elders, and they will declare it to you."

So, since you are the common father of all and an elder above all others, both in ascetic struggle and in learning, and a good teacher, we beg the height of your virtues to write to us, the unlearned, what you have seen in your vision of God on that same mountain, like the great Moses. Let it be written down, as on spiritual tablets, in a book composed by you, to teach this new Israel, who have only now come out from those invisible Egyptians and from the sea of this world. Just as you have worked many miracles with that God-speaking tongue of yours, in place of a staff, and by the grace of God, and have rescued many from the sea of this world, so now too, we beg you, do not consider us unworthy. Instead, with the Lord's help, write down well whatever befits the life of monks, as a great teacher, for all who enter this angelic way of life. And do not think that we say these words with any guile or double-mindedness, for you know, holy father, that [?]

such a thing is far from us; rather, we speak as is true and as is believed by all. Therefore we trust in God that we shall soon receive the spiritual tablets we are awaiting, so that they may lead without error all who follow them; and so that those teachings may be like a ladder leading up to the gates of heaven for all who follow them and hasten to ascend there, and so that through your teaching they may pass unhindered by the evil spirits, the world-rulers of darkness and the princes of the air. For if Jacob was a shepherd of sheep and saw such an awesome vision upon that ladder, how much more should you, who are a shepherd of rational sheep, show us the unerring way to God, not only by vision but in deed and in truth. Farewell in the Lord, honored and holy father.

Epistle of the holy and blessed John, abbot of Sinai, to which this writing, the Spiritual Tablets, belongs.

John greets John. Your honored letter has reached us, which was just as befitted your passionless and virtue-filled life and your holy and humble heart. You wrote to us poor ones virtuously, for just as your holiness is always accustomed to give us an example of humility, so for this reason you have done this too, in that you have asked from us, who are unlearned in both deed and word, a word of teaching, and have commanded of us a task beyond our strength. But I say this, that if there were not upon me the fear of the mother

[…] from him [?] of all the virtues, which is obedience — lest I cast off its yoke from me — I would not have ventured upon a task beyond my strength. For it was fitting for you, O wondrous father, if you inquire into such matters, to learn them from those who know the work of virtue well, since we are still at the level of disciples, not of teachers. But the God-clothed fathers and teachers of obedience say that obedience is this: that a person undertakes tasks beyond his strength without doubting, at the word of his superiors. Therefore I have humbly undertaken a task beyond my strength. I did not do it so that what I have said might be of any use to you. For I know, O holy father, as do all who have wisdom of mind, that because your mind is pure of all the darkness of the passions, it goes unhindered to that divine light and is illumined by it. But because I feared that death which comes from disobedience, I came to obey your holy command with fear and desire. I came as an obedient and faithful servant, poor and useless, of a skilled painter, with this small and worthless understanding of mine and with a thin voice and word [?]. I have only sketched the living words in ink. I have left it to you, O leader of teachers, to adorn well and bring out clearly what I have sketched, and to complete everything that is lacking, as the one who perfects the spiritual tablets. And as I said, I have not presented this writing to you for your instruction — far from it! For you, holy one, are able to teach many, and even us, and to strengthen them in divine matters and teachings. Rather, I have written it for that divine community,

which is with us under obedience to you, O teacher of teachers! For its sake, through your prayers and theirs and through hope in the Lord, I have been lightened a little of the weight of my ignorance, and I have raised the sail of my pen and given the rudder of our speech into the hands of your prayers. I begin to speak at your word. And I ask of all who come upon these words spoken by me: if anyone finds any profit in these words, reckon its fruit to this our holy father, who commanded us to do this, and pray for me only for the effort. Do not look at these words, for they are truly worthless and full of every kind of ignorance. Therefore pray for me on account of my zeal, for God gives the reward not according to the abundance of gifts and labors, but according to the abundance of zeal. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
The teachings of our holy and blessed father John, abbot of Sinai, which he dedicated to Father John, abbot of Raithu, for he had asked him to write down teachings for monks.

Chapter One: On Departure from the World. 1. With the help of our good, man-loving, and merciful God and King, let us begin the discourse, for it is good that we make God the beginning of a discourse addressed to the servants of God. For all whom that good and glorious God created are rational, and he honored them with free will. Because of this, some are his friends, some faithful servants, some useless servants, some wholly estranged, and others, though they are powerless, are even his opponents. Now by friends of God we unlearned ones understand, O holy father, those incorporeal and intelligible natures that surround him; by faithful servants, all who diligently do his will; and by useless servants, all who have received baptism and have not faithfully kept the vows they made to God in baptism. 2. And by strangers and enemies of God we understand those who are either unbaptized and unbelieving

…or those who believe wrongly. The fighters and opponents are those who have not only cast off the fear of the Lord from themselves, but also fiercely fight and oppose all who do the will of God. A separate, proper discourse belongs to each of all these whom we have mentioned, but we, poor and unlearned as we are, are not able to speak about each of them one by one. So we have come to those faithful servants of God who rightly compelled us, the unworthy, to stretch out our hand in unwavering obedience. From their understanding we take the pen of our word and dip it, as if in ink, in their sorrowful and radiant humility. On their hearts, smoothed and made white by virtue, as on sheets of paper, or rather as on spiritual tablets, let us begin to write those divine words and seeds of virtue, and let us speak thus:

3. God is found by all who desire and seek him, for he is the God of all and the life of all: unbelievers and believers, the righteous and sinners, the dispassionate and the passionate, the godly and the lawless, laypeople and monks, the wise and the unlearned, the healthy and the sick, the young and the old. As the spread of light, the sight of the sun and the nature of the air are over all, so he is the life of all and the giver of all this. Those who seek him find him, for there is no change in him, nor is there partiality before God.

4. An unbeliever is a rational and mortal nature that willingly flees from life and thinks that its own Creator, who is eternal, does not exist.
5. A lawless person is one who holds the law of God in his own wickedness and in heresy opposed to it, and thinks that he believes in God.
6. A Christian is an imitation of Christ, as far as is humanly possible, who believes rightly and blamelessly in the Holy Trinity in deed, word and thought.
7. A lover of God is one who keeps natural and sinless deeds without change, and who does not grow negligent in any good that is possible for him.
8. A self-controlled person is one who, in the midst of temptations, snares and tumults, strives to carry out the deeds of those who are removed from all such things.
9. Monasticism is the way of life and the work of the bodiless beings, carried out in material and mortal bodies.
10. A monk is one who does only what is God's and looks to God at every time, in every place and in every deed.
11. Monasticism is this: that one gives up his own will, gathers together all his scattered thoughts, and is watchful in everything.
12. Monasticism is a constant forcing of nature and an unfailing guarding of the senses.
13. Monasticism is an undefiled body, a pure mouth, and an enlightened and seeing mind.
14. A monk is a mournful soul, grieved by the constant remembrance of death, whether asleep or awake.

15. Separation from and renunciation of nature, out of desire for those good things that are above nature. 16. All who have abandoned the affairs of the world have done so either because of the multitude of their sins, or for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, or for love of God. But if not one of these three thoughts has become their guide, their departure is brutish; yet in every case our good King awaits the end of the matter, to see what it will be. 17. Let him who has gone out from the world to scatter the burden of his sins liken himself to those who sit by the tombs outside the city, and let him not cease from hot, fire-like, blazing tears and from the hidden lamentations of the heart, until he too sees Jesus come to him, so that the stone of hard-heartedness from his heart
he may roll away, and may loose his bound mind, like Lazarus, from the bonds [?] of sin;
when he commands his angels: "Loose him from the passions and let him go on the way of blessed passionlessness."
But if it does not happen in this way, his departure from the world will be of no profit to him. As many of us as wish to go out from Egypt and to flee from the bitter slavery of Pharaoh,
we too undoubtedly need some Moses as a mediator with God, that he may stand for us between action and contemplation;
and may stretch out his hands to God, so that those who follow him may cross the sea of sins and may become victorious over the Amalek of the passions,
for all those are mistaken who give themselves over to such battles and think that they have no need of a guide.
19. Those who [?] as their guide, while those who came out from Sodom [had] an angel. And now too those who the healing of the passions of the soul [?]

...seek, they are like those who came out of Egypt, who needed Moses as a physician. But those who wish to strip off the uncleanness of this wretched flesh need an Angel as a helper, that is, one equal to an angel, so to speak. For the greater and more festering the wounds, the more we need a skilled physician. Truly, great hardship and unceasing labor are needed by those who have set out to ascend to heaven in the flesh. This is true above all at the beginning and outset of their departure from the world, until our pleasure-loving habit and our pitiless heart come, through mourning, to love of God and to purity. Truly, great labor is required and much bitterness, especially for those of us who have grown accustomed to the passions. This lasts until, through meekness, steadfastness and freedom from anger, we make this mind of ours, which like a dog loves the flesh and loves filth, a lover of purity and a lover of wisdom. Yet let us who are passionate and weak not be without hope. Instead, with unwavering faith, let us hold out our weakness and the feebleness of our soul to Christ with our right hand and confess it to Him. Then we will without doubt receive help from Him beyond what we deserve, if only we bring ourselves down into the abyss of humility without ceasing. 21 [?]. Know
that those who approach the fierce and narrow, yet light, contest have come to enter a fire, since they expect to receive that immaterial fire within themselves.

But let each one examine himself. In this way let him [?] of that fruit of the field [?] mixed with tears, [?] so that his military service may not be to his own condemnation. If not every baptized person is saved, I will pass over in silence what follows. All who wish to become monks should leave behind every worldly affair, despise everything and renounce everything when they come to the monastic life, so that they may lay a good foundation. The good foundation is the three pillars of virtue: innocence, fasting and purity. Let all who are infants in Christ make their beginning with these practices. Let them take visible infants as their model, for in infants there is no cunning or perversity, no dissolute gluttony, no insatiable belly, and no heated or brutish flesh. But as I think, as they grow and are brought up, they also acquire this heat. It is truly hateful and deplorable when a soldier goes into battle and, as soon as he enters it, is undone and gives everyone an example in his own death. For when the others see that he went in and was killed, they no longer wish to enter that battle. Without doubt, by beginning our labors well and promptly, let us enter the monastic life; great profit

It is enough for us if, after some time has passed, we do not grow slack. For a soul that has grown slack and is then set free again by the memory of its former zeal is pricked as if by a spur. That is why this has often led many to give themselves wings. They were like eagles whose wings had fallen off, and afterward their wings grew out again and they rose to the height of heaven. When the soul betrays itself and loses its blessed and longed-for fervour, it should search carefully for the cause of that loss. Then it should turn all its zeal against that cause, for it cannot turn back through any other door than the one by which it went out. He whose departure from the world [?] is often like incense thrown into the fire: at first it gives off fragrance, but in the end it turns into smoke. He who has gone out to receive a reward is like a mill turned by a donkey. It keeps walking as it looks at the reward, and it always turns in one and the same place. But he whose separation comes from love of God

has gained that blessed fire as soon as he goes out. And when that fire enters the material, the further it advances, the higher it stirs up its flame. There are some who build [?]. There are others who set up pillars on sand. There are others who ran a little on their feet, so that their sinews and joints grew supple, and then they ran faster. Let whoever understands understand the meaning of the parable. Since we have been called by God and the King, let us run eagerly. Our life in this world is short, so let us not be found fruitless on the day of death and perish of hunger. Let us please the Lord as soldiers please the king. For once we have entered military service, faithful service is required of us. Let us fear the Lord as we fear wild beasts. I have seen men who went out to steal and had no fear of God. But when they heard the sound of dogs in that place, they took fright and immediately turned back. What the fear of God could not do in them, the fear of dogs did.

Let us love the Lord as people in the flesh love their friends. For I have seen men who had angered God and had no concern about it at all. And again I have seen those same men, when their friends had been embittered against them over some small matter, seek every means, try every device, show every kind of sorrow, and make every kind of confession, in person, through friends and through kinsmen, with gifts and with bribes, so that they might bring that friend back to the former state of friendship. At the beginning of our departure from the world, we certainly practise the virtues with labour, hardship and bitterness. When we have advanced in them, we practise them afterwards without distress, or with only a little sorrow and labour. But when our mortal nature has been swallowed up and mastered by zeal, then let us practise them with all eagerness and joy and desire and divine flame. As praiseworthy as those are who from the very beginning fulfil the commandments with all joy and zeal, so pitiable are those who have spent much time in the monastic life and still practise it with labour, even if they do practise it. Nor

let us censure a departure from the world [that comes about by circumstance]. For I have seen some fugitives who came upon the king against their will and met him, and afterwards went along with him willingly, entered the palace and sat at his table. I have seen seeds that fell to the ground by chance, and they sprouted, spread and brought forth abundant fruit; and others were sown on purpose, and they became fruitless. I have seen a man who came to a physician for some other need, and he was won over by the physician's readiness, and he was healed, and the mist that had spread over his eyes was stripped away. So these things that happen against one's will have often proved firmer and truer than some that are done willingly. Let no one plead the weight and number of his sins as an excuse and call himself unworthy of the monastic way of life. Let no one, out of love of pleasure, imagine that he is humbling himself, and make excuses on account of his sin. For where the wound is great, great healing is needed there too, so that the poison may be cleansed out; for it is not the healthy but the sick who come to be healed. If an earthly king called us to serve him in his presence, we would not delay, we would not make excuses, but we would leave everything behind and hurry there. So let us guard ourselves against disregarding [?] the King of kings, the Lord of lords and the God of gods, who calls us to the heavenly order. Let us not scorn it, and let us not part from him through our negligence and laziness, so that we may not be found speechless and ashamed before that great throne.

It is possible even for someone who is bound by the affairs of the world and shackled with the fetters of cares to walk, but only with difficulty. People whose feet are in fetters can also walk, but they often fall and get hurt by it. Someone who is unmarried in the world and bound only by its affairs is like a man whose hands alone are tied. So when he wants to run on the path of monastic life, he is not held back. But someone who is married is like a man bound hand and foot. I have heard some people who were living carelessly in the world say to me: "How can we enter the monastic life, when we are joined to wives and are caught up in serving public affairs?" I answered them: "Do all the good you are able to do. Slander no one, steal nothing, lie to no one, and do not be arrogant toward anyone. Hate no one, and do not stay away from church. Have mercy on the poor, and cause no one to stumble. Do not seize another's portion, do not touch a stranger's body, and let your own wives be enough for you. If you do all this, you are not far from the kingdom of heaven." Let us enter that contest and not fear our enemies, for they look at the face of our soul, even though [?]

[...] they cannot see; and if they see the face of the soul changed by fear, then they arm themselves more bitterly against us, for those crafty ones perceive that we have become afraid. Let us arm ourselves bravely against them, for no one makes war on one who fights zealously. By his providence the Lord has lightened the battles for those newly come, so that they may not return to the world immediately, at the very beginning. Therefore rejoice in the Lord always, all you servants of the Lord, and take this first as a sign of the love that the King has for you, and be fully assured that he has called you. God also often does this: when he sees brave souls, he lets battles loose on them at the very beginning, so that he may quickly crown them. The Lord has hidden from lay people the difficulty, or rather the ease, of this racecourse; for if all knew it, not many would become monks. Give the labors of your youth zealously to the Lord, and in your old age you will rejoice over the wealth of dispassion. Labors gathered in youth nourish and console those who have grown weak in old age. Let us labor fervently, you young men, let us run well, for the hour of death is unknown. Truly we have evil and wicked enemies, crafty and full of many devices, sleepless and cunning, bodiless and invisible, who have fire in their hands and strive to burn the temple of God with their flame. Let no young man accept the counsel of the enemies when they say to him: "Do not crush and waste your flesh in this way, lest you

[?] you fall into. In this generation few would be found who, wanting to put them to death, would only keep themselves away from many sweet foods [?]. But the devil, who suggests such a plan, has this in mind: that the beginning and the entry should be slack and free from struggle, so that the end would then turn out like the beginning. Above all, those who want to serve Christ well should look for this: that, with the counsel of spiritual fathers and with great discernment, they find places, occupations and rules suited to each person's way of life. Communities are not good for everyone, because of gluttony, and solitary places are not better for everyone, because of anger. Each person should understand what he is defeated by. All of monastic life is contained in three forms of withdrawal: either a person lives apart and struggles alone, or he lives in stillness with one or two others, or he stays patiently in a community. [?] says Solomon in Ecclesiastes. But let me walk on the royal road, for the middle way between the ones just mentioned suits many people. It is said about the one who is alone that when he [falls into] despondency, or sleep, or slackness, or [?] (Ecclesiastes 4:10), he has no one to raise him up. And the Lord says: (Matthew 18:20) [?]. Who, then, is that wise, faithful and blessed monk who has kept his fervor unquenched

until the day he departed from the body? Every day he did not stop adding fire to fire, longing to longing, fervor to fervor and zeal to zeal, until he came before the Lord holy and spotless. To Him be glory now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen. The first step of the ladder of virtues: let whoever has climbed it not turn back.

Discourse of the same blessed father of ours, John: On hatred of the world and of its possessions. Chapter 2. [1.] Whoever has truly loved the Lord, and truly seeks to reach that eternal kingdom, and has truly come to feel pain for his own sins, and has truly come to remember torment and eternal punishment, and has truly fixed in his heart the fear of his departure from the body, will no longer love, care about or worry over things needed for use, or possessions, or relatives, or the glory of the world, or friends, or brothers, or anything at all of the affairs of the earth. Instead he will throw off and hate all love and all care for all of this, and above all of it his own flesh. Naked, free of care and with courage, he will follow Christ, always looking to heaven and waiting for help from Him, as the Holy One said: "[?] of mine after you, and your right hand has received me," which that blessed one said [?]. 2. It is a great disgrace if we leave behind all that was mentioned above, and after the calling with which the Lord, and not a man, has called us, we are anxious about some matter that cannot do any good [?]
to us at the time of our distress, which is death. For this is why the Lord said: 3. The Lord knew how quickly we turn aside from the good way of life, we who have newly come out of the world;
and that, if we associate with lay people, we easily turn back to the world again. For this reason he said to the one who asked, "Let me go and bury my father,"
And the Lord said to him: [?] 4. After our departure from the world, the demons persuade us to call merciful and compassionate lay people blessed, and to blame ourselves,
as though we have stripped ourselves of all their virtue. But this is the intent of our enemies, that by that vain and untrue humility
they may either turn us back to the world, or, even if we remain in monastic life, cast us into despair.
5. There is a contempt of lay people out of pride, and there is again a contempt of them
when they do not hear, for the sake of fleeing from despair and acquiring hope. Let us hear what the Lord says to that young man,
who said that he had kept all the commandments: "Go, sell all your possessions and give to the poor, and become poor, and receive charity from others." Of whom [?]
[?] going, let us wisely understand that the Lord called even those living in the world, though alive, dead,
and he said to someone: "Leave the dead, the lay people, that they may bury those dead in the flesh who are among them."
8. That wealth did not in any way hinder that young man from baptism, and therefore some have surely erred who said that the Lord spoke to him about coming to baptism,
saying, "Sell your possessions." And such assurance as this is enough to convince us of the great glory of this way of life of ours.
9. It is to be examined why those who were engaged in vigils, fasting, and labor, when they come to become monks and withdraw from the world,
And when they come to the testing of their deeds, they are unable to carry on that former false and [?] vain striving of theirs.
10. I have seen many and various plants of the virtues, planted by those living in the world,
and they were watered as if from a channel of filth, and were dug around by vainglory and ostentation,
and that dung of [?] was poured [?] on their roots. And when they were transplanted to a land [?] trodden and traveled by lay people and [?] watered by that water of vainglory and stench,
they immediately withered, for plants accustomed to such watering do not thrive in the harsh and waterless land that is the testing ground of true ascetic striving.

11. Whoever has willingly hated the world has escaped sorrows. But whoever has love for any visible thing is not yet set free from sorrow, for how could he not grieve when that beloved thing is lost? 12. In everything we need great caution. Above all, let us guard with a watchful mind against the thing I intend to speak of. 13. Many people, through cares, anxieties, labours and vigils in the flesh, have escaped the fever and turmoil of their bodies. But when such people come to be monks, they become free of care, and the wretched ones are defiled by the stirring of the flesh. 14. Let us take heed for ourselves, lest we suppose that we are walking that narrow and hard way while we are actually keeping to the broad and wide way and going astray. 15. This narrow way is: [?] (probably restraint or mortification) of the belly; standing all night in psalmody; drinking water by measure; scarcity of bread; enduring shame and reproach; accepting mockery and scorn; cutting off one's own will; not murmuring at insult; patience in afflictions; submitting to abuse; bearing ill-treatment; not becoming angry at insult. If anyone robs us, let us forgive without a word. If anyone speaks evil to us, let us not be distressed but bear it with patience, forgive, and not seek revenge. And if anyone judges us, let us humble ourselves before them.

…without words, and this is the narrow way of monks. 16. Blessed are those who walk this way of the deeds described above, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. 17. No one will enter the heavenly bridal chamber crowned unless he achieves the first, second and third renunciation. The first is renunciation of the world, of possessions and of kinsfolk. The second is renunciation of one's own will. The third is renunciation of vain pride, and renouncing it brings about obedience. 18. For which of the people of the world has ever worked miracles anywhere? Who has raised the dead? Who has driven out demons? No one. For all these are the works of monks, which the world cannot hold and cannot achieve. If it could, renunciation and the monastic life would be useless and superfluous. 19. After we have left, the demons will inflame our hearts with memories of our parents and brothers. When they do, let us arm ourselves against them with prayer and inflame ourselves with the memory of that eternal fire. By remembering that fire we may put out the improper fire of our heart and kindle the divine fire within us. 20. Whoever thinks he has scorned something, yet is grieved when he loses it, wholly deceives himself. 21. All the young men who are inclined toward bodily love and pleasure, and to the monastic life…

let them take care with all diligence and remove themselves from every pleasure and wickedness, so that their last state may not become worse than their first. A harbor can become a place of captivity, and all who travel on the visible sea and all who travel on the invisible sea know this. This is a pitiable thing, when those who have escaped from the heart of the sea are sunk within the harbor. This is the second step of the Ladder of virtues, on which you have set your foot: imitate not the wife, but Lot in his flight.

On exile. Chapter 3: Exile. Exile [is ?] parents and all who lived in our country, who oppose and hinder that good intention of ours. This exile is separation from familiarity. It is unknown wisdom, unrevealed knowledge, a hidden life, invisible understanding and an unseen intention. It is a desire for humiliation and reproach, a longing for affliction and distress, a growth of divine desire, an increase of the love of God, a denial of arrogance and an abyss of silence. At the beginning this intention, which is separation from one's own, often comes through that fire from God, and it strongly drives the lovers of God to desire afflictions and sorrows. But this undertaking needs discernment and understanding in the same measure as it is great and desirable, for not every exile is good. If every prophet is without honour in his own city and fatherland, according to the word of the Lord, then let us also take care that exile does not become something that increases vainglory in us.

…exile [is] a mind made inseparable from God. True exile is the unforgetting love and practice of mourning. …exile, and let him flee from love of strangers [?]. When you are planning to take up the monastic life or exile, do not wait for world-loving souls. That thief, which is death, is impatient and grants no delay. Many have wanted to save the negligent and have perished along with them, when over a long time the fire of their soul went out and their fervour cooled. Once you have received the divine flame, run, for you do not know when it may go out and leave you in darkness. Not all of us will be judged for others, for why we did not save them. But all of us will certainly be judged for ourselves, for the apostle says that [?]. And again he says: While you are living in exile, beware of the demon of wandering about and of love of pleasure, for exile gives him an opportunity. Contempt for possessions is good, but its mother is exile.

Let everyone who has become a stranger for the Lord's sake no longer acquire carnal and unprofitable love, whether for possessions or for a person, so that his occupation may not be wandering about for the sake of the passions instead of exile. Let him who has become a stranger to the world no longer touch the world, for the passions love to return. Eve was driven out of paradise against her will, but the monk leaves his patrimony and his own land willingly. For she would again have desired the fruit of that tree of disobedience, and passion would befall this one daily from his kinsfolk and friends. Flee as from fire from those places of falling where sin has befallen you. For when we see those fruits of bitterness nowhere, we do not desire them again and again. Do not be ignorant of this device and craft of the evil rulers. They urge us not to separate ourselves from lay people, as though a great reward would be given us if we look at women and let loose the rein on ourselves. But let them not deceive us; rather, let us do the opposite. When we have been separated from our own people for some time and have acquired some small compunction or self-restraint, then the vain thoughts of pride come upon us. They tell us to return again to our own country for the benefit of many, as an example of good, and for the edification of those who knew our evil deeds and were scandalized by them. And if we have some word of teaching or some small understanding, then as

saviours of our souls they urge us to return to the world, so that what we had gathered well in the harbour we may wickedly scatter in the heart of the sea. Let us not resemble Lot's wife but Lot, by fleeing. For the soul that turns back to the place it went out from dissolves like salt and becomes an immovable pillar. Flee [?]; those who turned back again to Egypt did not see Jerusalem, that land of dispassion [?]. This also happens: when some who were infants went out from their own land and have been completely purified, it is good for them to return there again with this thought, that after their own salvation they may save others as well. For Moses too, the seer of God, was sent by God to bring out his own people, and he had many kinsfolk in Egypt, which is darkness. It is better to grieve parents than the Lord. For He created us and saved us, but they have often destroyed those they loved and handed them over to torment. He is truly a stranger who, while understanding, sits among people of foreign tongues as one who has no language. It is not, then, out of hatred for our own people and for our lands that we depart from there, far be it! Rather, because of them

…and also because of the harm that comes upon us, and because of being drawn away from ascetic struggle. As Christ became our model in every good thing, so also in this. For He too often left His bodily relatives. For this reason, when it was once said to Him: [?] At once our good Teacher and Lord showed a hatred free of passion, and said to them that [?]. Let that one be your father who labours together with you in bearing the burden of your sins, and who helps you and strengthens you. Let your mother be compunction and weeping, which is able to wash you clean of the defilements of your sins. Let that one be your brother who toils and runs with you in the race on the road that leads up to heaven. Take the remembrance of death as a spouse who never leaves you. Let your beloved children be the sighs of your heart, and take your body as a slave. Take as friends the holy powers, which can be of great benefit to you at the hour of death if they become your friends. Longing for God puts out the longing for parents. Whoever says, "I am able to hold on to both," deceives himself, for he does not understand what God says: that no one is able [?]. The Lord says that [?] father and mother against children, and

brothers against [?], for those who wish to serve me: enmity and division, separating the lovers of God from the lovers of the world, the immaterial from the material, and the humble from the lovers of glory. For the Lord rejoices in division when it happens for the sake of love for Him. See, see, and beware: when the whole world is being filled with water, do not become a lover of companionship with your own people and your parents. Otherwise you will not enter the ark of ascetic struggle, and you will perish in the flood together with love of the world. Do not let the tears of parents or friends move you to pity, so that you do not weep forever. When your own people surround you like bees, or rather like wasps, and lament over you, then firmly turn the eyes of your soul, without wavering, toward your deeds and your death, so that you may be able to drive pain away from yourself by means of pain. They would promise us — not our own,

saying: "We will do everything just as you wish and whatever you love." But this is their inner thought: that they might ruin that good race of ours, and then by some contrivance lead us to their own will. Let our departure from our country be to places

…harsh [places], where no bodily comfort is found and where we gain no vainglory there, but rather humiliation. If we do not do this, we are flying on the wings of the passions. Avoid revealing that you are the child of rulers or of noble rank, so that you are not found saying one thing with your mouth and showing another by your deeds. No one has given himself up to exile as unwaveringly as that great man who heard that he was being called to a foreign tongue and a barbarian land. It often happens that the Lord glorifies someone who, like that great Abraham, has gone into exile for His name's sake. But even if that glory is given by God, it is still good to turn it aside with the shield of humility. When the demons, or even people, praise us for our exile as if for some great virtue, let us then remember Him who came from heaven to earth and became an exile for our sake. Then we will find that even if we struggled and lived as exiles for ages upon ages, we could not repay what He did. Fleshly love is grievous and very evil, whether it is for our own kin or for some stranger. If we give it room, it can turn us back to the world and completely quench the fire of our compunction.
M [?]. Just as it is impossible to look toward heaven with one eye and toward the earth with the other, so likewise it is impossible

It is [?] that a soul would not be harmed if it has not become entirely estranged from its own people, whether in mind or also in body. A good habit grows in us through much labour and effort, and what has grown through the labour of many years can be destroyed in the moment of a single hour. For evil conversations and the indecent things of the world corrupt sweet minds and good ways of life. Someone who has left the world but still keeps company with worldly people, or stays near them, will without doubt fall into one of these traps. He may fall into the same snares he had fallen into before. Or his heart may be defiled by what he sees and hears of them. Or, if he is not defiled himself, he will judge those who are defiled, and so he is defiled.

On dreams. The mind of our understanding is weak and full of every kind of ignorance, and this cannot be hidden. For the palate tells foods apart, and the [?] (ears?) recognize the meaning of words. The sun shows up the weakness of eyes, and words show up the ignorance of the soul. Yet love compels a person according to his strength [?]. So I say what I understand, as something I suppose and not as something I define and affirm: after we go into exile, dreams make war on us. For this reason I wanted to say a little about dreams as well, together with the chapter on exile, so that we will not be ignorant of this device of our crafty enemies either.

A dream is a movement of the mind while the body is at rest. A fantasy is a deception of the eyes in the sleeping mind. A fantasy is an ecstasy of the mind while the body is awake. A fantasy is the sight of something bodiless that does not exist. The reason I wanted to speak about dreams together with the chapter on exile is plain to see. When we have left our homes, our kin and our other belongings for the Lord's sake,

And when we give ourselves over to exile for the love of God, then the demons trouble us through dreams, and show us our own kin as mourning, or as dying, or as imprisoned and afflicted on our account. He who believes dreams is like the man who chases his own shadow and wants to catch it. The demons of vainglory become prophets in sleep, for they announce future events to us; but of things to come they know nothing at all, except that they lie; or else an event takes place and they learn of it by some other means, or they have heard something about it in another place, or have seen it, and having learned of it as if by some trickery, they come quickly and tell us, and even that only by conjecture. If their word comes true, they rejoice; and if it does not come true, they are not troubled. When the dreams we have seen come true, we marvel, and as though we had drawn near to the gift of foreknowledge, we become greatly puffed up.
To those who trust the devil he often becomes a prophet, but to those who despise him he always appears a liar. He is a spirit, and he sees the things done within this air,

They learn of the death of someone who is dying, and they go and tell it to the foolish, and appear among them as prophets. They know nothing of future events by foreknowledge; otherwise sorcerers too would have been able to foretell death beforehand. They often transform themselves into angels of light and into the likeness of martyrs, and show us in sleep that we are going to them, and when we wake they fill us with joy and pride. Let this be the sign of their deception: true angels show us torments and judgments and the separation of the soul from the body, and when we wake we become trembling, frightened, and sorrowful. When we begin to trust the demons in sleep, then they mock us even when we are awake. He who believes dreams is wholly inexperienced, but he who does not believe them at all is wholly wise. All those dreams that show us judgment and torments: believe them. But if despair assails you, that too comes from the demons. The third step of the ladder of virtues, by the power of the Holy Trinity: you who have completed this holy stairway [?], look no more to the right or to the left.

Discourse of our holy and blessed father John. Chapter 4. On obedience, all-praised and beautiful. The time for our discourse has now come, addressed to the zealous and to the strugglers of Christ. Before every fruit the flower goes first, and before every obedience comes withdrawal from the world, whether in body or in will, without doubt. By these two virtues, as by two golden wings, blessed obedience rises to heaven without hindrance. Perhaps this is why that Spirit-clad prophet said, as he sang: [?] "by action, by contemplation and by humility." Let us now briefly set out in our discourse the figure of those valiant warriors and make known how they hold the shield of faith toward God and toward their own teacher. With it they turn back every thought of unbelief or of wavering of heart. They draw the sword of the Spirit and cut off every will of their own. They are clothed in the coat of mail of meekness and patience, and they remain unwounded by all the arrows of insult and contempt. They have the helmet of salvation, which is the protection of their teacher's prayers. And they do not stand with their feet together: rather, one foot is toward service,
they have stretched forth,

and the other they hold unmoved in prayer. Obedience is the renunciation of one's own soul, shown openly and entirely through the body. Or else, put this way: obedience is the mortification of the members while the mind is alive. Obedience is movement without examining, a voluntary death, a life without questioning, hardship without care, and an untrained defense before God. It is fearlessness of death, a voyage on the sea without drowning, and a journey made while asleep. Obedience is the tomb of the will and the resurrection of humility. The one who is dead through obedience does not answer back. Nor does he judge between what is good and what seems evil to him, for he who has put his own soul to death in the fear of God will give account for him. Obedience is the setting aside of the riches of wisdom and understanding while being rich in them. The beginning of the mortification of the bodily members and of the wills of the soul is hardship and pain. The middle is sometimes pain and sometimes painlessness. The end is complete painlessness and unawareness of pain. That living and blessed dead man feels pain and grief only then,

when he sees himself doing his own will, for he fears to bear his own judgment. All you who are prepared to enter this arena of spiritual martyrdom, as many of you as wish to bear the yoke of the Lord on your necks, as many of you as hasten to lay your own burden on another's shoulders beforehand, you who voluntarily [?]
desire to write a bond of slavery in your own hand, and in exchange wish to have freedom written for yourselves,

as many as, lifted up on the hands of others, are crossing over this great sea: know, you who are such, that you have begun to travel a short and harsh road, on which there is no error except one, which is called self-rule.
But whoever utterly renounces this, and does not do his own will even in whatever seems to him good and spiritual, has arrived before setting out,
for obedience is distrust of oneself in everything,
until the end of life. When we are zealous for the Lord's sake to bend our necks, with the thought of humility and of the divine life, then before our entry, if there is any wisdom in us

and sharpness of mind, let us search and examine, and, that I may say this also, let us test the guide with whom we are entering, so that we may not come to a sailor as to a master of sailors, to a sick man
as to a physician, to one subject to passions as to one free of passions, and enter the heart of the sea as if it were a harbor,

and soon meet with drowning. But after entering the arena of the service of God and of obedience, let us no longer judge our teacher and the guide of our good in anything at all, even if we see some deficiency in him,
as in a man. Otherwise, if we judge him in anything, know that we will gain no profit from obedience. It is fitting for those who wish always to keep toward their guides
[?] toward, to keep unwavering faith always, so that they may keep their virtues in their hearts, never to be erased, as a lasting remembrance, so that when the demons bring unbelief upon them,
they may drive them back by remembering those good deeds. For the more faith increases in the heart, [?]

so much also is the body vigorous and eager in service. But when it has stumbled through unbelief, it falls, as the Apostle says. When the thought comes upon you to judge your teacher, flee from it as from fornication,
and give no place at all to this serpent,
but answer that dragon and say: "O deceiver, it is not I who am judge of the superior,
but he is my judge, for it is not I who am his [?]

But he has carried my burden. [?] of the holy ones, and prayer as a wall, and those spotless tears as a washing bath. And they proclaimed blessed obedience to be martyrdom, and without it no one entangled in sins and passions will see the face of the Lord.
He who passes sentence on himself.
For if he submits completely for God's sake,

Even though it may seem to him that he has not taken off his burden, in fact he has cast it away entirely. But if he carries out his own will in certain matters, then even though he may think he has taken off his burden, he is still carrying it himself. This is all the more so if his teacher does not refrain from rebuking him. But if the teacher does refrain and leaves him unrebuked, I do not know what to say about this. Those who by [?],
walk on a good road, for they do not, by scheming and close scrutiny, stir up the machinations of the devil against themselves.
First of all, let us confess our sins to our good superior alone; and if he commands us, let us confess them before everyone as well,
for wounds, the more they are shown, do not grow hard but are healed. I once came to a monastery, and there I saw a terrible judgment of the good judge and shepherd.
For while I was there, a man from a band of robbers came to become a monk.
And that good shepherd and physician ordered that he be given complete rest for seven days, so that he might simply observe the rule of the monastery.
After that week the shepherd called him to himself and asked him whether it pleased him to stay with them.
And when he saw that the man promised this wholeheartedly, he asked him again about the deeds he had done in the world, and he saw that he confessed them eagerly and fervently.

Again he said to him, to test him: "I want you to confess all these sins of yours before all the brothers." But he truly hated his sins and despised all shame, and so he agreed to do it without hesitation, and said: "If you wish, I will tell them even in the city of Alexandria,"
Then the shepherd gathered in the church all those rational sheep, two hundred and thirty in number.

And while the holy man was celebrating the liturgy, for that day was Sunday, after the reading of the Gospel he brought in that reproached yet blameless man. Several brothers were dragging him and beating him lightly;
his hands were bound behind him, he was clothed in sackcloth of [?], and on his head
ashes had been sprinkled, so that at the mere sight everyone was astonished and lamented with weeping, for no one knew what he intended to do. And when he drew near the doors of the church,
that blessed and holy father called out in a loud voice and said: "Stand there, for you are not worthy to enter here."
But he was startled at the voice of the shepherd when he heard it from the altar. For, as he himself later assured us with an oath, "I thought it was the voice of thunder and not the voice of a man."
And at once he fell on his face, trembling and distressed with fear,
and lying on the ground he drenched the place with tears. And that wonderful physician again gave him a command,

he who in all things sought his salvation and made him a mirror of salvation and an image of true humility: he then told him to tell his deeds before everyone. And he confessed with trembling, one by one, all his astonishing deeds,
not only those that were carnal and according to nature, but also those contrary to nature,
and sorceries and murders, and other things that it is not fitting to hear;
And after the confession, he ordered that he be tonsured and numbered among the brothers. But I marveled at the wisdom of that holy man, and I asked him why he had done that strange thing.
And that true physician answered and said to me: I did this for two reasons. First, so that by this shame I might deliver him from the eternal shame,
and so it came about, for he had not yet risen from the ground, Brother John, before he had found forgiveness of everything.
Or will you be unbelieving about this? For one of the brothers standing there told me: I saw a certain terrible man who had paper and writing in his hands, and a pen,
and as the man lying prostrate spoke his sins, he too drew the pen across that paper and blotted them out; and rightly so, for it is written:
And secondly I did this because there are some here who have unconfessed sins, and I showed them this as an example, so that they too may come to confession,
for without confession no one attains forgiveness of sins. And I saw many other wondrous and memorable deeds with that shepherd and flock, most of which I will hasten to make known to you.
For I stayed there no small time and examined their way of life, and I marveled at how those of earth had been made like those of heaven.
For they were bound with the bond of love, indissolubly, and this is the wonderful thing: they were separated from all boldness and idle talk, and their struggle before all else was for this,
that they should not wound the mind of a brother in anything at all,
and if anyone showed himself a hater of his brother, that shepherd would send such a one away to the separate monastery,

as one to be punished, for there was a separate monastery for those who had sinned. And once a certain brother spoke evil of a brother in his presence, and immediately that holy man ordered him to be driven out altogether, saying that it is not right that there should be

in the monastery both a visible and an invisible devil. I saw among those saints astonishing deeds full of profit, a God-gathered assembly bound together by love, whose deeds and appearance alike were wonderful, for they so trained and shepherded themselves in the virtues
that they did not even need the reproof of the superior, but of their own accord they roused one another toward those divine works,
for they had divine rules and works established and firmly fixed. And if the superior was not there,
and someone began slander, or judging, or idle talk, another would secretly alert him with a sign and make him stop,
and if he did not notice,

or did not listen, the one who had made the sign would immediately rise, bend his knees in a prostration, and go away. And unforgettable among them, and I would say unceasing, was the thought and complete remembrance of death, and talk of the eternal punishment. I will not keep silent in telling you about the deed of their cook,
for when I saw that he had unchanging sorrow and constant tears in his service, I begged him to tell me how he had been made worthy of such grace;
And when I pressed him, he told me that he had never thought that he was serving men, but God,
"and I have considered myself unworthy of all stillness, and I keep this sight of this fire as a reminder of that eternal fire." Let us hear about another wonderful virtue of theirs,
for not even at table did they rest from spiritual works and contemplations, but by an established
hidden sign, by making a signal, those blessed ones reminded one another of spiritual prayer; and they did this not only at table,

but at every meeting and gathering. And if anyone committed some fault, the others would earnestly beg him to allow them to speak on his behalf to the abbot, and to take upon themselves the canonical penance and punishment for it.
The abbot knew this too, and for this reason he would give such men a light penance,
and would no longer seek out the one who had truly committed the fault. Where among them was any matter of idle speech or insolence to be found?
And if someone began a quarrel with his neighbor, a second brother would come and fall down before him on bended knee,

and would dispel that anger. But if he saw him still persisting in rancor, he would report it to the second after the abbot, and that one would thus strive that they be reconciled with one another before sunset.
If he again saw him still hardened, he would either impose abstinence from food until they were reconciled with one another, or expel him from the monastery.
And it was not in vain that this was observed and that they practiced such fine strictness; rather, it brought forth much fruit,
and it showed this among them. For many of those saints proved to be ascetic strugglers, knowers of hidden things, discerning and humble.
And an awesome and angelic sight was to be seen among them, for old men and elders ran to obedience like tender children,
and they held humility as their great boast. I saw men there who had spent more than fifty years in obedience,
whom I begged to tell me what fruit they had gained from so much labor, and some of whom
told me that they had reached the abyss of humility, by which they turn back every assault,
and others said that they possessed complete insensibility and freedom from pain amid insults and contempt. I saw others of good report among those beasts [?] who were likened to angels,
having reached the depth of simplicity and innocence, acquired through wisdom, voluntary and advanced in God, not anything brutish and senseless, like those mad old men of the world,
whom people call mad; rather, they were outwardly sweet, radiant, and kind, and their speech and manner were not contrived and crooked, but plain and cheerful.
one that is not found among many: inwardly, in spirit, their sense of smell was turned toward God and toward their superior,

like that of innocent children, and the eyes of their minds were wakeful and firm against demons and passions. The time of my life would not be enough for me, O holy father and God-loving community, to tell of the virtue
and the angel-like life of those blessed ones; but it is good that we should adorn this discourse of ours to you with their sweat and labors, and rouse you to zeal for the love of God,
rather than with our own words and teachings, for undoubtedly the lesser is adorned by the greater.
But this I beseech of you: let no one imagine that anything written by us is a lie, for little faith is accustomed to corrupt what is profitable.
But now let us return to our first discourse. There was a certain man named Isidore, one of the rulers of the city of Alexandria, and a monk

he became in the aforementioned monastery, which I too reached there. That holy shepherd received him, and saw him to be vehement and negligent, haughty and boastful; and the blessed one, with human skill, devised a stratagem against the machinations of the demons, and said to Isidore:
"If you wish to take the yoke of Christ upon your neck, I want you before all else to acquire obedience."
And he said to him: "As iron obeys the smith, so have I given myself over in obedience to you, O holy one of God." And the blessed man was pleased with the figure he had spoken,
and immediately gave a task of testing to that iron-like Isidore, and said: "It is my wish, brother, that you stand at the gates of the monastery,
and bend your knees to all who come in and go out, and say to them: 'Pray for me, fathers, for I am mad and full of gall.'" And he obeyed him,
as an angel of the Lord is obedient. And when he had spent seven years in that work, and had attained the depth of humility and compunction, the blessed man wished, after that period of seven years,
and because of his mighty endurance, to number him with the brethren and make him worthy of the blessing.
But he put forward many others, and me too, the feeble one, to entreat the shepherd to allow him to remain in that same work and to finish his course.
And by a hint in his words he indicated his departure from this world and the end of his life, and so it came to pass. Then the abbot left him in that same work,
and after ten days he passed to the Lord, from dishonor to glory,
and on the seventh day after

his death the doorkeeper of the monastery was also taken away by the Lord, for that blessed man had promised him: "If I find boldness before the Lord, you shall not be parted from me in that age to come, and I will soon take you away."
And so he did, as a sign of his unashamed obedience
and the Christ-like humility. While the great Isidore was still with us, I asked him what work occupied his mind when he sat by the gates of the monastery,
and that man of blessed memory did not hide what had benefited him, but told me: "In the beginning I trained myself to think that I had been sold for my sins,
and so I made my prostrations with hardship, toil and blood.
"And when a year had passed, my heart was no longer troubled, and I was waiting for God to reward my labour and obedience,

and when another year had passed, I had become firmly convinced in my heart that I was not worthy to be in the monastery, or to see and speak with the fathers, or to receive the holy Mysteries, or to look anyone in the face,

And for this reason I made prostrations in this way to those coming in and going out, and my eyes looked at the ground, and my mind increased in humility, and with a fervent heart I asked everyone for prayer. One day I sat at table with this great teacher;
and he brought his holy mouth close to my ear and said to me: "Do you wish me to show you a godly mind in a man aged and advanced in years?"

And I asked him to do this. Then that holy man called from the second table a certain man whose name was Laurence, who had spent forty-eight years in monastic life and was the priest next after the chief of the priests,
and he came up and bent his knees to the abbot, and the abbot blessed him, and when he rose, the abbot gave him no answer,
but left him standing before the table without eating, and this was just at the laying of the table, and he remained standing until the clearing of the table,
and I was ashamed to look at his face, for he was very old, about eighty-two years of age;
and when we rose from the table, the father sent him to the great Isidore mentioned earlier, to recite to him the beginning of the thirty-ninth psalm: "With patience I waited for the Lord."

But I did not neglect this; rather, I wished to draw out the old man, and I asked him what he had been thinking in his heart while he stood before that table. And he said to me: "I set it before myself in this way,
and I pictured the shepherd in my mind as Christ, out of my great faith in him. And it did not enter my mind at all that he was commanding me, but rather God.
And for this reason, father John, I stood not as before a table of men, but as before the altar of God, to pray to God,
and I did not conceive any evil thought at all against the shepherd, because of the abundance of my faith in him and my love for him, as it is written that love thinks no evil;
and know this, father John, that when a person gives himself over to simplicity of his own will, the enemy will find no place in him,
nor any time." As that good shepherd was, such a steward did the righteous Lord give him, a holy and meek man, such as is rarely found.
But one day that great father became angry at this man just mentioned, without cause, and ordered him driven out of the church; but I knew that he was innocent
of the matter for which the shepherd was rebuking him, and privately I spoke to the father about the steward, saying that he was innocent.
And the blessed man said to me: "I too know, father, that it is blameless, but just as it is not right to snatch bread from the mouth of a small, hungry child,

so the souls of the strugglers who were under his hand will be required from the soul of the shepherd if he is not eager to seek out occasions for them to be crowned at every moment, as far as they are able to bear it, whether by insults, reproaches, dishonour or humiliation. For he does harm in three great ways:
first, because he deprives him of that reward which is given through the shepherd's rebuke; second, because it was possible from another virtue [?].
the benefit of others, and not doing it. Third, which is harsher than these: lest those who were thought to be patient and burden-bearing be made negligent by the shepherd,
if for some time, as though they were pleasing to him, he should neither rebuke them nor put them to shame, and in this way they should lose the meekness and patience that they had.

For though land may be good and fruitful and rich, yet often the lack of the water of insult and shame makes thorns spring up in it, and the bull's-head weed of arrogance, fornication, and fearlessness.
And the great apostle Paul knew this, and for this reason he writes to Timothy,

that [?] And I said to the elder that this generation of ours is weak, and that many stumble at rebuke that is not true, or even at that which is true, and separate themselves completely from the flock.
But that all-wise man
answered and said to me: A soul that has been bound to the love of its shepherd for the love of Christ, and has been filled with faith toward him, will not separate from him even unto death;

and all the more if it has also benefited from him through the healing of its wounds, but will always remember the saying that [?] But whoever has not been thus attached and bound and nailed to that love, I think that for such a one to remain in such a place is vain and useless, for he is joined to an erring and untrue obedience.
And the great man did not lie in this; rather, he was a powerful teacher, and one who carried this out and offered spotless sacrifices to Christ. Let us hear of the wisdom of God,

and let us marvel at what is found in earthen vessels. For when I was there, I marvelled at the patience of many newcomers, which they showed under the humiliations and insults of the superior, and often even under persecution, and not only from the superior but also from those of lower rank.
And for this reason I questioned a brother for my benefit, who had been fifteen years in that monastery;
and his name was Cyrus, for I saw that the brothers constantly tormented him, and the servers many times drove him out from the table,
for that brother was by nature, in some very small degree, unable to restrain his tongue.
And I said to him: Why do I see you thus every day driven out from the table, brother Cyrus, and sometimes you even go to sleep without eating?
And he said to me: Believe me, father, these fathers are testing me, whether I am fit

to be a monk, and they do not do this to me in earnest, and I know their intention and that of the elder, and for this reason I endure everything without pain. And behold, for these fifteen years I have kept in mind what they told me at the very beginning, when they were bringing me into the monastery,
that they test those who become monks up to thirty years; and they do rightly, father John, for even gold does not become perfect without being tested.
And after my departure from that monastery, the valiant Cyrus remained two years and then went to the Lord, and at the time of the going forth of his soul he said to the fathers:
I give thanks to Christ, my fathers, and I am grateful to you as well, for since you were testing me for the sake of my salvation, I have remained untested by demons for these seventeen years.

And he died as a martyr, and that good shepherd buried him, as was fitting, there among the saints buried in that place. I would wrong those who are zealous for good things if I kept silent about the virtue of Macedonius, the archdeacon of that monastery.
This man, worthy of praise, once begged the shepherd, two days before the feast of the Epiphany,
to send him to the city of Alexandria on some business of his own. He promised to return before the feast in order to take part in its celebration.
But the devil, the hater of good, detained that archdeacon, and he did not return as he had promised the superior;

and one day after the feast he came to the monastery. And the superior removed him from his rank and placed him in the place of the newcomers. But the archdeacon accepted the father's command with patience. And with joy
and without distress, as if it were someone else and not he who was undergoing the punishment, he remained in that rank for forty days, and then the superior raised him again to his own rank;
and after one day he begged the superior
to return him again to that same former disgrace, and he said, "I committed a grievous sin in the city."
But the elder knew that he was seeking this out of humility, and that holy man gave leave to this good desire of his.

And I saw that old man, worthy of honor, standing with the youths and newcomers, and he begged each one to offer prayer for him, and he would say, "I have fallen into the fornication of disobedience."
And the great Macedonius himself told me why he desired this state of humility, and he said:
"Never have I seen in myself such relief from battles and such sweetness of that divine light
as I have seen in these days." It belongs to angels never to fall, and to human beings to fall and immediately rise again, however many times this may happen; but it belongs to demons,

after falling, never to rise at all. [?] of a certain monastery, he told me: "When I was young, I was employed in the care of the mules, and some spiritual fault and error befell me. But I had the habit of not hiding that serpent within me,
and I held it by its tail and revealed it to the physician. But he smiled and struck me lightly on the cheek,
and said to me, 'Go, child, to your service, just as you were, and do not be afraid at all.'

And I believed this with fervent faith, and after a few days I became fully assured that I was healed, and I went on in my service with joy and trembling." Every order and work of created beings has its distinctions,
and likewise in the community of those brothers there were differences of works and of minds. Therefore, when that physician perceived that some were making a show at the coming of lay people,

when such an occasion arrived, he would expose them before those who had come, and with shame he would reproach and humiliate them and assign them to a despised service. And thus he would strip them of this until, whenever they saw lay people, they would flee from them;
And a deed beyond nature was seen, for he drove vainglory away from himself and hid himself from men. May the Lord not deprive me of the prayer of that spiritual father,
for one Sunday before I left that holy place, that shepherd's second-in-command fell asleep in the Lord,
This man was wondrous, and his name was Menas. He had spent fifty-nine years in that monastery, and he had served in every kind of service.

On the third day we were performing the office for the departed one according to the rule, and during the morning prayer a fragrance was suddenly given off, and it filled the whole place in which the holy Menas was buried.
Then the father ordered that grave to be opened, and we saw that from both his feet, as from two springs, a blessing (eulogia) was flowing. Then the abbot said to the assembly: See

that the sweat of his feet and his labor have been offered before God as true myrrh. Those fathers also told me many other good deeds of the holy Menas, and they said this too: that once the abbot wished to test his patience,
which had been granted to him by God. When he went up to the abbot in the evening and bowed down, falling to the ground,
and asked for his prayer, as was his custom, the abbot neglected him and left him lying fallen on the ground until the ringing for matins,
and only then blessed him;
and he called him a show-off and impatient, and in this way raised him up. For that holy man knew that he would endure with courage, and for this reason he did this to him for the benefit of many.
And the disciple of the holy Menas told me

that he asked him whether sleep had come upon him as he lay below with bent knees before the abbot. And he told him: I completed the whole Psalter of David lying on the ground. I will not leave this crown of discourse unadorned by this emerald as well. For once I began to speak about stillness with some of those holy elders,
and they, with cheerful faces and kindly manner, answered me: We, Father John,

since we are weak and material, have taken up a life suited to our measure, and we have judged thus: that we should enter into battle according to the measure of our weakness. And we have considered the battle with people lighter,
who are sometimes angered and sometimes grow calm and comfort us, than that with demons, who are always armed with wrath against us. And one of those holy men, who
had great divine love toward me and boldness, said to me cheerfully and sweetly: O wise one, if you have firmly established within you the measure and the deed of him
who said that, if the Holy Spirit and the dew of holiness have come upon you, as he came upon the Virgin Mary.

And if you keep covered the power of patience from on high, gird your loins, as Christ God did, with the towel of obedience, and rise from the supper of your stillness, and wash the feet of the brothers with a humble mind. And set strong and watchful doorkeepers, unsleeping, at the doors of your mind, and hold fast that uncontainable mind within the body, in the unceasing service of the brothers.
Acquire stillness of mind with a body that moves about without rest in obedience; become quiet in soul amid the tumults of the people.
Put a bridle on the tongue that is quick to anger and dispute; fight that evil tyrant, the belly, seventy-seven times a day,

and nail to that wood of the soul, raised up in the form of a cross, the mind made firm like an anvil, so that it may be struck with sledgehammers and hammers whenever it is blamed and reproached, shamed and beaten,

and may not be loosened at all, nor be shattered, but may remain smooth, without lumps, and unshaken. Cast off your own will from yourself like a garment of disgrace, and, stripped of it, enter that place of struggle, for few are found to be thus.
Put on the chain mail of faith, so that it may not be loosened by unbelief nor be wounded. Hold the bridle of purity with both your hands against boldness,
which is improper touching. Bridle with the discipline of death the eyes, which wander about to gaze on the goodness and beauty of bodies;
rein in the mind that judges its neighbor, and turn it back to the care of itself,
and give it love, compassion and mercy as its work, and by this let all know, O beloved father, that truly [?] of brothers [?].
And stand thus in the community, and thus at all times [?] mockery as if it were living water, for David examined
every love that is under heaven and every beauty, and last of all said in wonder:

But if until now we have not been made worthy of the good things of such patience and obedience, then it is good that we should know our weakness and stand by ourselves far from the arena of those who struggle, and that we should call those strugglers blessed and pray for their patience.
But I was defeated by that father and good teacher, who contended with me from the Gospel and the prophets, with love.

and without doubt we gave the first place and the victory to honorable and glorious obedience. Let me recall one more virtue of those saints. Then let me leave the account of their deeds as one leaves paradise, and begin to speak to you my own worthless and unprofitable words, you who have gathered me [?] by the sight of their virtues.
We were once standing at prayer, and that shepherd looked at certain brothers who were conversing in the church,
and he removed them from the church for seven days, and commanded them always to bow the knee to those coming in and going out. And this was the wonderful thing:
that both were priests. I saw one brother standing at prayer with a more fervent heart than all,
and especially at the beginning of prayer, as if he were conversing with certain people. I asked him about his thought, and for the sake of benefit he concealed nothing, but said to me:
"Father John, I have the custom of gathering my thoughts and mind together with my soul at the very beginning of the chanting, and I cry out to them, and call them, and say:"
I saw their cellarer, for small tablets were hanging from his belt. I inquired and learned that he wrote his thoughts on them, and he holds them out before that shepherd,
And not only did he do this thing, but many others who were there did so as well, for this was the elder's command. Once that shepherd expelled one of the brothers,
because he had spoken ill of a brother to him, saying that he was a chatterer and a great talker,
And that brother stood outside the monastery for seven days, begging that he might forgive him

and bring him back into the monastery. But when that soul-loving superior was told that he had eaten nothing at all during those seven days, he sent to him and said: "If you wish to be in the monastery,

I will place you in the rank of the penitents." And when he saw that he accepted this with joy, he ordered that he be taken to the separate monastery where those who mourned for their sins were. Since I have mentioned that monastery, I wish to say a little about it as well. There was a place
about one mile away from the great monastery, which was called the Prison. That place is without comfort,
no smoke is ever seen in it at all, nor wine, nor oil, nor anything else, except bread and uncooked herbs. And into that monastery he would confine
those who, after coming to be monks, fell into sin, each one by himself, or two by two, until God should give assurance concerning each one;
and he had set over them a great man named Isaac,
and those who have been handed over to it hasten to prayer continually [?],

and they had palm fronds, which he gives them so that they may work at them to drive away despondency. This is the work, life and conduct of those who truly [?] Whoever marvels at the struggles of the saints does well, and whoever emulates their deeds saves himself. But whoever wishes to accomplish all their deeds at once is mistaken, for he will not be able to. When we are stung [?] by words of reproach,
let us call our sins to mind, so that the Lord may look upon our affliction, which we take upon ourselves for his name's sake, and may blot out the handwriting of our offenses,
and turn those pains that burn our hearts into joy, for it is written that
[?] in its own time. Do not forget those things which he said to the Lord, that after my fall, [?] Blessed is that monk
who endures trials and sufferings all his days for the Lord's sake,
