for he will rejoice with the martyrs and delight with the angels. Blessed is that monk who holds himself worthy of every insult and contempt, continually, as long as he is in this world. Blessed is he who has completely put his own will to death,
and has given himself entirely into the hands of his teacher, for he will stand at the right hand of the Crucified One. Everyone who removes and casts away from himself the reproof of his teacher,
whether just or unjust — such a one has renounced his own salvation; but he who endures reproof, with pain or without pain,
will soon attain the forgiveness of his sins. Show the Lord in your mind that faith and love,

which you have toward your teacher, and He Himself will invisibly make him full-hearted, so that according to your faith and love he may hold you dear and love you. He who exposes by confession every serpent, which are the passions, has acquired fitting faith; but he who hides it in pathless places

has gone astray and kills himself. He who wishes to know the measure of his brotherly love, let him understand well: he will know it when he sees his heart truly mourning over the error of his brother, and joyful over his progress and his good. Let everyone who wishes to establish his own word, even if he speaks the truth, know that he is afflicted and sick from the enemy with a diabolical disease;

and if someone does this toward his equals, perhaps he may be healed by the rebuke of the elders. But if he behaves this way toward elders and spiritual men, such a person cannot be healed by men. Whoever is not obedient in words, it is evident that
he is not obedient in deeds either,
for he who is unfaithful in little is unfaithful in much as well, and he labors in vain and receives nothing from his obedience
except punishment. He who has made his conscience pure in obedience to a spiritual father,
let it be known that he looks upon death as sleep, and rather as life, and that he has set his feet on the way to the kingdom;

and let it be truly known that such a one will not be given over to judgment, but his teacher will give account for him. Everyone who without compulsion receives a task from his teacher, and some harm befalls him in it, let him not blame the one who gave him the weapon, but himself, who used it badly;
for the teacher gave him the weapon to fight the enemy, but he struck his own heart with it;
but if he was compelled, and forced himself for the Lord's sake, and forced his own weakness, and told his teacher beforehand,
let him be confident, for even if he falls, he will not die. I forgot, O beloved, to set this bread of virtue before you as well.

For I have seen obedient monks who inwardly crushed themselves with insults and contempt, so that they would be prepared not to be troubled when insults and contempt came upon them from outside. Everyone who has firmly established that confession is due from him should let this thought be a bridle against every sin;
for whoever does not keep the thought of confession in mind sins fearlessly, as if in darkness. When we are away from our teacher,

And let us picture his face before us, and remember him as though he were with us. Let us keep away from every word and thought, and from food or sleep, which we know he does not want. Then we have come to know obedience without guile. The crafty disciple rejoices when his teacher is away,
but he who is a true son finds it hard

to be away from his teacher. I once asked one of the experienced men and said to him: How have you acquired humility in obedience, abiding in it constantly? And he answered me and said: Even if the true obedient man raises the dead, or acquires tears,
or is freed from battles, he thinks in this way: that it was by the prayer of his teacher that this grace was given to him;
and so he remains a stranger to vain arrogance, for how could he grow arrogant over what he says was not done by him,

but by the help of another. Does the one living in solitude not know these things said above? For they have many occasions for persuading him to arrogance, that it is by his own diligence that he does whatever he does. Whoever has overcome these two evils will remain from then on a servant of Christ, obedient forever. The devil strives greatly to fight those living in obedience, and at times he defiles them with fantasies and makes them hard-hearted,

and he stirs them up to unaccustomed disturbances, dries up their tears and makes them fruitless. He makes them gluttonous, negligent in prayer, drowsy and darkened, so that they may say: "No benefit has come to us from obedience; rather, we have truly turned back."

And in this way he would snatch them away from that struggle, and he does not allow them to understand that the frequent taking away from us of the things that seem good to us becomes, by God's providence for us, what wins humility for us. This devil has often been driven away by the patience of some, and then, while he is still saying this, another herald of wickedness arrives,

and strives to tempt in another manner. I have seen some in obedience who, by the prayer of their teacher, had become compunctious, kind, given to fasting, gentle and diligent, free from battles, and fervent; the demons came to them and told them, "You are now able to live in solitude, where you may struggle and attain dispassion through solitude."
And when they were deceived, they went out from the harbor and entered the heart of the sea,
fierce waves and violent winds rose against them, and they found no teacher to be their pilot, and they perished

in this bitter and foul sea, miserably. Let us examine and see in the sea, after a firm calm, the stirring and great rising of the waves. It cannot be for the sea, unless it were tossed and churned and agitated,
that it should cast out of itself all the wood and hay and all the foulness [?] and dung that enter it through the rivers, which are the passions,

and after that tossing you may see in it a great calm and firm stillness. A disciple who at one time obeys his father and at another does not is like a man who at one time anoints his eyes with eye-salve and at another with lime, as it is written. Do not deceive yourself, O son of obedience, with the spirit of pride,
so that, when you confess your sins to your teacher, you should lay the blame for your deeds on someone else;
for it is impossible to escape from shame without shame. Reveal your wounds to the physician; tell him openly, and do not be ashamed: "This sickness has come upon me through myself, father;

This wound of mine comes from my own negligence and has not befallen me from anyone else. No one else has become the cause of this evil of mine: not a person, not the flesh, nor anything else apart from my own negligence and slackness.

At the time of your confession, become in your appearance, your face and your mind like one who has sinned and been condemned. Stand before the judge with your head bowed toward the ground, and if it is possible, the judge's
…and you would drench the feet of the physician with tears, as though they were Christ's,
for this is the custom of the demons: to lead us either to make no confession at all, or to shift our sins onto others, or to blame certain people for our faults,

as though they had been the cause of them for us. If every deed follows habit, it is evident that the good follows habit all the more, for it has great help from God. If at the beginning of your monastic life you give yourself fervently to enduring insults and contempt,
it will not be long, my son, before your labor settles you in that blessed rest,
and in the end it will be settled among the martyrs through your obedience. Confess your sins to your spiritual teacher as to God, with an attitude of humility.
For I have seen condemned men who, by a pitiable appearance and by confession and supplication, bent the severity of the judge to mercy and changed his anger into sweetness;
and for this reason John the Baptist required confession, before his baptism, from those who came to him,

not that he had any need of it, but because he sought their salvation. Do not be surprised if even after confession the battles of the passions are waged against us, for the battle with the demon of fornication is easier than that with evil pride. Do not go astray, and do not be carried away by the stories of solitaries and spiritual teachers, for you, beloved,
are walking the path of Stephen, the first martyr, through your obedience. Do not flee from obedience, even if a fall should happen to you,

for at that very time you need the physician. As for one who had a helper and stumbled, it is evident that such a person, if he had not had a helper, would not merely have stumbled but would even have died. When a fall happens to you,
Then the demons come, as though they had found a pretext, and urge us toward solitude. But their inner purpose is this: to add a wound on top of our fall. When our physician says,

"I cannot heal you," then, because of that affliction, we must look for another physician, for without a physician few are healed. Is there anyone who will contradict what we say on this firmly and decisively?
that every ship which has a pilot and has fallen among the waves, if it had not had a pilot, without doubt

would have perished altogether? From obedience comes freedom from the passions, as has been said, that [?]; and since this is so, nothing prevents us from saying that from obedience comes freedom from the passions, through which comes about
the completion of humility; for obedience is the beginning of humility,
Just as Moses was the beginning of the law, yet the daughter brings her mother to perfection, as Mary [?]. The sick who went to a physician are worthy of great torment from the Lord

if they tested him and found great benefit from him for their illnesses, and then, while they were not yet fully healed, left him and looked for another physician. Beloved, do not flee from the hands of those who offered you to the Lord. For you will not feel such reverent shame before anyone else as you feel before him all the days of your life. It is not fitting for someone inexperienced to separate himself from the many,
and to enter alone into battle against the adversaries. So too it is improper, before being tested and well shepherded, for the passions of the soul to enter into solitary stillness;
for the former will die bodily, and the latter spiritually. Scripture says that, that is to say, that [?]
so that the son may be a fellow-fighter with the father against the adversaries, by the power of the Holy Spirit. A child who flees from his guide;

and a flock from the shepherd; and one gone astray from the teacher; and a child from his father; and a sick person from the physician; and a ship from the master of the sailors: destruction will come upon all of these,
and whoever engages the demons in combat without a helper will be killed by them. Those who go to a place of healing to be cured should have the relief of their pains as a sign

of healing; but those who enter into obedience should have humility as a sign of the release of their passions. For in those sick in body the relief of pains, but in those sick in spirit the increase of humility, is the sign of health. Let your conscience be the mirror of your obedience,
and this is enough. Those who obey a spiritual father in solitary stillness are fought by demons alone;
but those who are in a community are attacked in battle by both demons and men.
The former, because they constantly see their teacher, keep his commandments all the more strictly;
but the latter, at times when their teacher is apart from them, neglect his commandments a little.
But if they are zealous and patient, they make up what was lacking in their obedience by patiently enduring afflictions, and they receive a twofold crown. Let us guard ourselves with all vigilance,
for a harbor full of ships can easily wreck those ships, and especially through anger and boldness,

as when a worm secretly eats through their timbers and bores holes in them. Let us acquire complete silence and ignorance before our teacher, for a silent man is a son of wisdom and has found great knowledge. I have seen some in obedience who snatched the word from the mouth of their teacher, and I despaired of their obedience, for I saw that they had gained pride from their obedience, and not humility. Let us take heed with all caution, and be careful with all reverence, and with all
understanding let us discern when it is proper to give greater honor to work than to prayer, we who are in obedience,
for this is not fitting for us to do at every time. Take care of yourself when you are with the brothers, and do not hasten to show that you do some work beyond what they do;
for if you do this, you commit two evils. First, you harm them by your showiness and wound their hearts;

and second, you will certainly lead yourself captive to pride. Do not make yourself a show before others, either in appearance or in word. Do this only when you have ceased from judging and despising your neighbour. But if you are quick to judge,
be like your brothers,
then do not become like them [?] through pride. I saw an inexperienced disciple who was boasting before people about the goodness of his teacher. He thought that he would receive praise for this,

but he gained contempt instead, for everyone said to him: "How has a good tree brought forth a fruitless branch?" For it is not when we endure shame and contempt from our father that we are called patient, but when we endure them from all people,
for we feel shame before our father, and patience is also an obligation upon us. Thirst eagerly for reproach,
as for living water, from every person who wishes to give you to drink that medicine which cleanses from defilements,
and then the depth of purity will shine forth in your soul,
and the light of God will not be lacking from your heart. Let no one boast of himself when he sees a multitude of the brethren at rest,
and in his service. For thieves surround us from outside and hasten to destroy our labours and our zeal. Remember constantly,

who said: "But the judgment of our labors will be made known to us at the time of our departure from the world." A monastery is heaven on earth. So let us make our hearts like the angels who serve the Lord. Sometimes the hearts of those who live in this heaven become like stones,

and at other times they are comforted again by compunction, so that they may escape pride and their labors may be consoled by tears. A small fire softens wax, and a small insult often softens in an instant all the harshness and hardness of the heart, wiping it away and making it sweet. I once saw two men
who were hiding in a concealed place, listening to the groans and labors of those who were struggling. But one of them did this
so that he might imitate them, and the other so that, when he found the chance, he might reproach him and expose him before

him, and make that laborer of God stumble from that good work. Do not become silent like a dumb beast where silence is not fitting, and bring [?] turmoil and embitterment upon others; and do not be slow in manner and gait when they order you to hurry. Otherwise, you have become worse than the rabid and the senseless. I have seen such people,

as Job says, souls filled with pain and their own slackness, and many times they even claimed these willingly, and I marveled at how many-devised and many-colored wickedness is. One who is in the assembly

cannot gain as much from the psalmody as he gains from his own prayer, which he performs in his cell, for prayer involves more labor than psalmody. Strive unceasingly to gather your scattered mind back to yourself, and do not despair even if the mind is greatly carried away,

He who does not seek from those under obedience prayer with an undistracted mind. Do not be sorrowful when your mind is carried away, but rejoice when you bring it back to yourself, for complete freedom from captivity belongs to the angels alone. He who has resolved in himself not to depart from the place of his struggle
until his last day, even if a thousand deaths of soul and body should befall him,
nothing of this kind will easily befall him. For falls and stumblings always come from faithlessness of heart and from lack of trust in the place.
Those who are eager to move from place to place are untested in everything, for nothing produces fruitlessness as much
as impatience does. If you go to an unfamiliar place of healing,

be like a traveler and secretly test every matter there. And when you perceive, from both the practitioners and the attendants, benefit for your diseases and for those wounds of the soul, then present yourself, and sell yourself for the gold of humility,
and with the charter of obedience and the writings of service,

and with angels as witnesses. Tear up, tear up utterly at that moment the written bond of your will, which reverses and cancels the price by which Christ the Lord bought [?] you. Let the place where you settle be your grave before burial,

for no one comes out of the grave before the resurrection of all; and if some have come out, see, they have died. For this reason let us entreat the Lord that this may not come upon us. When the tasks of service are heavy,
then the negligent choose prayer, and when the services are light, then they flee from prayer
as from fire. There is one who is doing some task and, at the request and for the rest of another brother, gives it up to him;

and another gives it up out of his sloth; and another does not give it up out of his pride; and another does not give it up out of his diligence and zeal. If you come to some place and, without close examination, are carried away and enter there and make

the promise [?], and then you see in it deeds that are destructive and incurable for the soul, do not be slow to leave it. But the one who has been tested is tested in everything, just as the untested one is untested in everything. Slander and talkativeness have caused many separations in the world, but in a community of brothers gluttony causes many falls and insults. If you master your belly,
you will find freedom from passion in every place where you dwell;

but as long as it lords over you, wherever you go, except the grave, you will find affliction from everyone. The Lord enlightens the eyes of those living in obedience to see the virtues of their teacher; likewise the devil darkens the eyes of the disobedient to see the deficiency of their teacher, for such seeing is truly blindness. A good image of humility and obedience is,
O brothers, quicksilver, which rolls beneath everything
and remains untouched by any stain. Let the zealous guard themselves, so that they do not judge the negligent
and be condemned more than they. For, as I think, this is why Lot was made righteous: because he dwelt among such men

and it is nowhere shown that he judged them. At all times, and especially at the time of prayer, let us acquire silence and stillness, for the demons hurry to corrupt prayer by causing disturbance. Whoever carries out the services of obedience
stands before men in the body; but
in the mind, through prayer,
knocks at the doors of heaven. Abuse and reproach and things like them become, in the soul of the obedient, like the bitterness of wormwood;
but praises and honors are sweet like honey in the soul of the lover of pleasure;
Now then, let us consider the nature of these two: how wormwood purges bile and [?] from the body, whereas honey increases and multiplies bile. We ought to entrust ourselves without anxiety to those
who have taken on the care of us for God's sake, and to trust them even if we think that they are saying something harmful to our soul,
for it is then that our faith in them is tested,

as in a furnace of humility. This is the sign of true faith: when we see from our teacher things that we neither hoped for nor expected, and even in this we obey him without stumbling. From obedience comes humility, as I said before,

and from humility comes discernment, as the great Cassian said in the chapter on discernment; and from discernment comes knowledge of hidden things, and from knowledge of hidden things comes foreknowledge of things to come.
And who would not run such a good course, the course of obedience,
before which lie such great multitudes of good things? For this reason that great singer said

that "Your coming into his heart." Do not forget, all the days of your life, that great ascetic who for eighteen years did not hear from his teacher with his bodily hearing "[?]", but with his inner ears he always

heard from the Lord, not "[?]", for that is a word of prayer and uncertain, but he heard thus: "[?]", which is settled and firm. Some who were living under obedience deceived themselves, for they noticed their teacher's gentleness and sought from him things
that accorded with their own will; and the teacher gave way to their will and did not hold them back from what they asked for.

They imagined that they were doing it at the teacher's word, but let such people be assured that they have completely fallen from the crown of obedience, for obedience is estrangement from double-mindedness and from the fulfilling of one's own wishes. There is a man who receives an order from his teacher, but perceives his will, that he is not content with that thing being done, and he does not do it;

and there is another who knows that the teacher is not content with it, yet obeys without doubting and carries out his word. It is to be asked which of these acted better. It is impossible that the devil should oppose his own will; and understand this from those who live in negligence
and stay unmoved in one place, whether a place of stillness or a community. Let the temptation to leave our places be a sign to us of our progress in them,
for if the enemy did not see that we are fighting him, why would he fight us? It is not right for me to conceal and pass over in silence
that about which silence does not befit us: for John the Sabaite, who was a man from Greece, God-fearing,
holy and pure, related to us things that deserve to be heard.
But you, O holy one, know yourself that this man was raised above all the diseases of the passions, and above lying words, and above every unseemly deed.
He told me that in his monastery in Asia, for that holy man was from Asia, there was a certain elder, very negligent. I do not judge him, but say this in order to tell you the truth.
And there was with that elder a certain young disciple named Acacius, simple in nature and wise in mind, who endured so many evils upon himself from that evil elder,
many of which are astonishing even to hear, for not only with abuse and contempt, but with beating and blows he tormented him every day.
And I saw him every day in great beating and affliction, like a purchased slave, and whenever I met him, I said to him: Brother Acacius!
How did you get through this day? And sometimes he would show me his eye, swollen, and sometimes his neck, split open, or his head, [?];
But I knew that he was a good laborer of virtue, and I said: Beloved, be patient and long-suffering, for it will be to your profit. And he remained with that elder,
who had no mercy, for nine years, and after this that brother Acacius died and went to the Lord, and they buried him in the burial place of the fathers.
And after five days the teacher of Acacius went to a certain great elder who was in the same place, and said to him: Father, brother Acacius has died.
And when that elder heard this, he said to him: Believe me, elder, I do not believe that he has died. The teacher of Acacius said to him: Come and see.
And that elder arose and went with him, and when the two of them arrived at his grave,
that holy elder called out to him as to a living person, to him who truly was alive even after death, and said to him: Brother Acacius, have you died?
And that obedient disciple showed his obedience even after death. He called out to the elder and said: How is it possible, father, for an obedient man to die?
And when the teacher of Acacius heard this, he fell on his face with great weeping,

and he begged the abbot of the monastery to build a cell near that burial place, and there from then on he finished his days in holiness and always in humility, and he would say to the fathers: I have committed murder.
But I think, Father John, that this great John was himself the one who called to the dead man, and the dead man answered him;
for he also told me another story and attributed it to someone else, but he himself was the doer of that deed, as I truly learned later. And he said:
In Asia a disciple of a certain monk who was very gentle and kind and quiet,

and when that disciple saw himself being honored and being slighted [?] by that elder, he conceived a good plan, which is a stumbling block for many, and he implored the elder and asked for his release,
for there was also another disciple, and for this reason the matter was not very distressing, and so he went away from there and took

a letter from his teacher, and went to a monastery in the land of Pontus. And on the very first night that he entered the monastery, he saw himself in a vision of the night being called to account by certain men,
and after that terrible reckoning, he saw himself, that there remained upon him a debt of one hundred litrai of gold,
and when he awoke from sleep, he pondered that vision and said to himself: O wretched Antiochus, for that, he said, was his name, truly very much of our debt still remains upon us.

And so he spent three years in that monastery in great obedience, for all the brothers treated him with great contempt and oppressed him as a stranger; and there was no stranger in that monastery except him.

And again he saw in a vision of the night that a certain man gave him a written record of the remission of ten pounds of his debt. And when he woke up, he understood what he had seen, and he said to himself: Until now I have paid off only ten pounds; when, then, shall I ever pay off the rest that remains?
And he would say to himself: O wretched Antiochus, we need labor and greater reproach. And from then on he feigned foolishness and did not cease from serving.

And when those fathers, who had no mercy, saw him in such obedience, they all ordered him to do every task of the monastery, and he did it in silence. And when he had continued in this manner for thirteen years,
he saw the same men [?] who had been demanding an account from him in the first vision, and behold, they came to him again and wrote him a document of release
from all that debt. And he used to say this: However many times those living in that monastery afflicted me, I remembered that debt which I owed, and I endured with courage.
All this the all-wise John told me, Father John, as though about someone else; for this reason he called himself Antiochus, but it was he himself
who tore up that written record by courageous endurance. Let us hear further what discernment he acquired through his obedience.
For when he was living in the lavra of Saint Sabas, three young monks came to him, wishing to become his disciples.
And he received them with joy and gave them rest from the labor of their journey, and after three days the elder said to them:

"I tell you truly, brothers, I am a weak man. I am overcome by fornication, and I cannot receive even one of you." But they were not scandalized at all, because they knew what the elder's way of life was. When they had begged him earnestly and the elder still did not receive them, they fell at his feet
and begged him to teach them how they should live, or where it would be fitting for them to settle;

And the elder perceived that they would accept his word with faith and obedience. Then he said to one of them: The Lord wills, my son, that you settle in one place, in stillness and in obedience, with one father.

And he said to the second: Go, brother, and sell your will and give it to God, and take up your cross and endure in the midst of a community of brothers, and you will have a great treasure laid up in heaven.
He said also to the third: Acquire, so that it is inseparable from you,

like your breath, that word of which the Lord says that whoever endures will be fully saved. And go and seek, and if it is possible, do not leave anyone among the race of men harsher and more [?] than your teacher, and remain with him, and drink shame and insult every day like honey and milk.
But that brother said to the great John: And if that man is negligent, Father, what should I do? The elder said to him:
even if you see him in fornication, do not leave him,

but say to yourself, "Friend, why have you come?" Then you will see pride gone from you and hardness of heart made to vanish. Let us who desire this, the fear of the Lord, strive with all our strength, so that in that place meant for gaining virtues we may not instead acquire wickedness and evil, craftiness and guile, and anger. For this does happen, and it is no wonder;
for as long as a man is a laborer working the land, or a sailor, the king's enemies count him as nothing, nor do they arm themselves against him;
but when they see that he has received the seal and has taken up sword and shield and spear,
then they come against him gnashing their teeth, and they want to kill him. Therefore we ought to be careful and wakeful and not fall asleep. I have seen innocent and good children who went to school
so that they might learn wisdom and learning and gain profit from it,
but they acquired nothing there except craftiness, wickedness and [?] through mixing with others. Whoever has a mind, let him understand. For those who learn a craft it is impossible
not to advance in it day by day; and some perceive that advance, while others, by providence, are unaware of it. A merchant reckons up that day's gain
or loss, but he cannot know this unless he writes it down at all times, and in this way learns the profit of his trading;

so too, then, we ought to do, for daily examination of oneself enlightens the mind. When a foolish person is put to shame or reproached and burns with it, then he either begins to answer back or quickly bends his knees, not out of humility,
but rather so that he might calm that shame. If you are struck by your teacher, keep silent and accept those medicines of the soul,

and still more of the luminaries of holiness. When the physician has calmed down, then fall down before him, lest in a time of anger he not accept your prostration in repentance. Those who are in a community should stand against every passion,

but above all gluttony and anger, for these passions find their material among people. In those who live under obedience the devil plants a desire for virtues that they are unable to accomplish, and likewise to those living in solitude they suggest deeds that are unfitting for them to do.
Lay open the minds of untested disciples, and you will find among them errant thoughts:

a desire for solitude and severe fasting and for prayer with an undistracted mind, a hatred of vainglory, and a desire for unforgetting remembrance of death, and for constant weeping, and for freedom from anger,
for complete and great silence and for complete purity,

which by providence are not given at the very beginning; and for this reason they have gone astray, and some have left obedience to no purpose, for the enemy deceived them into being persuaded to seek all this before the proper time,
and the enemy did this for this reason: so that they might not persevere,

and in due time they will receive all this. The deceiver persuades those who are in stillness to call blessed those who are under obedience, for their hospitality, their service and love of the brethren, and their service of the sick, so that the deceiver may cast these too into impatience, like those former ones, and so that they may not complete their struggle and their endurance. Few are truly found
who live, as is fitting, in stillness; and they alone have acquired divine consolation to lighten their labours and to help them in their battles. According to the natures and forms of our passions,

let us also acquire obedience. If you are overcome by the heat of the flesh, let your teacher be an ascetic who gives little consolation through food, and not a wonder-worker who welcomes many to his tables;
but if you are overcome by arrogance and stiff-neckedness, let your teacher also be harsh and unyielding, and not gentle and sweet.

let us not seek those who know hidden things or prophets, but above all those who are humble and suited to healing our disease, both by their place and by their way of life. If you acquire the mindset of that blessed Cyrus mentioned earlier, that too is good: always remember that your superior is testing you, and never grow weary or become fainthearted. When your teacher multiplies rebuke and insult toward you,
and your faith and love toward him increase, then know, beloved, that the Holy Spirit has invisibly taken up dwelling in your soul and the power of the Most High overshadows you.
But do not boast and do not rejoice when you bravely endure insults; rather, mourn, for you have done something worthy of reproach and have distressed the soul of your teacher.
Do not be astonished at what I say, for Moses the prophet testifies for me that it is better for someone to sin against God than against the teacher;
for if we anger God, our teacher is able to reconcile God by asking on our behalf;

but if we anger our elder, there is no one who would entreat for us. Yet I say that these two are one and the same, the anger of God and the anger of the teacher. Let us take care, examine, and understand, when we are accused before the father, when it befits us to endure with thanksgiving and silence, and when we ought to set his heart at rest,
for I think that in every matter in which contempt falls upon us, silence is proper, for that is then a time of profit;
but in a matter in which a charge is made against another brother, let us set his heart at rest, for the sake of wondrous love and peace. As many as have left obedience,

they will tell you its benefit, for when they had been separated from him, only then did they realize in what [state] they had stood before. Everyone who seeks dispassion and God, every day on which he is not reviled and insulted,
has counted it as a loss. Just as trees shaken by the winds strengthen their roots all the more;

so too those who live in obedience acquire strong and unshaken souls. Whoever is in stillness and recognizes his own weakness, and comes and sells himself through obedience, is like the one who was blind and without labor received his sight toward Christ. Beloved!
Stand firm, and again I say, stand in your race, brothers, you who are in the struggle, and hear what is said about you
by the all-wise one, that what is a monastery [?], for his is the glory and the might forever and ever. Amen.
This step is equal to the number of the Evangelists. O striver, you who stand upon it, run fearlessly toward heaven. John once outran Peter in going to the tomb.
And likewise here obedience is placed before repentance, for he who outran [the other] to the tomb is a figure of obedience,
and the second is a figure of repentance, he who repented of his denial with tears.
Discourse on repentance itself, and also the life of the holy ones who were confined in that Prison. Chapter 5 [?].

Repentance is the renewal of baptism; repentance is a covenant with God for a new life. The penitent is a merchant who buys humility. Repentance is the complete cutting off of bodily consolations. Repentance is the chastiser of oneself: thought, and freedom from care about everything, and care for one's own soul. Repentance is the daughter of hope and the renunciation of despair. Repentance is the unashamed punishment of oneself. Repentance is reconciliation with God,
in a measure answering to one's sins, through the doing of righteousness. Repentance is the purification of the conscience,
which God created within man as an accuser of evil. Repentance is the door of consolation,
so that one may renounce one's own will,
and one's own wickedness. Repentance is the voluntary endurance of all afflictions and trials. The penitent is one who devises torments for himself
on account of his sins in this world. Repentance is the strong subjugation of one's belly,
and the constant accusing and shaming of one's soul, with firm fervor of heart. Repentance brings one near to God,
and removes one from sins. Gather and draw near,
come and listen, and I will tell all of you with whom God is angry; gather and see how much God has shown me, for the profit of your souls and of mine.
Let us set down here before all else, and honor with reverence, the work of the despised laborers.
Let us hear and keep and do it, you to whom some unexpected fall has happened; rise up and sit, you who lie prostrate from your falls;
hear my words, my brothers, and incline your ear, you who wish

to reconcile God to yourselves by true conversion. I, this weak one, heard of a certain strange way of life and the deeds of those who lived in that separate monastery called the Prison, which lay below that previously mentioned luminary of luminaries, whom we mentioned in the chapter on obedience; and while I was still there,
I begged that great superior that I might go there, and that blessed man, who never wished to grieve a soul, gave me leave. And when I reached that monastery of penitents
and the place of those true mourners, I saw there deeds

of which I will dare to say that the eye of a negligent person has not seen them, the ears of a dissolute person have not heard them, and they have not entered the heart of a slothful and passion-loving person.
Deeds and words which were able
to compel the goodness of God, and means and ways capable of quickly bending his love for mankind. For some of those who had been condemned, though innocent,
from evening until daybreak stand in the open air, placed there with their feet [?] unmoving,
and they were broken by sleep and swayed pitiably under the compulsion of this nature; and they did not allow themselves a single rest,

but they were angry with themselves and reproached themselves with shame and insult. Others gazed up toward heaven with longing and supplication, and asked for help from there with weeping and lamentation;
and again others stood like condemned men, with their hands bound behind their backs like robbers, and their faces bowed to the ground,
and they considered themselves unworthy to look up to heaven,

and from the abundance of the grief of their hearts they did not know what to pray, or what to say to God, or from where to begin making supplication, but they only presented their souls and minds wordlessly before God, and they had despaired of everything, and had hope in God alone.

Others sat on ashes and [sackcloth?], with their faces covered by their knees and their heads bowed to the ground. Others again ceaselessly beat their breasts and lamented their life with great weeping.
And some had soaked the floors of their cells with tears.

And some had no tears, and they struck themselves and mourned over their souls as over the dead, for they could no longer endure that anguish of their heart. And some gnashed their teeth from the pain
of the heart, and did not allow the sound of their lamentation to be heard, yet many times they could not endure it and suddenly cried out in lamentation.
I saw men there who were as though stupefied and [?] in appearance and in dejection, and as though out of their minds, from the great anguish of their hearts,

and their minds were sunk in the abyss of humility, and by that fire of the pain of their heart the tears of their eyes had been scorched, and their eyes were burned by bitter tears. Others sat sorrowfully and looked at the ground,
and ceaselessly shook their heads, and like lions they gnashed from the depths of their hearts and sighed,
and some of them asked God for forgiveness with great hope;

and others said with great humility: We are not worthy of the forgiveness of sins, and we have no word with which to answer God. Others asked of God that they might be tormented here and find mercy there in the age to come. And some, crushed by the weight of conscience, pleaded: Even if we are not worthy of the kingdom, only do not torment us, and that is enough for us.
I saw there humble and crushed souls, their heads bowed under the weight of their burdens, and they were able to soften even stones by those sounds and words
which they cried out to God, for, bowed down, they said thus: We know that we justly deserve every torment, and we are not able to give an account for that debt of ours;
Not even if we were to gather all creatures to ourselves for mourning [would it be enough]; but we take refuge in you, and by your great mercy we grow bold and beseech you, we, we,
that you not punish us according to the worth of our deeds, but with mercy. And it is [enough? the text has "a voice"] for us when from your great wrath,
and from the unspeakable and hidden torments, we escape, for we do not dare to ask for complete forgiveness.
And how could we dare, we who did not keep this vow of ours undefiled, but defiled it after that first loving-kindness of yours, the forgiveness granted before?
There the words of David could be seen plainly fulfilled, O beloved, for I saw there men bowed down throughout their lives and afflicted, and they were [uncared for?] by men.
And through the multitude of their griefs, [on the earth?] nothing else was heard from them except these words: "Woe is me, woe is me! What has befallen me, wretched as I am?"
"Justly, justly! Relieve me, relieve me, O Lord! Show mercy, O merciful one, and grant forgiveness, O Savior of all!" Brothers, I saw there [parched?] tongues,
which hung out of their mouths like those of beasts. Some tormented themselves in the heat; some by frost
were afflicted. And some would taste a little water, only so as not to die of thirst; and they would take some small amount of bread,

they immediately left it and said, 'We are not worthy of human food, we who have done the deeds of beasts.' Who could have seen among them laughter or self-indulgence, or an idle word, or irritation, or wrath? For they had completely forgotten wrath,
who did not even remember that there is such a thing as anger among people, for mourning had completely destroyed the wrath of the heart.

Where could there be found among them answering back, or boldness, or any rest for the body? Where could one have seen there a trace of insolence, or hope of comfort, or the remembrance of wine, or the taste of fruit, or the consolation of anything [?] or boiled,

or the sweetness of [form? the text is uncertain]? For the hope of all this had vanished from them in this present world. Where could there have been among them care for any worldly need, or the judging of a man? Far from it! But these words and cries were among them continually.
Some beat their breasts hard with their hands and, as if they stood at the gates of heaven, said to God:
"Open to us, O good Judge, open, open to us the door of mercy, which we shut by our sin, open!"
And others said, and another said: "To these poor ones [?]," and another said something else, for
"we are perishing and have been given up." And others said, "Brothers, may the Lord henceforth show his light upon us."
And others say, "Brothers, my [?] our debts [?]." And others said, "Beloved brothers, will the Lord henceforth grant forgiveness upon us? Or shall we hear his voice,
saying to us, 'You who are in [?] the indissoluble [?] and who have fallen into hell, because of your repentance I have forgiven you'?"
"Has our voice reached the ears of the Lord?"
And all had death before their eyes, and they said:
"Alas, what will our end be? Alas, what sentence will come upon us, or to what places are we going to go? Will there be forgiveness for us, these wretched, darkened and condemned ones?

Or has our prayer reached the Lord? Or has it rightly been turned back, ashamed and humbled? And if it has reached and come before the Lord, what has it accomplished? How far has it made Him merciful toward us, and how much profit has come of it,
since it did not come forth from pure mouths and bodies, and there is no power in it? Did it make the Judge fully merciful toward us, or only a little, or for half of our wounds,
for these are very great, and worthy of many labors and sweats? Have our guardian angels drawn near, or are they still far from us?
For if they have not drawn near to us, all our labor is vain and useless, for there is no power of boldness
to our prayer, nor the wings of holiness to enter before the Lord,

unless our angels draw near to us, take it, and offer it before the Lord." And again they would often say to one another in amazement: "Alas, brothers, what do you say? Will we attain what we are seeking?
Will our requests be granted us? Will the Lord accept us? Will He open His mercy to us?" And others would answer and say,
"Who knows, as our brothers the Ninevites said, perhaps the Lord will relent and deliver us from those many torments. But let us do our part, as much as we are able.
And if he opens to us in his sweetness, it is good; and if not, blessed is the Lord, who has justly shut us out.
But let us persevere and keep knocking until the end of our life.

And perhaps because of our great importunity he will open to us in his mercy." And again they would say to one another: "Let us run, brothers, let us run, for running is needed for us, and much running, for we have fallen away from that good company of ours. Let us hasten, and let us not spare these evil and defiled bodies of ours,
but let us put them to death, as they have put us to death." And this is what those blessed ones did.
I saw among them, brothers, knees hardened from the great number of prostrations, and their eyes were burnt by tears and sunk deep, and their hair had fallen away,
and their cheeks were scarred and wounded by the abundance of their hot tears, and their faces were wasted and yellowed, and they did not differ in any way from the dead;

and their chests were bruised from beating, and they would cough up fresh blood from beating their breasts again and again. Where among them could a prepared bed be found, or the wearing of good clothes? Instead everything was torn, patched and contemptible, full of [?] and lice, so that compared with their affliction, the affliction of the demon-possessed [?],
or the mourning of those who lament the dead, or the affliction of those who are in exile, or of those who have been arrested for murder?
Truly, the forced torment of all these is nothing compared with their voluntary scourging of themselves; and do not think, brothers, that these words of mine are empty.

Many times they would beseech their superior, that great and true shepherd, the angel among men, that they be fettered hand and foot, that he put a chain on their necks and secure their feet in the stocks, like the demon-possessed,
and that he not release them from these until they went to the grave.
I will not conceal this too: their crushed humility, their love for God, and their repentance.
for they expected to go to the Lord and to stand before His all-seeing throne, those good citizens of that land of repentance. When one of them saw that he was at his end, through their superior

who had been set over them he would send an entreaty to the great father, and adjure him with supplication not to consider him worthy of burial like a human being, but to throw him away like an animal to be eaten by wild beasts, or else to cast him into the rivers, and

Many times that luminary of discernment would listen to them, and would order them to be carried out without psalmody or honor. But hear what a terrible sight their last hour was. For when those holy penitents learned of the approaching end of one of them, while he was still conscious, they would stand around him, thirsting and eager, and with pitiful looks and compassionate words they would sway their heads, burning with pity for the one who was departing, and would question him, saying: What is it, brother and fellow penitent? What do you say, what hope do you have, what do you expect? Have you attained what you sought by your labors, or were you unable? Has the door been opened to you, or are you still guilty? Have you reached the goal toward which you were hastening, or are you still far off?

Have you received full assurance, or is your hope still uncertain? Has freedom been given to you, or is your mind still in doubt? Has any light come into your heart, or is it still darkened? Has that voice reached within you which says: [?]
Or [?] or else [?] or: Behold, you have been healed?
Or do you still hear that voice which says: [?] or else [?] or else [?] What do you say, brother,
or in what state are you? Tell us, we beseech you, so that we too may know what is going to happen,
for your time has now run out, and you will find no other forever. To these words some of those who were departing
among them would say: [?] And another would say: [?] And another would say with anguish: [?]
[?] the spirits of the air, for they were not yet confident, but were waiting to see what would happen at the judgment.

And another said something more bitter than this: "Woe to the soul that did not keep its vow undefiled; at this hour it will learn what has been prepared for it." But when I saw all this among them, I nearly gave up hope for myself, seeing my own disorderliness and their struggle:
for what the very air of that place was like: wholly dark, wholly foul, evil, and oppressive,
so that it was rightly called a dungeon and a prison, and the mere sight of the place was a lesson in all repentance and mourning.
But what seems hard and unbearable to others, those who have fallen from spiritual wealth and long for it regard as sweet and pleasant.

For the soul that has lost its former boldness, has fallen from the hope of dispassion, has corrupted the seal of purity, has become destitute of the wealth of graces, has become estranged from divine consolation,
has despised its own vow, has quenched the fire of its good tears, and is goaded by the remembrance of such things,
that soul will not only eagerly take upon itself all the hardships we mentioned earlier, but will not shrink even from its own death for God's sake.
If there is still a spark of love or fear of God remaining in it, as there was in these holy men we have mentioned, for they kept all this in mind,

they recalled the height from which they had fallen and said: "And the fire of our fervor and zeal, how it has perished and vanished!" And others cried out to God, those who showed zeal to our soul. And another again would say:
[?] of the light of my heart. In this way they recalled those former good things and their own good standing in them,
and over these things, as fathers over dead children, they lamented and said:
"Where is that purity of our prayer? Where is its boldness?
Where are those sweet tears, in place of these bitter ones? Where is that hope of virginity, and that perfect purity? Where is that expectation of blessed dispassion?
Where is that faith which we had toward the shepherd? Where are those graces which were upon us through his prayer?
We have lost all of it, and it has vanished as though it had never been.

And I heard that some of them asked God to send demon-possession upon them to torment their flesh; and some asked for the ruin of their faces, so that they might become a spectacle to all people, if only by some means they might escape those eternal
torments; and some asked that he send deformity upon them.
But as for me, brothers, when I saw what they did and that wondrous mourning, I forgot myself, my mind was carried away, and I could not console my soul.
And I spent thirty days with them in that prison, and then I, impatient as I am, returned to the great monastery, to the great father.
When he saw my changed and wasted complexion, he understood the reason for my change and said to me: "What is it, Father John?

Have you seen the labors of those strugglers?" I answered and said to him: "Yes, father, I have truly seen a terrible sight and been amazed, and I call those who have fallen and repent and mourn for themselves more blessed than those who have not fallen and do not mourn. For those who mourned have risen from their fall with a resurrection that cannot fall." And he said to me: "So it truly is."
And his unlying mouth told me: "Ten years ago there was a brother here,

very hardworking and zealous, and when I saw such fervor of his soul, I was afraid of the envy of the devil, the hater of good, lest in his swift running his foot should strike against a stone, as often happens to those who run swiftly; and so it came to pass.
For one night he came up to me and openly showed me a wound, and asked me for medicine and cauterization to heal it, and he was greatly distressed; and since he was worthy of mercy and forgiveness,
the physician saw it, for he did not wish to burden him with the canon. Then he fell to the ground and embraced my feet, and
washed them with tears, and begged to go to that prison which you have seen; and he cried out, saying that it was impossible for him not to go there,

and he compelled the physician's mercy to change into mercilessness, a thing rarely found among the sick. And so he went away to those penitents, and became their friend and a sharer in their struggle.
And his heart was wounded with sorrow and with the love of God, and on the eighth day he departed to the Lord, and he asked with entreaty not to be buried, but to be cast outside.
But I brought him here and buried him with the fathers, as one worthy; and so, after that week of days of his slavery, on the eighth day he was released and passed over to freedom forever.
And there is a man here to whom it was clearly made known concerning him that he had not yet risen from these contemptible and worthless feet when God forgave him that sin.
And this is not surprising, for when he acquired the faith of that harlot woman,

and like her with full heart soaked these worthless feet of mine with tears, for this reason he too found forgiveness, as the Lord said. I have seen souls defiled and maddened with evil love of the flesh,

and after this they acquired in their hearts the fire of repentance, and since they had been experienced in passionate love, they abandoned that evil and acquired toward God a true passionate love, resembling the former in its ardor. And they at once passed beyond all fear and pressed on to the love of God. For this reason the Lord

did not say of that harlot that she feared greatly, but that she loved much, and she was able easily to drive out love by love: that evil and violent love by divine and holy love. I am not unaware, O beloved brothers, that these struggles which I have told you seem incredible to many, and that others regard them as bringing despair,
But let the brave and prudent man take from these words a goad and a fiery arrow, and good zeal in his heart, in deed and not in word. But he who is unable to do these deeds,
let him recognize his own weakness and humility, if he wishes to gain [salvation] easily, and so let him follow after that first one,
though I do not know whether he will catch up with him. But let the negligent man not touch these sayings.

Otherwise he may, through despair, destroy even what he is doing, and the saying may be fulfilled in [?] him which says: "Know, beloved, that we who have fallen into the pit of sin cannot climb out of it unless we plunge into the abyss of the humility of the penitent." The mourning and sorrowing humility of the penitent is one thing,
who are still in sin and are punished by their conscience.

And another is that blessed and soul-enriching humility which comes from God upon the perfect. Let us not hasten to find this third by word, or else we labor in vain, for to know it by word is impossible; but the sign of the first is perpetual endurance of insult and contempt. The battle of former deeds and habits

It often overpowers even the one who mourns, and this is no wonder. The account of the judgment on those falls is hidden and inaccessible: which of them come from negligence, or which by the permission of providence, or which have befallen through God's turning away.
but someone told me this: that those who have fallen by [God's] providence quickly turn back from it,
for He who gave it to us for our instruction does not allow us to be tormented by the devil for a long time. Those of us who happen to fall,

let us hasten to fight the devil, above all at the time of prayer; for then he comes upon us and reminds us of our former boldness before God, and he wishes to ruin us and turn us away from prayer and supplication to God. Do not become grieved through despair,
even if you fall every day; but stand courageously and prudently in repentance itself, and your endurance will be pleasing to the Angel

who has been appointed as your guardian, and he will surely help you. While a wound is still fresh, it is easy to heal; but old and neglected wounds are hard to heal, and they need much labor and the knife, medicine and cautery, in this present life,

so that the soul itself may not be burned there because of them. Some wounds are not healed by length of time, but with God all things are possible. Before we fall into sin, the demons tell us: "God forgives sins"; and after the fall they tell us that
God is a righteous judge. Do not listen to the one who speaks to you about small errors, saying, 'If only you had not done some great thing; but as for this, it is nothing,'

for often a small gift has quenched the great anger of a judge. He who is in true repentance counts every day on which he does not mourn as if he had lost that day, even if he has done some other good on it. Let none of the penitents wait for the hour of death to repent well and receive forgiveness,

for every matter that is unknown and unseen is not certain. [?] by understanding on your part, hence doubtfully and with fear [?]. Know, brother, that where the Spirit of God is, all the bonds of sins are loosed. He who has complete humility, the bonds of his sins are loosed,
for let those who are far from these two things of which we have spoken not be deceived, for they are not loosed. Never will he judge or blame the fall of another,
the one who mourns for himself. When a wild beast bites a dog,

the dog becomes all the fiercer against it, and the pain of the bite blinds it into madness. Let us beware, brothers, lest perhaps our conscience has ceased from rebuking not because of purity, but because it has grown weary, and for this reason no longer rebukes us. The sign of remission is this, that one should always
a man should count himself as liable [?]. Nothing is equal to the mercies and goodness of God; therefore whoever has despaired
has killed himself by his own will. Everyone who has humility and mourning for his sins—such a one does not become negligent until the day of death;

But those who are outside these two deceive themselves. The sign of true repentance is this: that we reckon ourselves worthy of all afflictions and trials, visible and invisible. Moses, after the vision of God,
in the bush, returned again to Egypt, which is darkness, where the bricks of Pharaoh were being made.

But he went up again to the bush and reached even higher. Whoever understands this saying will never cut off hope. Job too became poor, but he became rich again, twofold. For the negligent, falls after the vow are hard, for they destroy the hope of dispassion.

And for them, merely rising out of that pit is a blessed thing. Let us not turn back again to the same road on which we went astray, but come, let us travel another, short and near. I saw two people at one time,
and on one road of God, walking along; and the one was an old man and foremost in labors,
and the other was the disciple of that elder, that disciple, of humility. Let us all be on our guard, and especially those who have fallen,
so that the disease of the godless Origen may not settle in our hearts; for that foul man puts forward the love of God for mankind,

and it becomes acceptable to lovers of pleasure and the negligent. And all the more in my repentance, of prayer [?], [?] the matter of the passions. Let the boundary, and rule, and pattern of repentance be for you those saints mentioned earlier, who were in the prison; and you will not have much need of a book,
until Christ the Son of God appears to you, at that resurrection of repentance; for his is the glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever.
Amen. Five steps you have climbed, O penitent, for you have purified those five senses through repentance,
and from that compulsory eternal torment, willingly in this very world,
and by the torment of yourself, you have escaped.

Discourse of the same on the remembrance of death. Chapter 6. Thought is the leader of every word, and the remembrance of death and of one's sins is the leader of all weeping and mourning; for this reason we have placed it in our discourse too, according to its proper order. The remembrance of death is
a daily death. 3. The remembrance of death is a perpetual sigh.
Fear of death is a natural thing, which came about through disobedience; but terror of death
it is a sign of unrepented sins. Christ feared death,

but He did not tremble, so that He might show the properties of both natures. As bread is more necessary than all other foods, so the remembrance of death is higher than all thoughts and exercises. Among those who live in the world, the remembrance of death gives birth to labors and struggles and to the acceptance of dishonor; but among those who live in solitude, it gives birth to pain of heart, and its mother [?] is blessed sweetness, from which come the abandonment of cares and unceasing prayer,
and the guarding of the mind; and these things are both its parents and its daughters. As the difference between tin and silver is clearly recognizable, even though the one resembles the other, so

the natural fear of death and the fear that is beyond nature are clearly recognized by those who have understanding. This is the pattern and sign of true remembrance of death: contempt for all the affairs of the world,

and the complete abandonment of one's own will. He who expects death every day is truly proven; but he who longs for death every day is rightly holy and perfect. Not every desire for death is good, for there are those who constantly stumble under the tyranny of habit and who in humility long for death to come, so that they may be delivered from that behavior; and there are others who, without understanding and in their folly, wish for death.
And there are others who do not want repentance and who rush toward death out of despair.
And there are others who out of pride regard themselves as free of passions, and for this reason they have no fear of death.
And there are others, if indeed any such are to be found now, in whom the Holy Spirit has taken up his dwelling, and by his power they long to depart from this world. Some inquire and say:
"Since the remembrance of death is so profitable to us, why has God hidden from us the advance knowledge of that hour?" And they do not know
that he did this wondrously for the sake of our life. For if people knew beforehand of their own death, no one would come to baptism or to the monastic life long before it,
but [otherwise] people would spend all their days in lawlessness, and at the time of death they would come to baptism and repentance. When you mourn,
do not accept that devil,

If someone comes to you and says, "Why do you mourn? God loves mankind, and he will forgive you even without mourning", know that his intention is to take mourning and the fear of God away from you. But if a spirit of despair is overpowering you, then do not avoid this consideration. Whoever wants to acquire the remembrance of death and the remembrance of God, yet gives himself over to bodily cares and distractions,

is like a man who has tied his own hands and wants to swim. The remembrance of death cuts off the pleasures of food, and when such pleasures are cut off with humility, the passions are cut off along with them. Hardness of heart makes the mind callous, and a great quantity of food dries up the springs of tears. Thirst and vigil press the heart, and when the heart is pressed it becomes mournful, and tears begin to flow. These words are harsh and heavy for gluttons and for faithless sluggards, but the man who works at righteousness will test them and find that the practice is good. Whoever finds this by experience, let him rejoice in it; but whoever is still seeking, let him be sorrowful until he finds it. Just as the fathers say of perfect love that it never falls, so I call the perfect remembrance of death fearless. The works of the mind for those who struggle are many: love of God, remembrance of God, remembrance of the Kingdom, remembrance of the zeal of the holy martyrs, remembrance

[?] of the vision of God, as it says, that the remembrance of those holy and invisible powers, the remembrance of death, of the encounter with God, of the torments and of that future judgment: we have begun from the great measures, and have ended with those who do not err and do not fall. An Egyptian brother told me: "After the remembrance of death had been firmly planted in my heart, I once wished to give my flesh a little comfort, for so it was needful; but that remembrance held me back like a bridle and kept me from the act. And this is the marvelous thing: I even wished to be parted from it, and could not." And another brother lived here, in the place called Thola, and many times because of this thought he would be utterly undone, and as if deprived of his senses,

or like one who has fainted, and as if lifeless; and the brothers who happened to be there would lift him up. Nor will I keep silent from telling you about the deed of Hesychius the Chorebite. For at first he lived in negligence and did not care for his soul at all. And while he was thus, a severe illness came upon him and he was caught up, and for one hour his soul truly went out of him. Then he came back to himself again and begged us who were there to go outside. And as soon as we had gone out, he got up immediately, walled up the door of his cell, and sat inside it enclosed for twelve years. And he answered no one a single word at all, neither small nor great, but only received bread and water in silence. And he sat continually, his mind caught up toward the visions which he had seen, and
he was in such mourning and sorrow that he never changed, as the Lord knows, his manner and appearance. But he always stood as one melted away, and hot tears flowed silently.
And when his end came, we opened the door and went in, and begged him earnestly to speak a word to us, and he answered us nothing else
except only this: "Forgive me, fathers, for there is no one who has acquired the remembrance of death who could ever commit sin."
And we marveled when we saw him, who had formerly been such a man, and had in an instant been changed by that blessed change.

And when that holy man had departed, we buried his body in the burial place that is near the monastery. And after a few days we looked into that grave and could no longer find his holy body, for the Lord had translated it to wherever he willed,

so that by this too he might assure all of them that his repentance had been accepted, and so that all who wish to come to repentance, even after negligence, might not be without hope. Just as they say of the abyss of the seas
that it is unfathomable, so too the purity and the practice of the remembrance of death are unfathomable,

and the holy man mentioned earlier will assure you of this. Such people acquire fear upon fear without rest, until even the strength of their bones is worn away. Let us understand that this too is a gift of God, together with all his other gifts,
for if not, how is it that many times we go even to the graves and stand there tearless and hardened; and many times
without seeing anything of the kind we become contrite, and we realize that that hour is a gift of God. Whoever has died to every bodily concern will acquire the remembrance of death.
But such a person, if he is still bound by love of affairs and cares, cannot stand firm in the remembrance of death, because he is his own enemy.
28. Do not wish to satisfy everyone with words out of your love for them; rather, ask of God that he may satisfy them in a way beyond words,

for otherwise your times will not be enough for you both to have fleshly love and to mourn, for these two are hard to find together. 29. Do not deceive yourself, O negligent and foolish laborer, by thinking that today you may be negligent and tomorrow you will accomplish today's work as well.
For a day is not enough even to accomplish what is due on that day itself, as is fitting toward the King. 30. People cannot pass even a single day in righteousness,

except in this way: that each of us says every day, "This day is the end of my times and years, and I am going before the thrones and the terrible [?], and I will meet the Judge of righteousness." 31. It is astonishing how even the pagans were so pleased with this that they said
that wisdom is the remembrance of death,
in which may we believers be found pure by the grace of the Lord,
to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. This is the sixth step.
Whoever reaches it will never sin again, for it is written: "Remember your last day, the day of your death, and you will never sin."
A discourse by the same holy father of ours, John. ON MOURNING, CHAPTER 7. 1. True, godly mourning is sorrow of soul and a grieving heart that always labours anxiously over things that cause pain,
and at all times toward its own beloved,

…they thirst, and when they do not attain it, they seek it with pain of heart, and after that they cry out in lamentation, with groaning and sighing. True mourning is a golden spur that pricks the soul at all times. It is stripped of all love of this world, of bodily consolation, and of all kinsfolk and one's own people, and its only work is what this God-loving sorrow has planted in the heart. Mourning is an unceasing torment of conscience, which through spiritual confession kindles the fire of the heart. Mourning is a forgetting of nature, as that blessed one who sings this forgot to eat his bread. True repentance is this: separation from all bodily consolation without being distressed by it.
True mourning is this: a grieving soul, pained by the fervor of the heart, and thirsting at all times in its search for him,
and when he shines forth upon it, it pursues him with labor, and with hardship and sorrow sighs after him,

And whoever is like this, that is mourning. Mourning is being stripped of everything in this world that one clings to. It is separation and withdrawal from everything, and following that perfect sorrow which brings good things, so that one's heart is like one wounded incurably by an arrow and longing for what it desires. Mourning is a persistent thought that always pricks the heart with compunction to confess sins,

…from the blaze of its fervour. For those who have newly entered into this blessed mourning and are set on making progress, the work is fasting and silence. But for those who have advanced in it, the sign is freedom from anger and not remembering wrongs.

And those who have been perfected in it, their sign is humility and thirst to drink disgrace, and hunger for voluntary hardships and involuntary trials, and desire for affliction, and keeping from judging sinners, and sharing with pain in the suffering of the brothers who are in hardship. The first are acceptable, and the second are praiseworthy;

but blessed and joyful are the third, who of their own will hunger for affliction and thirst for disgrace and reproach, for truly they have been filled with those delights that can never be sated. O you who have kept mourning, guard

…it with all your strength, and hold on to it firmly. For before it is planted in you and before its roots take hold, it quickly leaves you and flees, unless you guard it well. Turmoil and bodily cares, an easy life and pleasure, and above all much talking and self-indulgence make it melt and pass away quickly, as wax melts before fire. After baptism, the fountain of tears is greater than baptism, even though this is a bold saying:
for baptism is the cleanser of the sins we committed before it, but tears forgive the sins we have committed after our baptism.

And the baptism that we received in infancy we have defiled, but by tears we renew it as well; and if this had not been given by God, those who found life would be few. Sighs and mourning cry out to the Lord,
and tears that come from fear of torments intercede for us, while those that come from all-holy love reveal [?]
and make us confident in the offering of our prayers. If nothing assists humility so much as mourning, it is evident

that nothing opposes it so much as laughter. Hold fast, beloved, with all your strength to mourning and to that blessed compunction, and do not cease from it until it raises you above all the affairs of the world and presents you purified to Christ. Do not cease to picture in your mind
and to meditate upon the abyss of that dark fire, and the merciless servants who are there;
and that terrible and dreadful and [?]-eyed judge; and the caves and unreachable pits of the flame of the underworld; and the terrible places of darkness;

and those narrow and evil descents; and recall all such things, so that through great fear and trembling the burning of the flesh may be quenched, and our heart may be united to that incorruptible purity which shines more than fire

and illumines the soul. Stand in your prayer with trembling, like a condemned robber before the judge, so that both by your outward appearance and by your inward thought you may quench the wrath of that righteous judge,

For he does not disregard the mourning soul, which like a widow stands before him in sorrow and wearies him who cannot be wearied. Whoever has acquired spiritual mourning, for him every place is suitable for mourning and sighing,

but if someone practices mourning in an outward manner, then let him not cease to seek out places and manners that are conducive to mourning. As a hidden treasure is better safeguarded than one spread out in the market streets, so understand this manner of mourning mentioned above. Do not be like those
who have buried their dead, and who at one moment wail over them and at another drink and get drunk on their account,
but be like those who are in prison and are tormented every day by torturers. Whoever mourns at one time and at another

laughs and makes merry is like the man who throws loaves at the dog of gluttony: in appearance he drives it away, but in deed he invites it to come to him. Be sorrowful, beloved, and not one who displays it,

…but be sorrowful only within your heart, for demons tremble at sorrow as thieves tremble at dogs. Our calling here is not to a wedding, O beloved; that is in the age to come. Here, he who has called us has called us to mourn for ourselves. Some, when they shed tears and weep,

…force themselves in vain, while they have no thought at all in that blessed time. They do not know that tears shed without thought are the work of an irrational nature, not of a rational one. Weeping is the offspring of good thoughts,
and the father of good thoughts is the rational mind inflamed by the fear of God. Let your lying down on your bed be a representation of lying in the grave, and sleep little;

and let your sitting down at table be a reminder to you of that bitter table of the immortal worms, and manage to eat little and with measure. Whenever you drink your water, do not forget the thirst of the eternal flame,
and without fail compel your nature. At the time of anger and of insult from our teacher,
let us remember the terrible sentence of that Judge, and in this way let us be able to cut down that sorrow and brutish wrath with gentleness and patience, as with a two-edged sword.
With time the sea diminishes, as Job says, and likewise with time and patience these things that have been said take root among us little by little and become perfect,

and they make us perfect. Let the remembrance of that eternal fire lie down and rise up with you always, and may slackness never gain mastery over you at the time of prayer. Let even the form of your clothing lead you to mourning, for you are clothed in black, which is the sign of mourning,
for all who mourn for the dead put on black. If you do not have mourning,

mourn for this very thing, that you do not have mourning; and if you do have mourning, mourn for this, that you have brought yourself down from that toilless, honorable, and joyful state to a labor and a dwelling of affliction and torment because of your sins,
And for this you deserve much mourning and weeping and lamentation. As our Lord judges a just judgment in every matter, so also with regard to tears he takes into account the power of nature;
for I have seen small tears that were shed with pain, like blood, and again I have seen tears that came flowing down like springs, without toil,

but I admired those strugglers according to their toil and pain, and not according to the abundance of their tears, and I think that to God also those are more pleasing who weep a little with toil and pain than those who shed many tears without toil. Theology and discussion of heavenly matters and matters of the law are not profitable for mourners, for [?] all this dissolves their mourning,
for this is like one who sits on thrones;
but he who is in mourning is like those who sit on ashes and sackcloth. And for this reason David, although he was a wise teacher, nevertheless, when he mourned, spoke thus, saying:

…which are the passions that take the soul captive. When the soul becomes full of compunction and weeping by itself, without our effort or labour, and tears flow easily from our eyes, then let us make haste. For our Lord has come without being invited and has given us a sponge for refreshment and the water of life,
…which are the tears for washing away our sins,

which are written in that handwritten record of our deeds. Guard such a time like the pupil of your eye, brother, until it withdraws of itself, for it has far greater power for our benefit than what is gained by our own effort. It is not he who mourns whenever he wishes who has attained the excellence of mourning,

but he who [?] over whatever matter he wishes; rather, he who mourns as God wishes, he has true mourning. Many times that thankless passion of vainglory joins itself to our divine mourning. Let us understand this well at the time when we mourn and the passions still overcome us:
then let us recognize that the passion of vainglory is with us. True mourning is pain of the heart,
such that it does not incline at all toward ease and delight and the pleasures of comforting foods, but at all times looks only upon its own death, and
awaits that consolation of God which consoles humble monks, as a thirsty man awaits cool water.
