Those who acquired true mourning through pain of heart came to hate even this life as something grievous that brings tears and sorrows. But towards their own body,
…they were oppressive, like enemies. When we see anger and arrogance in those who mourn, let us count their tears and mourning as false. For the child of false and deceitful mourning is pride;
but the child of true mourning is consolation from God. As fire burns up a reed and makes it vanish, so pure tears burn up every poison and passion of the soul. The fathers say,
that true tears are hard to obtain, and especially for newcomers, for they arise from many different kinds of sources, such as from nature and from God;
and by trials and from grief, both from what is adverse and from what is good; and from vainglory,

and from fornication and from love and from the remembrance of death, and from many other things. But when we examine all of these, we find those holy and guileless tears that came from the remembrance of death,
for in them there is no error or vainglory, but rather purification and the growth of the love of God, the blotting out of sins and freedom from the passions. When tears begin from what is good and
turn to evil, that is no marvel; but this is a marvel and worthy of praise: when evil tears begin to flow,
or natural ones, and they then turn to good. And this saying is well known to those
who are overcome by pride. Do not trust your tears before complete purity, for wine is not to be trusted when it is only just flowing from the winepress,

but when it has aged and remained uncorrupted. No one disputes this, that all our divine tears are profitable; but what their profit is, we shall understand at the time of death. Whoever is in perpetual mourning in this world according to the will of God, such a one celebrates a spiritual feast every day;
but whoever does not cease from bodily feasts, eternal mourning awaits such a one. There is no joy for robbers in prison, and no festival on earth for true monks.

And is it not for this reason that the one who mourned well said with a sigh, "that he may rejoice in that ineffable light of yours"? Be like a king seated in your heart, exalted by humility, and command with authority:

tell that bitter laughter to depart, and it departs; and tell that sweet weeping to come, and it comes; and tell these slaves, our tyrannical flesh, "Do this," and it does it. Whoever is wrapped in this blessed and joyful mourning, like a bridegroom in a garment,
such a one has acquired that true spiritual joy. Who is such a monk, who has passed the days of his life in his monastic state with the fear of God, true repentance and piety,
and has not lost a single day or a single hour, and not even in the twinkling of an eye has fallen short of his profit,

but he has spent all his hours and days in a godly way, and every day he keeps in mind that the day that passes can never come back. Therefore he hurries so that it will not be spent in vain. Blessed is the monk who has toiled all his days and has spent his hours in humility and the service of God, and has not found rest even for one hour, but reflects and says: “This is the last of the days of my life in this world.” Blessed is the monk who can always see the invisible powers with the eyes of the mind.

But blessed also and truly unfallen are those who with these visible eyes bathe their cheeks every day with that blessed weeping, from the remembrance of death and of their sins. And I think that the first measure mentioned will not be found without this second one. I have seen troublesome beggars who with some nimble word,
And they quickly bent the hearts of the kings to mercy and to compassionate pain for them.
And again I saw those who were poor and had fallen away from the virtues,
who, not with bold words but rather with humble and pitiable words of affliction from the depths of the heart, and

as though their souls were in despair, cried out without shame and in pain to the King of heaven. By this pressure of theirs they compelled that goodness which cannot be compelled, and His sweet nature, to have mercy on them. Whoever takes pride in his own tears and condemns those who do not weep

is like a man who received a sword from the king to kill his enemies, but gave up the fight against the enemies, struck his own heart with that same weapon, and killed himself. Not that God needs it, beloved,
that a person should mourn and weep with pain of heart; rather, he wishes that the person's soul should rejoice in love for him. Beloved, blot out sin from yourself entirely,
and you will no longer need tears, for healing is of no use

where there is no cause of disease. There were no tears in Adam before the transgression of the commandment, just as there will be none in the righteous after the resurrection, when sin has entirely vanished,

for there is no pain or sorrow or sighing there. I saw mourning in some, and in others I saw mourning because they did not have mourning; and they did have mourning, yet thought that they did not have it, and through that good ignorance they remained free of pride,
and these are the ones of whom it is said that often the light-minded grow proud over tears;
and for this reason it is not given to some, who in their seeking of it blame themselves and punish themselves with sighing and grief and sorrow
of soul and pain of heart; and such forms are reckoned to them before the Lord as tears, even though they themselves do not think so,

and they count such forms as nothing. If we examine the matter, we find a laughable thing that the demons do to us: often when we have eaten our fill they make us compunctious, and when we fast they harden our hearts,
so that we may be led astray by those vain and false tears and give ourselves over to ease, which is the mother of all evils.

But it befits us, beloved, not to accept their deceit nor to yield to them, but rather to resist with all our heart and mind. I consider the nature of compunction and am amazed at how it is called mourning and sorrow,

and it is mingled in the soul with joy and gladness, and it is sweet like honey in the comb. And what do we learn from this except that such blessed compunction is truly a gift of God? No sweetness of bitter desire is found in the soul when the Comforter dwells within, in the hearts of those blessed broken ones. Let us hear, brothers, an account that is profitable for the soul and leads to compunction and repentance:
There was here a certain elder named Stephen, who lived the life of a desert solitary and of stillness, and had spent many years in monastic life,
and he was adorned with fasting and tears and was full of many other good deeds. And his cell was on Mount Sinai, the dwelling place of the holy
and of the God-seeing prophet Elijah, on that holy mountain. But his heart prompted him toward a higher and more exalted repentance,
and he went away to the dwelling place of the grazing hermits, to a place called Sidi,

which means affliction, and which is seventy miles distant from the monastery of Sinai, a place where there is no consolation at all, nor any road for people at all. And he lived there in hardship, with tears and severe repentance. After many years, when he had reached great old age, he returned again to his own cell on this holy Mount Sinai,
where he had two Palestinian disciples, very God-fearing men, who kept themselves in purity.
When the elder had spent a few days there, he fell ill with the sickness in which he also reposed.
One day before his death, his mind was caught up in rapture and his eyes were open, and he looked to the right and to the left of his bed,

and those sitting there heard his speech, for it was as though he were being judged by some beings. At one moment he would say, "Yes, it is true, but for this I fasted so many years." And again he would say, "You are not telling the truth, but you lie, for I did not do this of which you accuse me."
And again he would say, "It is true, but for this I wept and served." And again he would say, "You are not telling the truth, but you lie against me." And at one moment he said:
"Yes, truly, yes, you are telling the truth. And for this I have nothing with which to answer you, except that I have the mercy of God as my helper."

It was a terrible and frightening sight, an unforgiving and invisible judgment, and the most terrible thing was this: that they accused him even of what he had not done. Oh, what a wonder! For that recluse and
solitary said concerning some of his errors, "About this I have nothing with which to answer you," he who had spent forty years in the monastic life and had weeping and great mourning.
Woe, woe, beloved! Where then was the word of the prophet Ezekiel, that he might have said to them, "In whatever I find you, on that I will judge you," said the Lord?
Truly, he could say nothing of the kind. And why, O brothers? Glory to the only One who knows.
And some told me, the Lord knows, that with his own hand he gave food to leopards, lions and hyenas out in the desert,
and in the midst of such a judgment he departed from the body. And what his sentence was, or what kind of verdict went forth concerning him,

or what the end of that judgment was, was not made known. Like a widowed woman who has buried her husband and has an only-begotten son, and after God has him as her consolation, so also a soul that has fallen into sin
has no other consolation at the hour of death except the labor of hunger and thirst and tears. Let them never sing with a sweet voice,
such people by themselves, for such things are harmful to mourning,

and if you wish to summon mourning by such means, you will be all the further removed from it; for mourning is the settled pain of a burning soul. With many, mourning has become a forerunner of dispassion, when it has wiped out the matter of the passions and cleansed the soul.
A certain laborer experienced in mourning told me, "When I wished to incline toward vainglory,
or of anger; or of filling the belly, that thought of mourning in the heart pricks me within and says to me: Do not give yourself over to such things as these, or else I will flee from you.
But I answered and said to it: I will not be disobedient to you, O friend, until I have presented you before our Lord Jesus Christ. The abyss of mourning has found consolation,
and purity of heart has received divine radiance,
and radiance is an ineffable power,

which is known unknowably and seen invisibly. Consolation is the rest of a soul in pain and worn out, which weeps within itself like an infant and laughs radiantly. Rest is the lifting up of a soul bowed down by sorrow, when the tears of anguish are wondrously changed into joy. Tears that come from the remembrance of death give birth to fear, and fear gives birth to fearlessness,
and then joy shines forth, and when that unending joy is made complete, the flower of that radiant love appears. Crush yourself with humility and say in your heart

that 'I am not worthy of this joy' which comes upon you, so that you may not be too ready to accept it and receive a wolf instead of a shepherd. Do not accept visions when it is not the time for visions, but be patient
until it seeks you of its own accord because of your humility, and they follow you and go before you and remain with you to the end, forever,

in that holy and spiritual marriage chamber. At first, as soon as a little child recognizes its parent, it is delighted and filled with joy; but when the parent goes away from it for a time and comes back again, then the child is filled with both joy and sorrow: with joy because
it has seen the one it longs for, and with sorrow because it was deprived of that joy for all the time they were apart. A mother hides from her child,
and when it looks for her in sorrow, the mother watches it and rejoices, and in this way she teaches it never to go away from her.

according to the word of our Lord. A man against whom the sentence of death has gone out does not care about when there will be singing. In the same way, the true penitent and mourner does not give himself over to gluttony or to vainglory,
or to resentment and anger. Mourning is a constant pain in the repentant soul,
for day by day it adds pain on top of pains,

just as the pangs of a woman in labor are added to her pain. The Lord is just and loves justice, for He gives true mourning to the true solitary, and He always gladdens and consoles the truly obedient. Whoever properly follows either of these two ways has been delivered from eternal mourning. Drive away the dog that comes to you in the time of your mourning and calls God merciless and unforgiving, so as to cast you into despair. For if you consider it, that same dog, before the sin,
comes to you and presents God as merciful and forgiving. The constant remembrance of death gives birth to fear, and that fear brings about mourning,

But when mourning has been established in the soul by habit, it becomes like a second nature to it and passes away only with difficulty. Even if we perform great ascetic labors, if our heart is without compunction, let us know that we are in error. For I tell you the truth, brethren,

That those who have defiled their flesh after baptism need to be baptized again, with the tears of repentance, with the fire of fervor, and with the mercy of God. I have seen in certain people the perfect limit of mourning,
for from the pain of their heart they vomited blood from their mouths through the beating of their breasts;
and the saying came to my mind which says:
Tears that come from fear have within themselves trembling and protection; but tears of love, until perfect love has made one perfect, are more easily stolen away,
unless the fire of fervor burns beyond measure in the heart,

at the time of their flowing; and it is marvelous how the lower measure is the more unerring in its own time. There are some things that dry up our springs; and there are others that do not dry them up, but breed mire and beasts in the spring.
And through the first of these things Lot fell lawlessly with his daughters; and through the second the devil fell down from heaven. How many are the wicked devices of our enemies,

of ours, how by their devices they often turn the things that give birth to virtue into begetters of wickedness, and make the things that bring about humility appear as things that bring about pride. Withdrawal into the desert often brings us tears and compunction. Learn this from Jesus our Lord,
and from Elijah and John the Baptist, for they withdrew into the uninhabited desert to pray. I have seen tears stirred up even amid turmoil and in cities,
but the enemies bring this about so that we will think that turmoil does us no harm at all, and in this way we will draw near to the world.

And this is truly a deceit and a device of the demons. A single word often scatters mourning, but it is a wonder if a single word gathers it again. Beloved, at the hour of death we will not be held pitiable because we did not work miracles,
or did not speak about God, or were not seers of invisible things. But we must give an account to God
of why we did not mourn continually. Therefore it is fitting for us, brethren, to weep and mourn continually over our life and to hasten before God,
to whom be glory now and ever and to the ages of ages. Amen.

This is the seventh step. May the one who has been made worthy of it be a helper to me as well, for he himself no longer needs a helper. For through this seventh step, those who have reached it in these seven days of this passing life have washed away the defilements of the passions and have been made holy.
Discourse by the same author on freedom from anger and on wrath. Chapter 8. Just as water extinguishes the flame of fire,
so also the tears of true mourning extinguish every flame of wrath and anger.

Therefore let us join the removal of anger to mourning. Freedom from anger is an insatiable desire for reproach and dishonor, just as those who love vainglory are never sated with people's praise. Freedom from anger is a victory over nature and an insensibility to insults,

acquired through much sweat and great struggle. Meekness is a state of the soul that is not stirred up and that remains the same under insults and under praise. The beginning of freedom from anger is keeping the lips silent with a heart that is not stirred up;

And the middle is the silencing of the words of the heart during slight stirrings of the soul; and the end is undisturbed calm amid the blowing of unclean winds. Wrath is a stirring of hidden hatred and of unseen rancor. Anger is the desire to do evil to those who provoke one. Irascibility is an untimely inflaming of the heart. Bitterness is a distasteful stirring implanted in the soul.

Anger is a sudden disturbance of calm, and it is the ugliness of the soul. Just as darkness vanishes at the appearing of light, so at the appearing of humility all turmoil and anger vanish. There are some men
who, when they become angry, calm down again in a moment, and for this reason they are negligent about struggling against this passion of theirs and healing it,
and the wretched ones do not remember the saying
which is written: "A certain mill is quick, and in a moment grinds more than another does in a whole day," and it swiftly crushes the wheat and all the fruit of the soul,

and for this reason great caution is required of us. Many times a great flame is kindled by the violence of the wind, and in a single moment it burns up [?] and lays waste the field of the soul more than another flame, gently kindled, does in a whole day. Let us not be ignorant of this, O beloved: that many times the demons suddenly withdraw from us, so that we may neglect those great passions as though they were small, and so be weakened by them beyond healing. Just as a rough stone, thorny and knobby,

when it rolls among many stones, is rubbed and made smooth, losing its roughness and unevenness, so too a soul that is sharp [?], harsh and wrathful, when it mingles and lives with many men who are strong and harsh ascetics: such a one will unfailingly meet with one of these two things:
either it will be healed of that passion through patience, or it will withdraw from them and come to know its own weakness.

The wrathful man is mad by his own will, for he has been overcome by his former habits, and without being aware of it he falls into raging. Nothing is worse for the penitent than anger, for the great humility of repentance is what helps him;
but anger is the image of all pride. This is the great depth of meekness: when the one who troubles him is close by, and his heart is at peace, and he does not diminish his love for him;

and again, this is the great evil of anger: that even if a man is alone he rages and fights against the one who troubled him. Just as the Holy Spirit is the peace and calm of the soul, so anger is the disturber and destroyer of the Spirit,
and for this reason nothing so hinders the coming of the Holy Spirit to us as anger. We know that

the offspring of anger are many and evil, but there is one of its offspring alone that, against its will and fierce though it is, nevertheless sometimes becomes useful. For we have seen men raging with anger, who revealed the rancor that had been hidden among them for a long time, and by a passion they were delivered from a worse passion, when the one who troubled them gave them satisfaction in the matter or else asked forgiveness.
And I saw others who had a bestial long-suffering, and by that silence they fed and filled their hearts with the remembrance of wrongs,
and I considered those wretched ones worse than the demon-possessed and the rabid, because of their own accord they made themselves enemies of the good, as the hawk is of the dove.

Beloved, it befits us to take great care and caution against this serpent, wrath, for it has even nature as its helper, as fornication also does. We have seen wrathful people who, from the abundance of their bitterness, have abstained from food and added venom upon venom by that bestial fasting.
And I saw others who took their anger as a pretext and gave themselves over to gluttony, and they hurled themselves down as if from a high cliff into a deep pit.
And I saw others, wise ones, who like skilled physicians mixed both,

and from both, through that measured consolation, they gained great profit. Measured chanting of the office sometimes calms the anger of the soul, and sometimes it assists the love of pleasure, when it is done without measure and out of season; therefore let us use it according to the proper time and measure. A gentle answer calms anger, and a harsh answer increases anger, and therefore it is necessary that we have humility with us in all things. I was once outside my cell for some need,

and I heard certain solitaries who, from the excess of their fury and anger, were in their cells, all by themselves, pecking and struggling like partridges in cages, and lunging back and forth at the face before them in their rage, as though the one who had offended them were standing right there in front of them;
but I spoke to them and advised them, with the fear of God, not to live in stillness in complete solitude at all, lest they be changed from human nature and become demons.
I have also seen hearts full of passion and filth, lovers of the flesh, dissolute, lovers of singing and luxury, inclined to companionship with young men and fond of adorning their faces,

for whom I chose solitude as the enemy of such passions and filth, so that they would not turn from human nature into the nature of beasts. But some told me that people are pitifully defeated by both of these,
and these I completely kept from living according to their own will, and I lovingly advised their spiritual fathers that sometimes in stillness
and sometimes among the community they should order their way of life,

and we left everything to the spiritual father, so that he might order things as he wishes, according to their passions. Love of pleasure harms only itself, and perhaps, besides its one partner, harms someone else as well;
but wrath many times, like a wolf, throws the whole flock into turmoil,
and that it wounds many humble souls. The darkening of the eyes of the soul by anger is evil, as the speaker says,
and it is worse still when the soul's wrath shows itself through the lips as well. But raising one's hands is entirely hostile and foreign to the monastic

way of life. If you want to remove the speck from your brother's eye, take care not to wound him with an arrow instead of a probe, meaning a retort and a harsh, evil expression. The probe is instruction given with meekness and reproof given with long-suffering. The apostle says “rebuke”; he did not say “beat.” But if it cannot be done without beating, O superior,

So from time to time, not by his own hand but by the hands of others. If we look into it, we have found many irascible people who zealously practise fasting, vigils and solitude. For this is the devil's purpose: to persuade them, under the pretext of repentance and ascetic struggle, to multiply among themselves the things that feed that passion. If one wolf, as we have said, is able to throw the whole flock into turmoil
with the help of the devil, then surely one wise brother too is able, like a flask full of oil, to calm the waves,
with the help of an angel. And just as the former will receive great punishment,

so this one will receive a great reward from God and become a model of benefit for all. The beginning of blessed freedom from anger is to endure shame, reproach, and insult with bitterness and pain of heart; the middle is to be among them without distress; and the perfection is this: when someone is found who counts insult as praise.

Rejoice, you who are first; live, you who are second, blessed are you by the Lord; and be glad, you who are third, perfect in measure. I saw a pitiable sight among the irascible, which came upon them secretly from pride: for they would become angry,
and then, because they had been defeated by anger, they became angry again,
and I was amazed as I watched them punish fall with fall and take vengeance on sin with sin, and I pitied them; and at the devices of the devil
I was so amazed that I nearly gave up hope for myself. Whoever sees himself defeated by anger and pride, by wickedness and duplicity, and wishes to draw against them the two-edged sword of meekness:
let such a one go to a community of harsh brothers and enter there as into a fuller's house, which washes away filth

and [to the place] that saves the soul, and let him stay there if he wishes to be completely cleansed of the passions. When his mind is beaten by insults and dishonour, or even when his body is trampled and pounded and crushed like a garment, then all the filth

that is in the garment of his soul will be cleansed and thoroughly washed. Let even the saying of worldly people convince you, and understand that dishonour, shame and insult wash away the passions of the soul. For when worldly people have badly insulted someone, they boast to one another, "I washed him, I bathed him," and truly it is so. The freedom from anger that comes through mourning among beginners is one thing;
and the complete extinction of wrath and the imperturbability of the perfect is another, for in the former the passion is bound by tears and mourning, as if with a bit and bridle;

But by these second ones it has been killed, like a serpent, by the sword of impassibility. I saw three monks who were insulted together by certain people. The first was distressed because he had been insulted, yet he kept silent. The second rejoiced over his own insult, but was grieved for the one who had insulted him,

because that man had harmed himself. And the third pictured in his heart the harm done to his neighbor and wept fervently. And in those three could be seen workers moved by fear, by reward, and by love. Just as the heat of a fever [?] is spoken of by one name,
yet has many causes and not one for its arousal, so too is the arousal of anger and of our other passions, for many

and diverse causes belong to each one. For this reason it is not possible for us to prescribe the treatment of them in a single manner. Rather, we say this: let the one who has the disease strive to make the treatment accord with the disease and with its causes. Above all it is necessary

that each one search out the cause of his own disease, so that when he finds the cause in it, he may also receive the medicine and the cure, by the help of God and by the diligence of spiritual physicians. Let us therefore gather in spirit, as in a figure and a parable, and make an inquiry into the causes of this disease:

where it comes from, and what the manner of its cure is. Those of you who wish, come to this spiritual and invisible tribunal of ours. Let us sit down and investigate this aforementioned passion of wrath. How then shall we find the causes of this disease, O brothers, or how shall we learn who is the parent of this invisible enemy? But come, let us strive and bind this tyrannical anger. Let us send against that invisible one invisible marvelous ones as well, and let us press it hard with meekness, for this is the bond that pacifies it.
Let us strike it down and scourge it with long-suffering, and let us deliver it into the hands of all-holy love, and let love drag it forth
and stand it before that invisible tribunal. And then let us question it with the mouth of the mind and say to it: Tell us, O senseless and foolish and dishonorable and restless one,
tell us, what is the name of your father, and what is your wicked mother called, who so evilly gave birth to you?

Or what are the names of those evil and foul sons and daughters of yours? Or which are the deeds that fight against your fierceness and kill it? And let it answer and say to us: My parents are many, and my father is not one;
for my mothers are vainglory, love of money, gluttony, and sometimes fornication too. My fathers are haughtiness and usury. My children are remembrance of wrongs,
hatred, enmity, and insisting on one's own word. My enemies, by whom I am now bound, are freedom from anger and meekness.
And the one who fights me and destroys me is Humility;
but as for who her parent is, ask her yourselves in her own place. May God give us, brothers, Humility, the destroyer of this passion, by the grace of God,
to whom belongs the glory forever and ever. Amen. In this eighth Step is found the crown of Freedom from Anger,
and whoever has this crown by nature may perhaps have no other;
But he who has acquired it by sweat and toil has conquered all eight of these passions.
Discourse of the same blessed father of ours, John, on the remembrance of wrongs. Chapter 9. The virtues of the saints are like that ladder which Jacob saw,
for, as one enters into them one after another, they lift a person up to heaven;
but evil deeds are like those chains that fell from the apostle Peter.
For in this way the passions hang one upon another, and they drag the soul down to hell;

For this reason too we heard from unholy anger, when it said that remembrance of wrongs is its offspring; therefore now, after the parent, let us also speak about its wicked child. Remembrance of wrongs is the venom of anger, the keeper of sins, the hatred of righteousness, the destroyer of virtues.
It is a deadly poison of the soul, a worm that devours the mind. It is a shame to prayers, an estrangement from love, a nail in the soul; it is a thing
without savor, beloved by the wrathful for the sweetness of its bitterness; it is a perpetual sin, a sleepless lawlessness, a wickedness at every hour and always.
One of the passions, I mean remembrance of wrongs,

is among the offspring and not the parents, and even more among the parents too; and for this reason I do not wish to say much about it. He who has become victor over anger has abolished remembrance of wrongs,
but as long as the father lives, it is impossible that he should not have a son [?]. Whoever has acquired love has become a stranger to envy,

but whoever harbors enmity will have no end of vain toil and destruction of the soul. The table of love dissolves hatred, and a pure gift soothes and calms the soul. An unguarded table is the mother of boldness, and through the window of love gluttony enters. I saw hatred that loosed a long-standing bond of fornication;

and there too I saw remembrance of wrongs, which from then on kept that bond of fornication unbound, and I marveled at how a demon drove out a demon. Could it be that this is a work of God's providence, and not of laborers? Firm natural love is far removed from remembrance of wrongs, but it must be guarded against, for fornication easily approaches it, and the louse of fornication appears, hidden in the dove of love. If you remember wrongs,
Bear grudges against the demons, and if you are to be anyone's enemy,
always be an enemy to your flesh. The body is an ungrateful and treacherous friend: the more we give it rest, the more it harms us.
Remembrance of wrongs is an evil interpreter of the Scriptures, for it brings them in to testify to its own wickedness. Let the prayer of the Lord Jesus put it to shame,

which we cannot say if we hold it within us. When you struggle hard and still cannot drive that passion completely out of your heart, then make your peace again and again with the one who has troubled you,
and outwardly show him love, so that by doing this you may be shamed by the reproof of your conscience and fully take love for him into your heart as well. Do you want to know

whether you are completely healed of that passion? Take this as your sign: not when you pray for the one who troubled you, nor when you ever gladden him with gifts, nor when you invite him to receive honour;

But when you hear of some spiritual or bodily trial that has befallen him, and you grieve and weep as if it had befallen you, then know that you have been freed from the remembrance of wrongs. A solitary who remembers wrongs is a hidden asp, carrying its deadly venom within its own head. The remembrance of Christ's sufferings will heal the remembrance of wrongs, for it will be put to shame by his freedom from rancor and his gentleness. Worms breed in soft wood, and the remembrance of wrongs befalls solitaries who are slack and harshly silent. Whoever puts it far from himself will find forgiveness of sins, but whoever clings to it,
is far from the mercy of God. Many have given themselves over to severe labors so that their sins might be forgiven, but a man free of rancor

outruns them; for the Lord says: Forgive, and your sins will be forgiven you. The sign of true repentance is freedom from rancor; but whoever has rancor and thinks that he is repenting is like a man who wishes to truly run in his sleep. I have seen rancorous people
who were reproving other rancorous people for their rancor, and were put to shame by their own words,
and ceased from that passion. Let no one think that this wicked passion is a small one, for it is so great that many times it brings down even those who struggle and are spiritual.
But let us call upon the Lord to deliver us from it. For his is the glory for ever and ever. Amen. This is the ninth Step; let whoever has acquired it boldly ask Christ for the forgiveness of sins.

Discourse on slander and judging. Chapter 10. I think that no one with understanding is unaware that slander is born of hatred and of remembering wrongs. For this reason I have placed the offspring after its parents, in proper order. Slander is the offspring of hatred. It is a subtle, hidden disease that creeps in secretly. It is a leech that sucks out the blood of love and makes love disappear. It is a divided heart, it breeds defilement and heaviness, and it destroys purity. Once I heard some people speaking evil of someone. I became angry and told them to stop. But those who were doing this evil answered me and said, "We do this out of love for him and the concern we have for him."
I answered and said to them, "Stop this kind of love, so rough and harsh, so that you do not make a liar of the prophet who says,
If you love him, pray for him,
and do not speak evil,
for God helps him through prayer and has mercy on him. Consider this, brother, and see: Judas was in the company of the disciples, and the robber in the company
of murderers; and in a single moment, wondrously, the one was saved and the other perished;

and if you always bear this in mind, it will be of great profit to you for not judging your neighbor. Whoever wishes to overcome judging, let him not attribute to his brother the error he sees in him, but to the devil who suggested it to him,
for no one wants to sin against God, even though we are overcome through our own negligence, and no one is overcome by force. I have seen people who sinned openly and repented secretly,

and those whom I had judged as fornicators were holy before God, for they had been purified through repentance. Do not show deference to someone who speaks evil of a brother to you. Instead, say to him,
"Stop, brother. Every day I do worse things myself, so how could I judge him?" In this way you will gain two benefits,

for you will both profit your own soul and heal your neighbor. This too is one of the ways that lead quickly to life, namely, not judging one's neighbor, for the Lord says: [?] And therefore let us strive, beloved, not to judge our brothers,
whatever error we may see in them. As water is foreign to fire, so is judging one's neighbor foreign to repentance. Even if you see someone in sin at the hour of death, do not judge him even then,
for God's judgment is unknown to men. Many have committed great evils openly,
but have done greater good deeds in secret, and they were mistaken,

lovers of judging, and they held smoke in place of the sun [?]. Listen to me, listen, O you evil judges of sinful people: if it is true, as the word the Lord spoke is true, then it is clear that in whatever matter
we blame and judge our neighbour, we fall into that same thing ourselves, whether it is bodily or spiritual. Those who are hasty and quick to judge the sins of others

fall into this passion for this reason: they have no true remembrance of and concern for their own sins. For if someone were to cast off that veil of love of the flesh and properly see his own evils, he would care for nothing else in this world,
but would reflect and say: "All the days of my life are not enough to mourn for my sins." And he would train himself in this even if he were to live a hundred years,
and even if he were to see tears flowing down from his eyes like the river Jordan. I have examined and seen true mourning,
and I found no trace in it of slander or judgment. The demons have many devices: either they strive to cast us into sin,
or, if they cannot do this, they then labor to make us judge sinners, so that by this second thing those wicked ones may defile the first as well. This is the sign of slanderers and the envious:
when they hear some teaching, or some good virtue of another, or good words, they immediately begin to disparage it, and they [?] and come to hate it. I have seen some who in secret many
and great evils were committing, and no one saw them,
and since all people presumed them to be pure, for this reason they harshly rebuked and judged those who committed a small error. Judging is the seizure of the honor of the Only-Begotten
and the destroyer of the soul. As pride by itself, without any other passion, is able to destroy us,

so judging one's neighbor alone is able to destroy us completely, as this alone condemned and destroyed that Pharisee. A wise gatherer of grapes eats the ripe grapes and does not look at the sour ones,
and likewise a wise and discerning mind, if it sees certain virtues, gladly takes them to heart and does not look at errors;

but the foolish look only at the errors and evils of their neighbour. For it is said of this that [?]. But you, brother, even if you see a brother's sin with your own eyes, do not judge. The eyes are often deceived too. Sing praise to the Lord instead, to whom be glory forever and ever.
Amen. This is the tenth step; whoever has overcome this passion is a worker of love or of mourning.
Discourse of our holy father John on silence and talkativeness. Chapter 11. In our earlier discourse we said
that judging is evil and deceptive.
Now let us also say a little about talkativeness, which is its cause and its door,

the door through which slander and judging come in, and even more often go out. Talkativeness is the throne of vainglory, where vainglory sits and shows itself. Talkativeness is a sign of a lack of understanding and the door of slander. It leads the way to insolence and is the servant of lying,

…the destroyer of compunction and the bringer of despondency, the forerunner of sleep and the scatterer of good thoughts, it makes mourning vanish, cools fervor, and darkens prayer. Silence with understanding is the mother of prayer and the gatherer of the mind from its captivity [of distraction], the guardian of that divine fire, a teacher, the keeper of divine thoughts, one who stands over the fervor of the thoughts; it is a watchman who always keeps watch on the enemies;

it is the bond of mourning and the friend of tears, it is that which reminds of death and depicts the torments, it is a training for the coming judgment and a servant of godly grief, it is the enemy of
insolence and the companion of stillness, it guards against the love of glory and multiplies understanding, it is the enemy of falls and the finder of those spiritual visions.
It is an unseen advance and an invisible ascent. Whoever has recognized his own fall, let him guard his tongue; but the talkative person does not know himself as he ought.

6. The lover of silence draws near to God, and the nearer he comes to him, the more he is enlightened by him. 7. The silence of Jesus put Pilate to shame, and the spirit of a silent man has dispelled vainglory. Peter said one word and wept bitterly,
and he mourned over it, because he had forgotten the saying of that speaker who says: [?]

And again the one who said: "It is better to be thrown down from a height [?]". I do not wish to speak at length about this, even though the many kinds of passions compel me to speak at length about them,
but I once heard from someone who was discussing silence with me, for he said that much speaking comes from these two things:
either from upbringing and bad habit, for since the tongue is a member of the body, as it has been accustomed, so it seeks out its habit;
or else from vainglory among those who practice asceticism; and it also arises from gluttony;
for this reason many bridle their belly with hunger and through this have silenced their much speaking. Whoever remembers death will hate idle words, and whoever has acquired mourning,
…let him flee from much talking as from fire. Whoever has loved stillness
has guarded his mouth; but whoever loves going about

He will be driven from his own cell by that passion. Whoever has seen the taste of the sweetness of our Lord Jesus Christ and has smelled the fragrance of that heavenly fire flees from people as a bee flees from smoke; for as smoke drives the bee away, so the disturbance of people opposes this work. It is hard and difficult to hold back water without an enclosure and mortar,
and harder than this is the silence of the tongue,

without fasting; but with God all things are possible, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. This is the eleventh Step. Whoever overcomes this enemy has destroyed the multitude of passions from himself.

Discourse by the same author on lying. Chapter 12. The offspring of iron and stone is fire, and the offspring of much talking and jesting is lying. Lying is the destroyer of love and the mother of false swearing, which is the denial of God. Let no one who has understanding think
that the sin of lying is small,

For the Holy Spirit spoke fearfully about it through the mouth of David the prophet: "He who speaks lies shall not prosper before my eyes." If the prophet David says to God that he will destroy those who speak lies, what then will be done to those who add an oath to the lie? I have seen some men who rejoiced in lying, and by frivolity and idle talk stirred up laughter, and so destroyed the way of life of those who mourn. When the demons see that one of them wants to leave a gathering of people who are full of laughter and jesting, they speak to him deceitfully and lead him astray with two thoughts:
first they say, "Do not offend the speaker"; and second, "Do not make a show of loving God more than your neighbors do." Flee from such people, and do not linger there,

or else thoughts of laughter and jesting will come upon you in your prayer and darken you. Do not only flee, but if you have the strength, also break up that evil conversation and bring in the remembrance of death and judgment; for it is better, even if a little vainglory should spatter you from this: only strive to be of benefit both to yourself and to all those others. Duplicity is the mother of lying and its work, for duplicity is nothing other than training in lying

and the devising of vain oaths. Whoever has acquired the fear of the Lord has become a stranger to lying, since he has within himself a [?]-eyed judge, which is conscience. Just as there are distinctions of punishment for all the passions,
so also for lying, for one punishment belongs
to him who lied out of fear of torture, and another to him who did it without any hardship, out of lack of fear of God. One lied for the sake of food;
another for love of pleasure; another in order to bring laughter to those with him;
and another in order to do evil to his brother. By the chastisement of superiors lying is wiped out,
but by an abundance of tears it perishes completely and is destroyed. The speaker of a lie gives as his excuse that he acts out of discernment,

and he would count that destruction of his own soul as righteousness. A lying man claims to be doing the deed of Rahab the harlot, and says that by his own destruction he is purchasing the life of others. If we purify ourselves entirely of lying,
then even if some affliction should come,

and we should wish to summon a lie, even then it will flee from us. An infant child does not know lying, nor does a soul that has separated itself from evil. And when wine has gladdened [?] the heart of a man,
he speaks the truth even against his will; and those who are filled with the compunction of tears

do not know lying, for they ever glorify the Lord, whose is the glory, now and ever and unto the ages of ages. Amen. This is the twelfth Step; whoever has become victor over this serpent has acquired the root of good things, which is truth.

Discourse of the same on despondency. Chapter 13. This passion of despondency too is one of the branches of talkativeness, as we said above, and indeed is its firstborn offspring; for this reason we have assigned it its fitting place, within that evil torment of the passions. 2. Despondency is a slackening of the soul,
a weakening of the mind, a neglect of ascetic struggle, a hatred of the monastic life; it calls laymen blessed, and accuses God of being merciless and not good;
it is slack in psalmody, feeble in prayer, tireless in bodily service, unsparing of effort in handiwork, hypocritical in obedience.
3. An obedient man has no experience of despondency, for through things visible he has gained what is invisible. 4. The gathering of those who live in community is opposed to despondency;

but for the man who lives alone, it is for life. 5. It does not leave him before his death, and he does battle with it every day until he goes to the grave. 6. The demon of despondency saw the cell of a solitary,

and smiled, and came near to him and settled down with him. 7. A physician visits the sick at dawn, but despondency comes upon solitaries at midday. 8. Despondency reminds solitaries of welcoming strangers,
and urges them to give alms from their handiwork.

9. It zealously urges going to the sick, and brings to mind the saying which says: "I was sick and you came to me." 10. It urges going out to the afflicted and the faint-hearted, and that faint-hearted one devises the consoling of the faint-hearted. 11. When we stand for prayer,
they remind us of necessary tasks, and use every means in their haste to draw us away from there,
like cattle [led] by a halter [?] by that brute. 12. The demon of despondency brings on shivering, a burning heat in the head, and stomach pain, until the third hour. 13.
When the ninth hour draws near, it relieves him a little; and when the table is set, he springs up from his bed; and when prayer comes, his body grows heavy again. 14.

When we stand at prayer, it plunges us in sleep and constant yawning, and snatches the verse from our mouth. 15. The other passions are each abolished by the virtues opposed to them, but despondency is in every respect death to the monk. 16.
Courage of soul raises up a dead mind, but despondency and sloth scatter all wealth.
17. Since this too is one of the eight evil thoughts, and the heaviest of them all, let us examine it as well, following the same order as the others. But for now I will say only this.
18. When there is no psalmody, despondency does not
appear, and when we have completed the canon of prayer, then our eyes open.

19. In the hour of despondency those who force themselves become manifest, for nothing adds to a monk's crown as despondency does, if he does not yield to it. 20. Take note and you will find [?] that it fights you continually at the time of prayer and of sitting, telling you to lean against the wall and to look out through the window of the cell, and making us imagine the footsteps of someone walking. 21. Whoever has gained true mourning, the spirit of despondency will not touch him. 22. Come, beloved, and let us bind this tyrant too, by the remembrance of death and of sins; and let it be beaten with handiwork and be dragged by the remembrance of the eternal good things,
and let it be brought before that spiritual tribunal, and ask it: Tell us, you too, O slack and negligent one!
Who is it that bore you for evil? And who are your offspring? And who are those who fight against you? Or who is it that kills you?
And it says: Among the truly obedient I have nowhere to lay my head, but I dwell with those who live alone, and my parents are many:

sometimes hardness of soul, and sometimes forgetfulness of the heavenly good things, and sometimes even excess of labors has summoned me. And my offspring are many: moving from place to place, brought about by me;

and disobedience to the spiritual father; and forgetfulness of the eternal judgment; and often even the complete abandonment of the monastic vow. And my opponents, by whom I am now bound, are psalmody and handiwork;
and my enemy — [?] of death
remembrance.
But what kills me is prayer with hope in those eternal good things.
And as for who is the parent of prayer, ask prayer itself, for it sings to the Lord and calls upon him.
To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. This is the thirteenth. It is a victory over the passions; whoever has gained this victory has been proved in all things.
Composed by the same holy father of ours, John of Sinai. On gluttony. Chapter 14. I wish to speak a little about gluttony too,
as with those other passions; but we are addressing these words to ourselves,
[the things] we are saying about gluttony of the belly, for I am amazed
if anyone has become free of it before taking up his dwelling in the grave. Gluttony is the hypocrisy of the belly: when it is full, it claims to be in want,

And when it is filled and bursting, it cries out that it is hungry, and eagerly seeks to receive still other food. Gluttony is the inventor of foods and the source of the love of delicacies. When you stop up one of its springs, it appears somewhere else; and when you do away with that one too, it overpowers you from yet another side. Gluttony deceives the eyes: the belly holds little, but gluttony makes one imagine swallowing everything at once. Being full of food is the father of fornication, but affliction of the belly leads to purity. One who often gives rest to a lion may even tame it,
but one who gives rest to the flesh makes it more savage. The Jew rejoices over the Sabbath and the feast, and the gluttonous monk over Saturday and Sunday.

A year beforehand he counts up to the time of filling himself, and ahead of the time he prepares the foods. The slave of the belly considers with what foods he will keep the feast, and the true servant of God considers
with what divine graces he may be enriched. When a stranger comes to the glutton, he receives him with joy and at once lays the table,
and he counts his own relaxation of the rule as love for a brother. When some people from outside come, he wishes for a dispensation for wine,
And he thinks that he is concealing virtue, but he is a slave of passion. Often vainglory is at enmity with gluttony, and as over a purchased slave,

so they quarrel over the wretched monk. The one compels him to relax the rule, while the other tyrannically presses him to display his virtue. The wise monk escapes both, for at the proper time he drives away the one by means of the other. When the battles of the flesh overpower us,

then let us torment the flesh at every time and in every place; but if we have put the flesh to death, which I do not know ever to have happened before one goes to the grave, then let us conceal our virtue. I have seen aged priests

who were mocked by the demons and who at meals urged young men who were not under their obedience, and by adjuration and by making the sign of the cross released them to take wine and other foods from which they had been abstaining. If such priests are attested by all for fear of God and ascetic struggle,

[?] concerning their crucifixion [?], let us relax our rule a little when we find ourselves in such a place; but if they are negligent, let their crucifixion [?] not be counted to us at all, and especially if that fire of the flesh [?] is overpowering us. The wretched and pitiable Evagrius thought that he was wiser than the wise in speech and understanding, but that senseless man was mistaken,
and he was found more foolish than the foolish in many matters;
and in this one especially, for he says that when our soul desires many foods,
then let us restrict it even in bread and water. But this is as if someone were to say to a small child, "Climb to the top of the ladder in one step."
But we oppose his statement and say that when our soul desires various kinds of foods, it is seeking something natural;

therefore let us use a stratagem against that one of many stratagems, unless at that moment we have heavy battles and fear of a fall; and let us carry out our stratagem in this way: let us first cut off fatty foods, and then heating ones, and then tasty ones,
and if possible let us give the belly food that is filling and easily digested, so that by that fullness we may drive away its insatiable mind,

and by that quick digestion we may escape the heat of the flesh as from a fire. If we investigate, we shall find that most windy foods also arouse the flesh. Laugh at that demon who says to you after supper that you should make a promise to fast tomorrow, for when the ninth hour of the next day arrives, he renounces that promise of his.
The fast of those who have not fallen into a fall is one thing, and that of those who have fallen is another; for the former have as their sign the deadening of the arousal of the flesh,

while the latter, even until death and the end, are implacable and give no consolation to their flesh and belly. The former must always keep the balance of their nature unharmed; but the latter, by sorrow of soul and wasting of the flesh, make God merciful toward them. The time of consolation and joy is for the perfect.

[?] a time of freedom from care in everything; but for the one who struggles, the time of joy is the time of battle and of victory over the enemies; while for the one ruled by passion, the time of joy is the feast of feasts and the gathering of gatherings. Dreams and memories of foods and dishes
are in the heart of gluttons; but dreams and memories of eternal judgments and torments
are in the heart of those who mourn. Master the belly before it masters you, and then you will fast with shame. Those who know this saying,
who have fallen into that unspeakable pit of fornication,

but eunuchs have no experience of this. Let us bridle our belly with the remembrance of that eternal fire, for many became obedient to their belly, and in the end even cut off their members and died a double death. Let us search and consider, and we shall find without doubt that among us this alone has caused those evil shipwrecks. The mind of one who fasts prays vigilantly, but
the mind of the glutton is full of unclean idols. Fullness of the belly dries up the springs of the eyes,
but affliction of the belly makes the springs of tears flow. One who gives rest to his own belly and thinks that he has overcome the demon of fornication
is like a man who quenches fire with oil. When the belly is constrained,
[?] the heart is humbled; but when the belly is given rest, the mind is exalted and the thoughts are scattered. Examine yourself, brother, at dawn,
at midday and in the evening, and before taking food, and you will see for yourself the benefit of fasting. At dawn the thoughts are troubled and scattered,
but when midday comes they weaken a little, and when the sun sets they are then completely humbled. Constrain your belly and without doubt you will silence your mouth,
for the tongue grows strong from an abundance of foods and begins to talk much. Be most vigilant toward it,
and fight a hard battle against it, for if you labor a little, the Lord will help you at once. Skins, the more they are kneaded,
[?] they spread out all the more; but if they are disregarded and not stretched [?], they cannot hold so much. One who forces his belly to eat every day widens his intestines;
but one who struggles with fasting narrows them, and when they are narrowed they can no longer hold much, and then we shall keep the fast naturally. Thirst often quenches thirst,

but to cut off hunger by hunger is difficult and impossible. When the belly overpowers you, overcome it with the labor of fasting; but if you are unable to do this because of weakness, torment it with vigils. When your eyes grow heavy with sleep, take up handiwork,
but if sleep is not overpowering you, do not do so,
but pray, for it is impossible to hold the mind on God and on mammon, that is, on God and on handiwork. Be aware

[?] that sometimes the demon settles on a person's stomach and makes it insatiable, so that the person thinks that even if he ate all Egypt and drank the river Nile, he would not be satisfied. After we have eaten our fill, that unclean demon of gluttony departs and sends the tyrant of fornication against us,
and tells him all our affairs, and says: "Hurry, quickly, [?] stir him up [?],

for his belly is full, so do not worry, you will not have to toil much. The demon of fornication comes upon us with fury, and when he sees us sated he smiles, and he makes our hands and feet tremble [?] with sleep, and he does whatever he wishes, for he sports with us as he pleases, and he defiles soul and body with fantasies and with flows of filth. O, what an astonishing thing, brothers!
How is that bodiless and immaterial mind defiled and darkened by material flesh;
and how, again, is that immaterial one purified and refined by this clay, and made to see clearly! If you have made a vow to God,
and in order that you may walk the narrow way,
constrict your belly, for

know that as long as it is at ease, you have transgressed your vow. Hear what the Lord says, that [?] of the belly, of fornication, [?] how of fasting, and few are [?]. The prince of demons is that star fallen from heaven, and the prince of the passions is the satiety of the belly. When you sit at a table full of food, bring the remembrance of death and judgment into your mind, and even so you will barely restrain the passion of gluttony a little. When you take drink,
do not forget the remembrance of that vinegar and gall which your King took, and then you will either abstain, or sigh and humble your mind,
and blame yourself. Do not reproach yourself, brothers, for you cannot escape that invisible Pharaoh, nor will you see that heavenly Passover,

unless you eat unleavened bread and bitter field-herbs in this world all the days of your life. The bitter herbs are the privation and the labor and the pain of fasting; and the unleavened bread is the lowly mind, which nowhere accepts the leaven of arrogance. Let the word of the one who speaks be nailed into your thought, he who says that the demons
Fasting is the constraint of nature, and the undoing of the palate's tastes, and the extinguisher of the body's burning.
And it is the cutter-off of evil thoughts; it is freedom from filthy dreams, and purity of prayer, and it is the lamp of the soul,

and the guardian of the mind, the undoing of hardness of heart, and the door of compunction, the supplier of humble sighs, and it is a good crusher of the heart, and what makes idle talk vanish; it is the cause of stillness, and the guardian of obedience, and the driver-away of sleep; it is the health of the body, the guide to dispassion; it is the remitter of sins and the door of paradise. Come, brothers, and let us question this too,
and above all that evil passion of gluttony, foremost of all, that leader of evils, the fall of Adam, the ruin of Esau,
the slayer of the Israelites, the disgrace of Noah, the burner of the people of Gomorrah, the guilt of Lot, the destroyer of the sons of Eli the priest, and the supplier of defilements,

let us question it and investigate, so that it may tell us where it is born from, and what its offspring are, and who is the one that crushes it, or who is the one that destroys it completely. Tell us, O teacher of all fleshly people,
you who have bought everyone with the gold of insatiability: from where do you make your entry among us,
and after your entry what sort of offspring do you bear among us, and what is your departure from us? But that wicked one thus answers us, who were questioning it with scorn and abuse,
saying, "Why do you revile and despise me, you who are under my authority,
or how do you hasten to separate yourselves from me? And I am by nature bound together with you.
[I] am. My door is the abundance of foods, and the cause of my insatiability is long-standing habit, and mercilessness of soul, and forgetfulness of death.
But since you wish to know the names of my offspring, I will enumerate them,
and they have multiplied more than the sand of the sea; but hear the names of my firstborn and beloved children:

My firstborn son is fornication, and after him harshness of heart, and the third is sleep, and then a sea of thoughts, and waves and stirrings of defilement, and an abyss of unspeakable and untold impurities comes forth from me.
And my daughters are: sloth, much talking, forwardness, dissipation, laughter,
contention, stiff-neckedness, disobedience, mercilessness, captivity of the mind, and loftiness and arrogance, and love of the world,
which is followed by defiled prayer and scattering of the mind, and many times unexpected trials, which beget despair, the worst of all.
I beget passions and multiply falls and cause death to be forgotten.
The remembrance of sins fights against me, but cannot overcome me;
and the remembrance of death is strongly hostile to me, but nothing among men can do away with me completely. But one who has acquired the Holy Spirit
cries out [?] to Him against me and entreats Him, and He lays me waste and no longer lets me,
so that I might do anything passionately. But those who have not tasted the sweetness of that Comforter,
with them my sweetness will surely become sweet, for He alone is the one who destroys me, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
This fourteenth Step is a great and valiant victory over that evil passion; whoever is able to overcome it, it is evident that he is going toward perfect purity and dispassion.
By the same author.
On incorruption, [attained] through labours,
and sweat of corruptible men, and on the purity and virginity acquired by them. Chapter 15. We have just now heard from that wicked tyrant gluttony,
for it said that the warfare of the flesh is its offspring, and this is not surprising, for our first father Adam also teaches us this;
for if he had not been overcome by gluttony, he would not have known his wife at all, whom he knew when he was cast out of paradise. And now those who keep that first commandment
do not fall by that second fall, but remain unshaken in the sonship of Adam, diminished;
and this also so that evil may not remain immortal, as the great Gregory the Theologian says,

Since this beautiful purity follows upon victory over the passion already spoken of, we have therefore set it in its fitting place, so that we may speak about purity as far as we are able. Purity is a property of the bodiless nature. Purity is a temple pleasing to Christ, and a heaven of the heart upon earth. Purity is a renunciation of nature that goes beyond nature, and an emulation of the bodiless, marvellously achieved in mortal and corruptible flesh. Pure is he who by love [drives out] love

...drove out, and quenched fire with immaterial fire. Pure is the one who, even in sleep, perceives no stirring or movement of the mind. Purity is a name common to all the virtues. Pure is the one who has acquired perfect reverence,

and who can find in himself no trace of the passions at all. This is the rule and boundary of perfect purity: that the mind should not change in any way at the differences between bodies, but should be the same toward animate bodies and inanimate ones, rational beings and brute beasts. Let none of those who have acquired purity suppose that he acquired it by his own power,
for to conquer one's own nature is among the things that are impossible. Where nature has been conquered, there undoubtedly the One who is above nature has taken up his dwelling,

for beyond all dispute the lesser is destroyed by the greater. The beginning of purity is the complete guarding of the thoughts, the destruction of fantasies and of the sight of evil images, and of repeated emissions, except that over long intervals of time an emission may occur in sleep without fantasy. The middle measure of purity is natural stirrings without fantasies, and free from emission.
But the perfect measure of purity is the mortification of the body,
through the prior mortification of the thoughts. Truly blessed is the monk who, toward every colour and every body,

toward every face and every beauty, has gained complete freedom from passion, so that he cannot detect anywhere within himself any trace of passion toward such things. For it is not he who keeps this clay undefiled who is pure,

but he who has wholly subjected its members to the soul. Great is he who remains free from passion when touching, and greater than he is the one who remains unwounded by sight and overcomes the fire of sight by remembering those good things and the beauties of heaven. He who drives off that dog by prayer is like a man who fights a lion;
but he who fights it by answering back and by the resistance of the mind is like a man
who is chasing his enemy. But he who has completely disregarded its approach, even if he is still in the flesh, has already risen from the grave. If this is the mark of true purity,

to remain unmoved in the fantasies of sleep [?], then this is surely the limit of great passion and filth: that while one is awake an emission should occur from a thought. He who fights this tyrant with labour and bodily sweat,
is like a man who has bound his enemy with a rope of hay;
but the one who engages it with fasting and vigil is like him who has fettered his adversary with iron;

and the one who stands against it with humility, freedom from anger, and thirst is like him who has killed his attacker and buried him in the sand. Understand the sand to mean humility, for it does not
grow any pasture for the passions, but is wholly earth and ashes. One is he who [?] by his own ascetic struggle; and another [?], and another, who by humility;

And another is he who has bound that tyrant by divine gifts and revelation. And the first is like the morning star, and the second like the great moon, and the third like the shining sun, and the dwelling of all of these is in the heavens. First the dawn rises,
and then the light spreads, and only then does the sun shine forth,

so too understand those things said above. The fox deceitfully feigns sleep, and the demon of fornication feigns a cessation of battle; the one in order to catch a bird, and the other in order to hunt and destroy the souls of men. Do not believe, brother, in a cessation of the battle of your flesh,

and do not trust it all the days of your life, until they present you before Christ. Do not trust in fasting because you have not fallen through it, for he who ate nothing at all fell down from heaven; so will your abstinence from food really keep you from falling? Certain men of understanding have said well that monastic life is this:
enmity toward one's own flesh, and warfare against one's own belly. Among newcomers, falls of the flesh come about through comfort and rest;

but among those in the middle [?] they come about also through pride, and among newcomers too they come about through pride; but those who have drawn near to perfection suffer this only from judging their neighbor.
Some call blessed those who are eunuchs by nature from their mother's womb, as being at rest from the warfare of the flesh; but I call blessed those
who make themselves eunuchs every day, and cut off from themselves thoughts of filth as with a two-edged sword. I have seen some men who fell against their will, and I have seen others

who wished to fall of their own will and could not, and I judged them more wretched than those who fall every day, because they could not, yet they still longed for that stench. Pitiable is he who falls;

but more pitiable is he who causes another also to fall, for he bears the weight of both falls and of the lust. Do not try to turn back the demon of fornication by reasoning and dispute, for it has many pretexts against us,
since it fights us by means of our own nature. Whoever wishes to fight and conquer his flesh by his own strength labors in vain,
for unless the Lord destroys the house of the flesh and builds the house of the soul,

in vain does he keep vigil and fast who wishes to destroy it. Show the Lord that sickness of your nature, acknowledge at all times your own weakness, and you will receive from the Lord, invisibly, the grace of chastity. There is among lovers of pleasure, as someone who had fallen into it told me after he had come to his senses, a certain awareness, so he said, of carnal love arising among them, and there enters into them some shameless and wicked spirit, which sits upon the sense of the heart, and bodily as well,
with pain of heart, as if from a furnace of fire, it afflicts that man
who has no fear of God, and the remembrance of torments
he despises as if it were nothing, and he loathes prayer, and he regards the sight of the dead as looking at lifeless stones, and it makes the man with whom it is

like one foolish and robbed of understanding, and it makes him drunk with desire toward bodies, both rational and irrational, so that if these days of such warfare and of that wicked spirit were not shortened, no soul would be saved that is clothed in this clay flesh, joined with blood and foul [?]discharge,
for how could it be saved, since every kind longs insatiably for what is akin to it,
blood for blood, and worm for worm, and likewise flesh for flesh;

even though, by seeking out means, we strive to deceive that deceiver, we who force nature and love the kingdom. Blessed are those who have remained wholly untested in this first warfare of which we have spoken,

and let us pray to the Lord that we too may not be tested by it, for those who have fallen into that pit need hunger and great labor in order to be able to climb that ladder of the virtues. Let us consider and discern whether among those enemies of ours, the demons, in their warfare against us, each one of them is appointed to one particular deed and battle, which is a marvel. I set my mind to observe those
who are in battle, and I saw falls
greater than falls. The demons have a custom, especially toward struggling monks, that many times all their contrivance and treachery,
and he directs his strength and his zeal against the passions that are contrary to nature, to wage war on them, and not against the natural ones,
and for this reason many, when they are with women, are not assailed by warfare at all, and so they call themselves blessed; and the wretches do not understand that where a greater fall comes about,

there the demons do not strive for the lesser. I think that those murderers of ours [urge?] these wretched ones toward deeds contrary to nature [?]: first, because the material for that fall is found by all of us; and second, because it carries a great and surpassing punishment. He knows this saying who at first commanded the wild asses and ruled over them, but at last, through those wild asses, was made subject to the soul-destroying demons and was mocked.
and who was nourished with the bread of heaven, but at last was deprived of that good.

And this is a marvel: after he had come to repentance, our leader Anthony said with grief and bitterness, "A great pillar has fallen." But that all-wise man concealed the manner of his fall, for he knew that it was a fornication of the body
even without touching another's body. There is among us a certain death and perdition of falling, which dwells among us and with us
always, and especially in the time of youth, which I have not dared to write about, for he restrained my hand who says
that of some things, the writing and the hearing [?] from deeds. The great Paul named my flesh death, for he says that [?]; but the blessed Gregory the Theologian
called him passionate and a slave of darkness; and I longed to learn why those holy men gave him such names. If the flesh is death, as has been said, it is evident
that whoever has prevailed over it will not die, of the defilement of his flesh. Tell me, I beseech you, who is greater: the one who died and rose again, or the one who did not die at all?

And he who calls the second blessed says that Christ died and rose again. But he who calls blessed the first, the one risen from the dead, then let him not cut off hope for anyone who has fallen and is among the dead. This hater of mankind, the enemy, the demon of fornication, names God the Lover of mankind, and says that He readily forgives this passion as being natural;
but let us observe the wiles of the demons, for after the fall they speak of Him as a just judge and merciless;
for before the fall they used that device in order to draw us toward sin; but after the fall they have devised this in turn, in order to

bring us to despair. As long as that thought of sorrow and despair is fighting us, let us not give ourselves over to falling; but when it fades away, that tyrant who calls Him "lover of mankind" arrives again. Just as the Lord is incorruptible and all-holy,
so He rejoices in the purity and incorruption of our bodies. The demons rejoice in nothing so much as in the stench of fornication,

and there is no passion they love as much as the defilement of the body. Purity is the property of God and likeness to Him, as far as is possible for man. The mother of sweetness is the earth and dew, and the mother of purity is stillness together with obedience. Those who have overcome their flesh by stillness and have gained such dispassion, if they come near the world, the passions stir up against them again;

but dispassion gained through obedience is tested in every place, and is firm and unshakable. I saw, and I recalled that saying, that a fall is the herald and offspring of pride, while a fall often becomes the occasion of humility for those who wish it. Whoever wishes to overcome the demon of fornication by gluttony and satiety
is like a man who feeds a fire with oil.
Whoever strives by fasting alone to calm the warfare of the flesh is like a man who swims with one hand and wishes to cross the great sea. Join humility to fasting as well, for without the second,
the first is useless. Whoever sees himself being defeated by some passion, let him arm himself against it before all else,
and above all against this enemy, fornication, for if it is not defeated, there is no profit in defeating the others;
but if we are able to kill this Egyptian, then we too shall see God in the bush of humility. At one time I was being tested, when I perceived this wolf of fornication,
how he was bringing brutish joy and tears and consolation into the soul by guile, and I supposed, with a childish mind,

that I had some fruit, and not fruitlessness and corruption. Truly, every sin that a man commits [?] for this reason, because he defiles the nature and substance of the flesh by that flow of uncleanness,
which does not happen with any other sin. I ask how it is that we say, concerning every sin,

...that so-and-so has erred, but of fornication we say with pity that so-and-so has fallen. A fish flees from the hook, and the pleasure-loving soul from solitude. When he wishes to bind certain people to one another with the bond of evil love, then

he tests both parties and casts into both of them love for one another; and if from the first they do not accept the thoughts of passion, then he begins first under the pretext of spiritual love, and afterwards, according to his own will, he kindles that furnace. Often those who were inclined to the love of pleasure

are merciful and tender-hearted, abounding in tears and loving; but those who strive for purity do not have these qualities in the same way as the former. A wise and intelligent man once asked me a question, saying to me:
Which sin is the heaviest of all sins, after murder and the denial of God?

And I said to him: falling into heresy. When heretics come to the catholic Church, to orthodoxy, and renounce and anathematize that heresy with all their heart, the Church immediately deems them worthy of communion in the holy mysteries,
but those who have fallen through fornication, even when they come to confession and abandon the deed, the canon of the apostles and fathers separates from communion for some length of time.
And I marveled at this hidden matter, and that hidden thing remained hidden and unexplained:

for what reason this happens. Let us search out and examine minutely, and understand, in the singing of the psalms, which is the sweetness that comes to us from the demon of fornication, and which is that which comes from the words

of the Holy Spirit and from the grace and power that are in them. Do not be deceived, O brother, you who are in your youth, for I have seen certain people who prayed with all their heart for those they loved, and did this with love and with the thought of fornication, and they supposed that they were fulfilling the remembrance and rule of love. Bodily defilement also comes about through touch, for more than that of the eyes and more than that of the hearing,

this sense of touch is heavier and is quickly able to bring on passion. Remember your own hand, and you too be afraid to put your hand even to natural things, both to your own natural parts and to the flesh of others. I suppose that no one is truly called holy
until he changes this earth and clay into gold, if only he is able, for it is difficult. When we lie down on our beds,
then let us be watchful, for then the mind alone, without the body, fights the demons,

and if it is a lover of pleasure, that mind quickly becomes a traitor to the soul from within. Let the remembrance of death lie down with you always, and prayer to the Lord Jesus, for there is no other such helper in sleep,
as these, nor will you find anything like them. Some say that battles and discharges come only from foods, but I see many who are gravely sick, and also those who fast rigorously, and
they are greatly defiled by discharges and battles. I once asked about this matter a certain experienced and discerning monk, and that blessed man taught me well,
that a discharge occurs in sleep,
from an abundance of food and from rest; and sometimes it comes from pride, when we grow arrogant because we have gone a long time without stumbling; and it comes also from judging one's neighbor,
-- and those two come upon the sick as well, though I think even all three do.
— But if someone sees himself cleansed of these causes and a fall still befalls him, blessed is that laborer of dispassion,

for it befalls him through the envy of the demons, since God permits this to befall him from time to time, so that through a sinless temptation he may gain lofty humility. Let no one dwell by day on the fantasies seen in sleep, for this too is a scheme and a device of the devil, so that through dreams they may defile us even while we are awake. Let us hear another device of the demons as well,
