for just as foods harmful to the body often harm us days and hours afterward, so sometimes it happens with the spiritual too,

for I have seen men who were living in comfort and rest and drinking wine, and at that time they had no battle, and they did this many times, and afterward, through this same cause, the enemies defiled the man's soul. I saw also men who ate and associated with women and felt no evil thought whatever in their hearts,
and as those deluded men grew confident and became carefree, at the time when they supposed that they had peace
and freedom from error in their own cell, then in an instant ruin came upon them.

But what that ruin is which comes upon us spiritually and bodily when we are alone, he who has experienced it knows, and he who has not experienced it has no need to know. At such a time a good help for us is the wearing of sackcloth,
and sitting on ashes, and standing firmly in prayer with hands raised, and hunger for bread,

and parching of the tongue with thirst, so that we moisten it only by measure, and staying among the tombs, and above all humility of heart, and, if we have the means at that time, take with you a spiritual father, or some elder, or a zealous brother who has acquired the mind of an elder, for I would be amazed

if a man alone could bring a great ship out of the deep into harbor. Often one and the same sin befalls two people, and the same fall is a hundredfold heavier for the one than for the other, owing to place and upbringing and spiritual measure, and many other things. Falls occur from many causes and in various forms, for some occur through being near harmful persons, and through looking at them;

and others from food; and others from arrogance; and others from many other causes. Someone told me of a marvelous deed and a measure of perfect purity, and he said that a certain man saw the face of a very beautiful woman and greatly glorified the Creator,
he marveled at the wisdom and power of the Maker, at what beauty he had made from clay and from nothing; and by the mere sight of her he came to a great love of God, and there flowed from him streams

[?] of tears; and it was a wondrous thing to see, for what was the ruin and downfall of others became for him a cause of crowning beyond nature. If such a person always has such a measure and such a mind in such matters,
then surely he has already risen with that incorruptible resurrection before the resurrection of all. The same thing happens with hymns and the services of the hours,
for the lovers of God come away from the singing into spiritual joy, love of God, and tears,
but the lovers of pleasure into passion and error. As we said before, the demon of fornication fiercely attacks some who have withdrawn and live in the desert, and this is no wonder,
for demons dwell much in deserts, since the Lord drove them out into the desert and the abyss for the sake of our life. The demons attack the solitary monk powerfully,

in order to persuade him that he has gained no profit from living in the desert, and so to lead him away into the world. The demons withdraw from us for a little while when we are among lay people, so that we may convince ourselves that we suffer no harm and may stay there, so that in this way the enemies may arrange the right moment for themselves and easily strike us down. In whatever matter and place the demons attack us, there let us also fight them, for if that matter and place were not grievous to them, why would they attack us over it?
But if, when they attack us, we do not fight but submit, it is clear that we are becoming their friends.

Many times, when we have gone out into the world for some need, the right hand of God shelters us through the prayer of our teacher, so that the name of God may not be blasphemed on our account; and sometimes, from hardness of heart, we do not perceive the warfare while we are in the world,

And because we had become glutted with looking and with harmful thoughts, we could not perceive the passion, since we were full of passion; or else [they say] that the demons of fornication depart from us of their own accord,
and leave us the demon of pride to fill their place. Hear further the device and machinations of that deceiver, all you who wish to gain purity,

for someone experienced in their deceits told me that many times the demon of fornication withdraws from a monk, and at the time when he is sitting with women it makes his heart tender, gives him a fountain of tears, and suggests to him that he teach them about the remembrance of death and judgment, and about purity and ascetic struggle,

so that through those words of compunction and that outward show they may run to that wolf as to a shepherd; and when familiarity and boldness have developed, then the fall comes upon that wretched man. Let us flee, brothers, let us flee, so as not to see
or hear of that fruit about which we have made a vow, and not to see its taste;
for I am amazed if we consider ourselves greater and stronger than David the prophet,
which is impossible. So great and lofty is that virtue of purity that the holy fathers even dared to give it the name of dispassion.
Some have said that it is impossible for a person to be called pure after falling into sin,
but I oppose them and say: Yes, it is possible. Just as it is possible and easy for anyone who wishes to make a wild olive tree domestic by grafting the sweet and good olive onto it,
so too purity is possible after sin. If the keys of the kingdom had been entrusted to someone who was a virgin in the flesh, those mentioned earlier might say so; but he puts them to shame
who had a mother-in-law, and yet became pure and was given the keys of the kingdom. Many are the stratagems of the demon of fornication, and many are his devices.

Those who have no experience of falling into sin, he instructs and tells them: “Try it just once, and then never go near it again.” But those who have fallen and have experience of sin, he reminds of the taste they experienced when they tasted it. Many who have no experience of sin feel no desire for it, because they do not know what the act is,
and there are many who have experienced that act of filth
who loathe it and do not even want to go near it;

and again, many who have no experience of it long to try it, while those who have experience are under attack through the memory of that taste and are overpowered by it. Many times we fall into a good sleep and rise in peace, for the holy angels invisibly protect us, especially when we have fallen asleep with prayer and much supplication; and many times again we fall asleep well,
and rise troubled by evil visions from the wicked demons.
And the one agitated and swollen within me [?] through fasting, as formerly his anger within me, in his place [?], when I humbled my mind,

[?] within me, its trace [?]. Whoever has conquered the flesh has conquered nature, and whoever has conquered nature has become higher than nature. And whoever has reached this measure is only a little lower than the angels,

and perhaps not lower in anything at all. It is no wonder [if …] fights [?]. But this is truly a great wonder: that one who is material, with this adversary [the body] and this heavy matter, overcomes immaterial and bodiless enemies. Know this too, beloved:
that this too God arranged out of his great care and mercy for us: that he placed upon women dread, shame and concealment,
and as with a bridle he "unbridled" [?] them by this, for if they had the boldness to approach men forcibly, no flesh would have been saved. One thing is the slight approach of a thought,
another is the mind's conversing together with the thought, another is assent, another is captivity, another is battle,
and another is what is called passion, as the holy fathers say; for thus the blessed ones say, that the approach
of a thought is this: when some trifling word, or some newly seen image, comes upon the heart;
and [the conversing] of the mind is this: when the mind begins to converse with that image that has come to the heart, whether with passion or without passion.
And [?] is a nod of desire by the soul toward what was seen. But this [?] is either the forced and violent seizure of the heart,
or a thought that has settled in us and corrupts that good order of ours. And there is [the state] when that thought and the person fight on equal terms, either conquering or being conquered.
But that is meant which has nested for a long time in the soul and in the thought, so that the mind has come to be accustomed to exercising itself in it,
and of its own accord goes toward it. And of all these, the first is without sin;
but the second not greatly so; and the third depends on the measure of the one who struggles; but the struggle becomes for him the captor [?] of either a crown or torment;

And captivity is judged one way at the time of prayer, another way at a time of leisure, one way in the case of evil thoughts, and another in the case of idle ones. But passion without doubt requires repentance equal to it, or else it is liable to eternal torment.

Now therefore, whoever contemplates the first without passion cuts off all the others at once. There is also spoken of by discerning fathers another thought, subtler than these, which some call a "flash" [?] of the mind,

which, without lapse of time, and without word, and without image, more swiftly than the recollection of all this, show to the soul in a hidden way some form of bare passion; and it makes its coming by some subtle and
timeless and untraceable recollection, and by some it is not perceived at all. Whoever has found such subtlety of it,
he is able to reveal to us and teach us whence or how there comes about, by the mere sight of the eyes,
and the touch of the hand, and the hearing of a voice,

without any thought, a fornication of the soul, passionately. Some say that from the thoughts of the heart the flesh comes to passion and arousal; and again others say that from the senses of the body evil thoughts are born;
and the first say that if the mind had not led the way for passion, the flesh would not have followed.

But the second bring forward the wickedness of bodily passion in support of their argument, and say that often through the sight of a face, or the touch of a hand, or the smelling of a fragrance, or the hearing of a sweet voice, thoughts come into the heart.

Whoever has power from the Lord, let him reveal to us and teach us the truth of these matters. For knowledge of such matters is very useful to those who struggle with understanding. But those who live their lives in simplicity and plainness

and in simplicity of heart have no need to investigate such things. For not everyone has understanding, nor does everyone have blessed simplicity. Rather, this is useful as armour (literally, “a chain”) against the cunning of the enemies. Some passions pass from the mind to the body,
and some again from the body to the mind, and the latter occurs with those in the world, but the former with those dwelling in the desert, for there are not
among them the material objects of the passions in visible form. -- But on this matter I,
say thus: when we fight hard against that demon of fornication, and drive him out of our heart with the stone of fasting, and torment him with the sword of humility,
then he remains in the body like some worm, and with untimely and idle arousal he stirs us up and wishes to defile us,
and this comes especially upon those who have yielded to that demon of pride. For since evil thoughts did not come continually into their heart, for this reason they came to pride.
And that this saying is true: when such people are in stillness, let them then examine themselves well, and they will find some thought in the depth of the heart,

like a snake hidden in dung. These passions suggest to people that they have achieved that small degree of purity of heart through their own strength and zeal. The wretched ones do not understand the saying
that it is given freely, whether by God’s grace or through the help and prayer of others. It is fitting for them that with great zeal [?]

drive this aforementioned snake out of their hearts with great humility, so that when they are freed from it, then perhaps they too may be able to strip off those garments of skin, and may sing to the Lord the victory hymn of purity, as once did those innocent children
who went out to meet Christ, the Lord of all; and when they are thus able to strip off those evil garments of skin,
they will not be found naked of their innocence and humility. This demon too lies in wait constantly, more than all the demons, and especially when we are unable to labor with the body,

and to pray well; then the unclean one fights us. Those who have not acquired true prayer of the heart are greatly helped by the bodily labor of prayer, that is, the stretching out of the hands, the beating of one's breast, gazing toward heaven with a fervent heart, much sighing, and forceful bending of the knees, which they are unable to do when they are in the company of people,
and for this reason, at such a time, the demons raise war against them,

since they are not yet able, by the invisible power of prayer and vigilance of mind, to overcome them and to strengthen themselves, and for this reason they are often defeated. Withdraw a little from people at that time, if it is possible,
hide for a short time, and lift up your gaze with the eye of the soul,

and if you cannot do this, then do so with the bodily eye: lift your eyes to heaven, stretch out your hands in the form of a cross without moving, so that by that figure too you may put Amalek to shame and prevail over him. Call out to the Mighty One to help you, not with worldly words but with words of humility,
crying out before all else, for then you will see power from on high, and you will invisibly drive away those invisible enemies with invisible help.

And whoever grows accustomed to fighting the enemies in this way will soon learn to overcome them by the spirit alone, without the body, for in place of the first this second is given by God to the laborers of righteousness.

I once went to a gathering of brethren, and there I saw a very zealous brother who was troubled by thoughts of fornication. And since he found no hidden place suitable for prayer, he made a pretext of going to the outside place where one goes for the needs of the body, and he stood there,
and for a long time he prayed, in order to fight the enemies;
But I reproached him for praying in such an indecent place. He told me that to drive out impure thoughts, in such a

foul-smelling place I prayed, so that I might escape the foulness. All the demons first strive to darken the mind. Then, once they have darkened the mind, they make a person do whatever they wish. For if they did not blind the eyes of the mind,

they could not steal that treasure. The demon of fornication does this more than all the others. Often he darkens the ruling mind and makes people do and say things in front of others, deeds and words that even madmen do not do.
For this reason, afterward, when they awaken in their minds, not only before those who saw them,

but even before themselves they are ashamed of those deeds and words and those obscene gestures, and they marvel at that blindness of theirs; and many, through such distress as this, have ceased from evil. Turn away and do not listen to that wicked one,

who, after a fall and the doing of some evil, would hinder you from prayer and fasting and vigil and cut off your hope. Rather, remember the word of the Lord which he spoke, that because of the importuning of that soul overpowered by the passions and afflicted by evil habits [?] from its enemies.

Drive away, beloved, that wicked enemy too, who says to you: "Satisfy that desire of yours, and afterwards you can turn to repentance, prayer, fasting and vigil; you can mourn again later and set your soul right." Drive him away from you. Many have done evil and were never able to come to repentance. Once their desires took hold of them, they could no longer free themselves, or else sudden death overtook them. Fornication hinders prayer, destroys boldness before God and darkens the mind. There is no one
who has conquered his own flesh except the one who has broken his own heart.

And there is no one who has broken his own heart except the one who has denied himself. For how can the heart not be broken once the self-will has completely died? There is a passionate man who is more passionate than the passionate: he confesses even his own defilements with relish and with passion. The foul thoughts of the heart, all of them about fornication, are born of the devil. Fasting heals them and drives them away,

and so does treating them as nothing, along with vigil, humility of heart and casting oneself down before God. But what am I to do now about all this? If I somehow bind this friend of mine, the flesh, and judge it as I would those other tyrants, I do not know how. Before I can bind it, it is set loose, and before I can torment it, I give in to it [?],
and before I have condemned it, I relent. How shall I become victor over what I love by nature? How shall I be freed from that to which I am forever
and I am bound. How can I kill what is to rise with me? How can I make incorruptible what has received a corruptible nature? What excuse can I give to something that has so many excuses?

If I bind it with fasting, I judge my neighbor, and I am handed over to it again. If I stop judging and win the victory in this, my heart grows proud again and I fall back into its hands. It is both my helper and my opponent, both friend and enemy, both supporter and adversary.
When I give it rest, it fights me, and when I press it hard, it grows weak. If I indulge it, it destroys me; and if I torment it, it does not endure it.
If I afflict it, I too fall into distress, and if I weaken it, I have nothing else by which to acquire the virtues.
I both fight it and love it. I both pursue it and hold it dear. O wonder, what is this mystery of mine,

What is this account of my compound nature, how I am both my own enemy and my own friend? But tell me, you yourself tell me, O my spouse, O my nature, for I do not wish to learn about you from another, but tell me yourself how I may escape from you unwounded,
how I may be able to drive away the natural battles that come from you, since I have promised Christ to be your enemy.
How may I become victor over your tyranny, since I wish to be the one who compels you? But it speaks thus to its soul: I will tell you nothing of such a kind

of which you are ignorant. But this much we both know: I have my own rest and comfort as the father of the outward heat, and deeds done before and habits as the father of the inward arousal. When I have conceived, I give birth [?]

falls, and they, once born, give birth through despair to death. If you understand and rightly recognize my weakness and yours, you have bound my hands; if you enslave the belly, you have bound my feet, so that I can no longer go forward.
And if you join yourself to obedience, you have parted from me, and if you acquire humility, you have cut off my head, for you have help from the Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever.
Amen. This is the fifteenth step. Whoever is in the flesh and reaches this step of chastity has died and risen again, and has already received here the image of that eternal incorruption.
Discourse by the same author on love of money. Chapter 16. Many wise men and spiritual teachers, after the tyrant mentioned before,
placed this many-headed dragon in their discourses,
and so that we unwise ones do not change the order set by those wise men, we have now followed their order. So let us say a little about this disease first, and then speak about health. Love of money
is the worship of idols and the daughter of unbelief. It foretells sickness, falsely fears old age and announces famine [?].
a foreteller of drought, and the mother of all evils. Love of silver is a despiser of the Gospel, a willing transgressor of its commandment. Whoever has acquired love has scattered his wealth,
but whoever says, "I have both,"
deceives himself. Whoever mourns for himself

has come to hate even his own body, and if the time comes, he will not spare even that. Do not say, "I am saving for the poor," for the kingdom of heaven was bought with two mites. A hospitable man and a lover of money met each other, and the second called the first foolish and wasteful out of vanity. Whoever has conquered this passion
has [?] cares [?]
... cut off; but whoever among them is bound can never pray with a pure heart. The beginning of love of money is the thought of almsgiving,

and its end is hatred of the poor. As long as he is gathering, he preaches almsgiving; but once he has gathered the wealth, his hands are closed. I have seen people poor in possessions who became rich in spirit, and through that joy they forgot bodily hardship. The monk who loves work is a stranger to listlessness, for he works every day,
and he remembers the saying of the Apostle, who says: "I ..." [?]
This is the sixteenth victory over the passions. Whoever has won it has gained love and has cut off cares.

Discourse of the same, on poverty. Chapter 17. Poverty is separation from cares and freedom from anxiety about life; it is an unhindered journey, faith in the commandments of the Lord, and estrangement from sorrow. The poor monk is a king of this world,
and his care is directed toward God,
and by his faith all are his servants; he says nothing to anyone about his needs,

and he receives everything from the hand of God. The poor monk is a son of dispassion, for what he has he counts as though he did not have it, and if he sees harm to the soul in a place, he counts those possessions as rubbish.
But he who feels sorrow over some bodily matter is not poor. The prayer of the poor monk is pure,

but the lover of possessions prays with his mind on the material things of the world. Those who live in obedience are strangers to the love of money, for those who have denied their very selves, what else could they acquire as their own? There is only one thing the poor must beware of,

for those who do not have an abundance of possessions are quickly overcome by going from place to place. I have seen possessions teach a monk patience through his love for them, but I, more than these,
call blessed those who go about for the Lord's sake rather than those who stay put for the sake of possessions,

yet if their patience is for love of the Lord, they are blessed. He who has tasted that heavenly sweetness will easily despise possessions, but he who has not tasted it rejoices over wealth. He who is poor out of ignorance, senselessly and like a beast, suffers loss on both counts, for he has lost this world and has not attained the eternal one. O monks, let us not be less in faith than the birds,
for they do not worry, nor do they gather, and they trust in him

who feeds them, the Lord of lords. Great is he who has left possessions for God's sake, but holy is he who leaves his own will, for the former will gain a hundredfold, whether in possessions or in graces, while the latter will inherit surpassing glory in eternal life. The sea will not lack waves, nor the lover of money anger and sorrow. He who has despised possessions
is freed from disputes, quarrels, and turmoil, but the lover of possessions will fight to the death over a needle. Firm faith destroys cares,
and the remembrance of death renounces even the body. There was in Job not so much as a trace of the love of money, and for this reason, when he lost everything, he remained untroubled.
The love of money is the root of all evils, and it is rightly so called, for hatred, thefts, murders, turmoils, enmities,

slanders, mercilessness, and envies are its doing. With a small fire some have burned a great deal of material, and by one virtue many have escaped all these passions; it is called hatred of possessions,
and it is born from tasting the knowledge of God and from concern about the account that is to be given at the time of our death. He is not ignorant,

Whoever has read carefully the words of the mother of all evils, which is gluttony — for that wicked one said that her second offspring is insensibility and hard-heartedness — [will know this]; but the many-headed serpent of idol-worship held me back from giving it its proper place,
for it has received from the fathers the third place in the chain of the eight evils, about which we have said this little;

and now we wish to speak about hard-heartedness and insensibility, and then about sleep and vigilance, and further about evil fearfulness, for all these are diseases of newcomers, from all of which may the Lord deliver us, to whom be glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.
This is the seventeenth step; whoever has gained this will ascend to heaven without hindrance.
A work of our holy father John, abbot of Sinai,

On hard-heartedness and insensibility, which is the death of the soul before the death of the body. Chapter 18. Hard-heartedness is the death of the mind and the slayer of the soul. Hard-heartedness is born of long-continued negligence, and negligence from idleness of heart and from love [?] and of sloth. Insensibility is confirmed negligence,

blindness of the mind, and the mother of evil habits, the snare of zeal and the trap of spiritual struggle, the enemy of compunction and the door of despair, the mother of forgetfulness, and the child of fearlessness toward God.
And after giving birth, it is the mother of its own mother. The hard-hearted and insensible man is a foolish philosopher,

The teacher is self-condemned, one who speaks against himself; the guide is blind: he does not see himself, yet he teaches others to see. He speaks of healing wounds, yet he keeps wounding himself without pause; he speaks of curing disease, yet he does not stop eating what is harmful. He curses the passions, and at once, right there, he turns back to the evil deed. He becomes angry,
and the wretch is not ashamed of his own words. He knows that he is doing evil, yet he stays in it; with his mouth he promises to do good, and in deed he does evil.
About death, wisely

he speaks, and conducts himself as though immortal; he sighs over the departure from this life, and slumbers as though [life here were] eternal and unending; he speaks about fasting, and strives after gluttony; he reads about judgment, and begins to smile.
He reads about pride, and in the very reading he is proud; he hears about vigilance, and gives himself over to sleep;
he extols prayer, and flees from it as from fire; he calls obedience blessed, and is himself disobedient before anyone else;
he praises hatred of possessions, and over a worthless rag he is not ashamed to make a disturbance. When he is disturbed, he grows angry,
And because of his anger he becomes angry again; he adds defeat upon defeat and does not notice it. When he has eaten his fill he repents, and as soon as an hour has passed he eats again.

He calls silence blessed, and praises it with much talking; he teaches about meekness, and in the middle of his own teaching he becomes angry. When he wakes up he sighs and shakes his head, yet he stays in the same passion. He hates laughter, yet he teaches about mourning while laughing.
before men he accuses himself of being proud, and by that self-accusation he buys praise from men.
He willingly looks at a face and teaches about purity; he praises recluses, and himself lives in the world and is not ashamed;

he glorifies the merciful and reproaches the poor; he constantly becomes his own accuser, and does not wish to come to understanding. I have seen many such people, who heard about death and the eternal torments and wept,
and while the tears were still in their eyes, they ran quickly to the table,
and I marvelled at how this bitter queen, the belly, that treasury of stench, strengthened by insensibility, had overpowered even mourning.
According to my small and feeble power I have revealed the wiles, wounds and deeds of this tyrant, who is like a rock and harder than iron,
for I am not able to say very much about it. But let whoever is able, by the Lord, to lay a remedy on those wounds,

not neglect to apply the remedies that come from him, for I am not ashamed in this matter to bear witness to my weakness, as one held fast by it; nor could I by myself have come to know its devices and wiles, unless I too had myself pressed it to confession.
But when I tortured it with the torture of the fear of the Lord and by unceasing prayer,
for this reason that tyrant and evildoer said: "My friends laugh when they see the dead, and in prayer they are like stones, hard-hearted and darkened.
And when they stand before the holy altar they are without understanding, and when they receive the holy mysteries they are as if eating plain bread.
I am the enemy of compunction, and I have learned from my father to kill all those good things that are born of courage and zeal.
I am the mother of laughter. I am the parent of sleep and the friend of satiety.

I am the companion of ostentation. When I am reproached I feel no compunction, nor do I heed anyone's teaching." But when I, wretched as I am, heard this, I marvelled at those words of that raving one, and I asked the name of its mother,
and it said: "I do not have one birth, but my birth is manifold and unstable. Satiety gives me strength, length of time makes me grow, evil habit strengthens me,
and whoever has it cannot be freed from me. But exercise yourself always, with much vigilance,
on the eternal judgment; perhaps you may find a little relief; and discern within yourself my mother, from where I am born, and fight against her,
for it is not from one mother that I am born in everyone.

Pray continually in the tombs, and inscribe the images of the dead indelibly on your heart, for if you do not write this within you with the pen of fasting, you will not overcome me forever and ever."
This is the eighteenth step of victory; whoever overcomes it has acquired mourning and tears.
Discourse of the same author.
On sleep and on prayer with many. Chapter 19. Sleep is a stay of nature,
and it is an image of death and an inactivity of the senses. Sleep is one, yet it has many divisions, just as desire does.
For it arises from nature, and from foods, and from demons, and sometimes from excessive fasting, by which the flesh is weakened,

and then let them console themselves with sleep. Just as heavy drinking depends on habit, so too excessive sleep comes from habit; for this reason let us struggle against it especially at the beginning of the monastic life, for it is hard to uproot a habit. Let us pay attention and we shall discover: when they sound that spiritual trumpet, which is the ringing for the hours,
then the brothers gather visibly for prayer, and the enemies gather invisibly for battle. For this reason, after the ringing the demons come up to us and say to us:
"Rest for one moment, until the first psalm has been said, and then go to church."
And again there are other demons who, when we have come to prayer, engulf us in sleep, and repeatedly draw us toward the needs of the body, to go outside beyond what is customary;
others urge us to chat in church, and others carry off our mind toward defiled
thoughts, and others make us lean against the wall as if we were weakened, and often send immoderate yawning upon us,
and some of them strive to provoke laughter during prayer, so that by it they may stir God to anger against us. Others

press us to hurry in saying the Psalms. Others make us proud over the singing of the office; others stir up in us a love of pleasure from the singing of the office; and again some of them fall upon our mouths,

and do not allow us to open our mouths and pray. Whoever sets it in his mind with firmness of heart, and so sees that he is truly standing before God when he prays, such a one stands unshaken like a pillar,

and is not harmed by even one of those things mentioned before. The truly obedient man, when he stands for prayer, often becomes wholly illumined and filled with joy, for he has been prepared beforehand by that blameless obedience and service.
And that struggler has been set aglow by it. I think that prayer in a multitude is possible for all, but for many it is better to pray with only one other person,
for praying alone is for very few. When you pray with a multitude, you cannot accomplish that immaterial and lofty prayer,
but let your mind have as its work understanding the words that you sing, or else have some set prayer, so that while your neighbor finishes the verse, you may say it in your
heart, when you sing verse by verse in turn. It is not right for anyone at all to do manual work during prayer, for the Angel who came to the blessed Anthony taught us this well,
for he does his handiwork and afterwards rises for prayer. Fire tests gold,
and standing in prayer tests a monk's reverence
and his love for God, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. Whoever has found blessed prayer draws near to God and is delivered from the demons.
By the same author: on bodily vigil, from which vigilance of the soul is born. Chapter 20. Before the kings of the earth,
some stand unarmed and in honor, and some with staffs, and some as swordbearers and armed men;

But great is the difference between the first and the last of these, for they are in far higher honor and rank than these second and third, because they are the beloved and intimate friends of the king.
And let us too come and see how we keep our standing before God and the Master in the prayers of evening, of day and of night.
For some, in the night vigil, stand in prayer with hands outstretched, immaterial and stripped of every care. Others complete their vigil with psalmody, and others are [?] in the reading of books,
and others do battle with sleep by means of handiwork,
and others complete the night with the remembrance of death, so that through it they may obtain compunction.
Of all these, the first and the last keep vigil with a great measure of the love of God; but the second and the third, who sing psalms and read, are on the very path of the monastic life,
while those who keep vigil at handiwork hold to a lesser path. Yet God accepts labors according to intention and ability, and gives graces. A wakeful eye has purified the mind, while

much sleep has hardened the heart and darkened the soul. The wakeful monk is an enemy of fornication, but the sleeper is its friend. Vigil is the crushing of hardness of heart and deliverance from dreams; it brings forth weeping and humbles the heart;
it is a guardian of thoughts and a digester of foods; a tormentor of demons;

a bridle of the tongue and a driver-away of fantasies. The wakeful monk is a hunter of thoughts, and in the stillness of the night he can easily see them and seize them. The God-loving monk, when they ring for the hour of prayer, will say:
"Hurrah, hurrah, for it is good!"

but the negligent and sluggish one says: "Woe is me, woe is me, for I am sleepy." The setting of the table tests the gluttons, and the struggle of prayer tests the lovers of God. When the glutton sees the table, he rushes to it leaping for joy,

but the one who loves prayer is late [?] in going to it. Much sleep brings forgetfulness, but vigil purifies the mind. The farmers' wealth is gathered on the threshing floor and in the winepress, but the wealth and understanding of monks are gathered in the prayers of the night
and in the contemplations of the mind. Much sleep is an evil spouse, for it robs the negligent of half of their life. The inexperienced monk stays awake for idle tales,
and when the hour of prayer arrives his eyes grow heavy. The dissolute monk is practiced and eager in much talking,
and when the reading of a book is brought forth, he can no longer lift up his eyes because of heavy sleep. The sound of the trumpet raises the dead,

and idle words awaken the negligent and dissolute. The tyrant of sleep is a treacherous friend, for at the time of eating and drinking it draws away from us, and at the time of fasting and prayer it fights us mightily. At the time of prayer it prompts us to do handiwork,
so that by this it may drive sleep away. It fights hard against those newly come to the monastic life, so that from the very beginning it may teach them dissoluteness,
or so that it may prepare them for the demon of fornication. Until we are freed from this, let us not neglect prayer together with the many,

for many times we have not let ourselves sleep out of shame. The enemy of the hare is sleep [?], and the enemy of sleep is the demon of vainglory. After trading, the merchant counts his profit; and the vigilant and zealous monk, after his rule of prayer, counts his profit. Stay alert after prayer, with zeal,

And then you will see a multitude of demons set upon us, so that they may sow among us filthy thoughts of the heart, for they take revenge on us because we struggle in prayer. Again, sit as a watchman, and you will see those who

are always ready to snatch away the firstborn fruits of the soul. Many times, out of habit, we have practiced the words of the psalms in our sleep, and again, many times the demons do this, so as to bring us to pride;
but the third thing I did not wish to say, yet someone compelled me to say it: that the soul which unceasingly practices the words of the Lord even in sleep,
remains in the same,
for the Lord, on account of the first, graciously grants this second as a means of driving away the fantasies of evil spirits. If you are living in a community of brothers,
and there carry out the virtue of vigil,
the demon of cowardice will not fight you much; but if you are living in solitary, remote places, strive that the offspring of vainglory and daughter of unbelief may not rule over you,
which is fear, which we will overcome if we always flee to the Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. Whoever has climbed the twentieth step receives light in his heart.

Discourse of the same, on cowardice. Chapter 21. Cowardice is a childish habit in a vainglorious soul. Cowardice is a turning aside from faith through expecting things not to be expected. The coward imagines hardships before they happen. The coward crushes his own heart with fear of fantasies. Cowardice is the destroyer of hope. The proud soul is a slave of cowardice,
for it trusts in its own strength, and when it hears some sound, it immediately trembles. Those who mourn and are pained in heart do not know fear at all;
but many of the proud have been driven out of their wits by fear,
for the Lord justly hands over the proud to chastisement, so that others too may become afraid because of them,
and may learn humility. Every coward is vainglorious, but not everyone who is unafraid is humble,

for robbers and grave-breakers too are not quickly frightened. As for places in which you are afraid, do not hesitate to go there at night, for if you give way to this demon, this childish and contemptible habit will grow old with you. As you go, arm yourself with prayer, and when you reach
that place,
stretch out your hands and scourge the enemies with the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

for there is no weapon stronger than it, either in heaven or on earth. When you are freed from this sickness, glorify the Savior, for if you give thanks to him he will protect you forever. You cannot fill your belly once so that you never again need food, and neither can you conquer cowardice once so that it never comes upon you again. In proportion to mourning, this is driven away, and as much as mourning diminishes in us, cowardice increases.
[?] my [?], said Eliphaz, concerning the devices of this enemy,
And so I too say this. Sometimes the soul is the first to be afraid, and sometimes the body first, and the second shares in the passion of whichever received it first. When the body trembles,
and that fear does not enter into the soul, then deliverance from this sickness is near.

But when, with a heart crushed by all kinds of unexpected afflictions and apparitions, we expose ourselves without fear and count all of it as nothing, then we have truly been set free from fear. It is not the darkness of the night or the desolation of the place that makes the demons strong against us, but the barrenness of the soul,
and sometimes also, by divine dispensation, the instruction that comes through God's permission. Whoever is a servant of God fears only his own Master, but whoever does not fear Him,
that one will be frightened even of his own shadow. When an evil spirit comes upon a person, the body trembles;
but when an angel comes, the soul rejoices in humility;
therefore it behooves us to recognize his coming by this sign, and at that moment to hasten immediately to prayer, for a good guardian has come to us from the Lord,
to whom be glory now and always and unto the ages of ages.
Amen.
Discourse of our holy father John, on vainglory. Chapter 22. Some say

that vainglory and pride are separate from one another. For this reason they name eight chief passions: first they name the passion of gluttony; second, fornication; third, love of money; fourth, anger; fifth, despondency; sixth, sorrow; seventh, vainglory;
the eighth pride. But Gregory the Theologian and many others, on the other hand, speak of seven of these passions;

for they count vainglory and pride as one, and I am more inclined to agree with them, for there is no one who has conquered vainglory who would then be conquered by pride. For these two differ from each other only as much as a small child differs by nature from a grown man, or wheat from flour. For the first is the beginning,
and the second is the end. Now then, concerning this beginning and end of the passions, this unholy haughtiness, let us speak briefly at the proper time,
for whoever philosophizes about it at length is like a man who weighs the winds. Vainglory in its outward form is a change of nature, a perversion of good customs, and
a flight from blame. But by its nature it scatters a person's labours, wastes his sweat, steals spiritual treasures, and is the offspring of unbelief,
and the forerunner of pride. It is shipwreck inside the harbour. It is an ant on the threshing floor, for it is small, yet it spoils all fruit and all labour. The ant waits for the wheat to ripen,

and vainglory waits for the monk's wealth to be gathered. The ant rejoices so that it may find and steal, but the vainglorious one rejoices so that he may destroy and scatter. The demon of despair rejoices over a multitude of evils, but the demon of vainglory over a multitude of virtues. The daughter of the first is a multitude of wounds,
but the daughter of the second is a multitude of labours. Pay attention and you will find that wicked thing never leaving you until the grave, in your clothing and in your gait,
and in every deed. The sun shines ungrudgingly upon all, and vainglory is found in all deeds; for when I fast my mind is exalted, and when I break my fast,
so that my fasting may not become known, my mind is exalted again over this, because I am wise;

when I put on fine clothing I am exalted, and when I put on old clothing my mind is exalted just the same; when I keep silent I am exalted, and when I speak I am the same. Wherever one throws this wicked caltrop, on every side its spike is found pointing upward to wound the soul. The vainglorious person within Christianity is an idol-
[?] a servant, for he supposes that he believes in God, but he hastens to please people and not God. The vainglorious person shows off everything. His fasting brings no reward,
and his prayer brings no profit, for he does both for people's praise. The vainglorious ascetic suffers a double loss,

for he torments his own body and has no reward. Who would not laugh, and even more, who would not lament, at the one who labours for vainglory? For because of it, at prayer, he sometimes laughs and sometimes weeps in front of everyone. God often hides from us whatever virtues we may have, so that we may acquire humility. For the person who praises us,

or rather the one who leads us astray, by that praise opens our eyes to see our wealth, and once our eyes are opened, all that wealth perishes and vanishes. The person who praises someone to his face is an apostle of the devil and a guide to pride. He destroys compunction,
destroys good things, and leads people astray from the way, as the prophet Isaiah says. Great is the person
who takes insult upon himself with joy; but holy and honourable is the one who turns himself away from praise without being harmed. I have seen mourners who were insulted by others,
and they were moved to anger, and as in a market they bought passion with passion.
Therefore let all be ashamed who

praise a person to his face. When you hear that your friend has spoken ill of you, then show love toward him. It is a great thing to drive the praise of men from the soul, but higher still is to be rid [?] of the praise of demons. Humility has been shown,
not by one who humbles himself, for how would he not bear with himself? But that person has shown humility,

who is reviled by others and endures it and does not change his love toward them. I set my mind to observing the demon of vainglory, and I saw that he suggested thoughts to one brother, then went and revealed to another brother what he had suggested to him, and then sent the first brother to the second so that he might tell him those thoughts, and then he called them blessed, as one who knows hidden things. Often that unclean one also touches the members of the body,

and sows his wiles among them, and through the twitching of the members deludes a person with fantasies about things to come. When he suggests to you the office of bishop or of superior, do not accept it, for it is hard to drive a dog away from places where there is meat. When we have spent a little time in the desert in solitude and in peace, then our enemy tells us to go to the world, and says to us: "Go, so that you may rescue those perishing souls and save them." The appearance of an Indian is one thing, and that of a white man is another;
and likewise the form of vainglory of those who dwell in monasteries is one thing, and that of those who dwell in deserts is another.

When people of the world come to the monastery, the demon of vainglory gets there ahead of them and persuades the foolish monks to go out and meet them. He persuades them to fall down before their feet, and they lay claim to humility,

though full of pride, and they adorn themselves before them with an appearance of meekness, but their minds are bound by those people's riches, in the hope of getting something from them; and they call them lords, and tell them that after God we have no life except from your hands. When they sit down at table, vainglory tells them to fast, and they mercilessly rebuke those lesser than themselves. When they stand up to pray, it makes the lazy vigorous, the voiceless fine of voice, and the drowsy wakeful,

and they ask the steward of the church for the honor of distinction: the reading of the book, the leading of the psalm and the presenting of the hypakoe; and they call him teacher and father until those laymen depart. If they are honored by the steward as they requested, they become proud, and if he slights them, they bear a grudge against him for a long time. After the departure of the laymen, that demon of vainglory turns their hearts to disobedience and makes them wrathful and quarrelsome toward everyone. Vainglory often brings disgrace instead of honor, for when their disciples become angry, they bring great shame upon them. Vainglory often changes the harsh into the meek.
It advances upon natural qualities, and through them it often casts down the wretched;

I saw a demon that afflicted and drove out his fellow demon. For certain brothers became angry with one another, and while they were still in the uproar, some people arrived, and they immediately ceased that uproar, not for God's sake but for vainglory's sake; and they came out of anger and were sold to vainglory,

for those wretched ones could not serve both at once. The vainglorious person conducts himself among monks in rule of life and in body, but in mind and in deed he is among the people of the world. Beloved, if we hasten toward heavenly goods,
Let us also taste the glory of heaven,

for whoever tastes that glory will despise all the glory of the earth. For I would marvel if anyone were to despise this vain and passing thing without having tasted that glory. Many times vainglory has taken us captive, and then we turned back and took it captive in a better way,

for I have seen some who began spiritual work out of vainglory, and though its beginning was bad, its end became good and praiseworthy, when those who were doing it changed their mind from pride to humility. Whoever is proud on account of natural things,

that is, on account of being well educated, and of skillfulness, and of reading well, and of knowledgeable understanding, and of a good voice and beauty of face and stature, and of things similar to these, such a person will never attain those good things that surpass nature, for

Many men have crushed and worn down their bodies in order to conquer the passions, and they acquired the grace of working miracles and the power of prophecy, yet they did not acquire humility, and the wretched men did not understand that it is not labors, but rather humility, that is the mother of such things. Whoever asks God for gifts as a reward for his labors has laid a bad and weak foundation for himself,

But whoever counts himself liable to tribulations and labours will receive that great wealth at an unexpected and unknown time. Beloved, do not accept the demon of vainglory when he tells you, "Make your virtues known, so that it may be of benefit

to those who see them." For what benefit would it be? Nothing builds people up as much as humility, a good bearing, and sweet and gentle words. Such a bearing also becomes a model for others, and not a model of vainglory. What could be of greater benefit than this? A certain holy and experienced elder related,

and he said: I was once in an assembly of the brothers, and the demons of vainglory and of pride came, one on my right and one on my left. And the one kept poking me in the side with his vainglorious finger,
and urging me to tell those present some vision or ascetic struggle that I had undertaken in the desert. But I drove him away and said to him: [?]
And immediately the second one spoke into my left ear, saying: [?]
for you have become great, in that you drove away that shameless mother of mine and conquered her;
But I answered him with the verse that follows the one quoted earlier,
saying: [?] do. I asked that same elder, and said to him: How is vainglory the mother of pride? And he answered and said to me: Praise lifts up a person's soul,
and when the soul has been lifted up, then pride seizes it and raises it up to heaven, and from there brings it down to the abyss,
and to the lowest depths of hell. There is a glory given by God, as it is written: [?] And again there is another glory that comes by the contrivance of the devil,
as it is said: [?] If you wish to recognize the glory that comes from God, you will recognize it in this way: when you regard that glory as harmful, and flee from it by every possible means,
and conceal your way of life wherever you go;

But diabolical glory is recognized in this way: when you wish that people may see your virtue. That foul one persuades us to lay claim before people to virtues that we have not acquired, and he reminds us of the word of the Gospel, which says:

Many times God delivers those who love him from vainglory by means of the reproaches and humiliations that come upon them from people. The beginning of freedom from pride is guarding the mouth and loving humiliation and reproach; the middle is giving up every deed that brings vainglory;

but its perfect measure, if indeed it can be found at all, the end of the abyss, is this: that a person should seek with all his strength insult, reproach, and contempt. Do not conceal, beloved, your faults, the showing of which might be thought a stumbling block. It is not right to apply one medicine to every wound,
but one medicine is needed when we ourselves attract glory to ourselves, and another when it comes to us from others without our attracting it. When we undertake to do deeds
of any kind that bring vainglory, then let us remember our mourning, and the fear of standing in prayer in our cell,

and without doubt we will put that shameless one to shame, if only we take care for true prayer. But if we cannot acquire this disposition of heart, then let us remember the shame that follows vainglory, both here and in the age to come. When those who praise us, and still more those who deceive us, begin to praise us,
then let us inwardly remember our sins and the multitude of our iniquities, and so recognize our unworthiness. Often the vainglorious ask for something, and
it is fitting that their request be granted them; for this reason the Lord anticipates them and gives them the thing before they ask, so that they may not obtain it by their own prayer

and add to their pride. The simple do not fall much into this venom, for vainglory drives away simplicity, and it is a life filled with guile and crookedness. There is a certain worm which, when it has grown,
puts forth wings and flies up to the heights;
and vainglory, when it has been brought to completion, gives birth to pride, the beginning and completer of all evils. One who does not have this disease is very near to salvation,
but one seized by it appears far from the glory of the saints.
On the twenty-second step: whoever is not seized by haughtiness will not fall by senseless pride, the enemy and hater of God.
On pride,
[?] together with which it also speaks about blasphemy. Chapter 23. Pride is the denial of God and friendship with demons. It is the despiser of people,
mother of judging, offspring of praises; a form of barrenness, driver-away of God's help, forerunner of bewilderment, and bringer of loss of reason;
cause of falls and of madness; source of anger; door of faithlessness; stronghold of demons;
the guardian of sins, the mother of mercilessness, ignorance of mercy, a bitter answerer, a merciless judge, the adversary of God,

and the root of blasphemy. The beginning of pride is the end of vainglory. Its middle is contempt for one's neighbour, shamelessly proclaiming one's own labours, praising oneself in one's heart, and hating reproof. Its completion is rejecting God's help, rejoicing in one's own deeds, trusting in one's own strength, and a demonic mind. Let us all hear

all who wish to escape from this evil pit: at first this passion takes its beginning from thanksgiving to God, for it cannot at the outset shamelessly suggest to a person that he deny God. I have seen people
who thanked God with their mouths and exalted themselves in their minds, and a witness to this is that Pharisee who said:

Wherever a fall has occurred, know that pride first took possession there, for this second thing is the herald of the first. I heard a man, one of the teachers, saying: "I have understood it in this way: as if the number of the unholy passions were twelve,
if you willingly accept one of them, namely pride, it will fill the place of the other eleven." A proud monk is talkative and quarrelsome,
but a humble one is altogether quiet and silent. As a cypress never bends its height to the ground, so a proud monk never acquires obedience. A proud monk longs for leadership,

for in no other way does he find destruction so quickly. He regards himself as humble, yet he is overcome and filled with pride. If so, who then could have mercy on such wretched people? If so, who else would love him? The chastisement of the proud is a fall into sin, their tormentor is the devil, and their sickness is complete departure from the mind and madness;
and the first of these may perhaps be healed even by people,
but the second is incurable by people. Everyone who flees from reproof and is agitated by it testifies, being such a person, himself
to his own passion; but whoever hastens toward reproof is quickly released from his bonds. If, without any other passion, through pride alone the devil fell from heaven, let us understand
that it is possible to ascend to heaven through humility alone, without any other virtue. Pride destroys the sweat of one's labours and one's spiritual wealth.

because they cried out in pride, because they did not cut off the causes of the things they were crying out for. A certain spiritual elder was instructing a proud brother, but that blinded man answered, "Forgive me, father,
I am not proud." But the all-wise elder said to him, "What is this, child? May the Lord forgive you. Now you have convinced me that you are proud,

for you yourself testified to it when you said, 'I am not proud.'" For such people, obedience, a humble and despised way of life, and reading about the virtues of the fathers that surpass nature are very beneficial. Perhaps in this way they may have some hope of salvation. It is shameful to be vain about someone else's adornment, and it is utter folly to be proud of the graces and gifts of God. If you had some good thing before your birth and your coming into the world, then be vain about it,
If not, the graces acquired after birth God has given you, who granted you both that birth itself and the coming from non-being into being.
As many virtues as you have accomplished apart from your mind, without your mind being of use to you in them, for those exalt yourself, for they alone are yours;

but as many as your mind has served you as a helper in, those are not yours, for the mind is given by God. As many labors as you have performed without your body, those alone have been done by your own diligence,
but those that you have done with your body are not yours, for the body is not yours but was created by God. Do not be confident about your days,

until the sentence concerning you has gone forth, since you hear of him who, after entering the wedding chamber and [?] sitting with those who were invited [?]. Do not exalt yourself, however much you may labor, O clay and earth-born one,
for many who were bodiless and immaterial fell down from heaven. When the devil finds a place among his workers,
then he comes to them in sleep, or even while they are awake, as if in the form of an angel or of a martyr, and reveals mysteries to them and bestows graces,

so that the wretched one may be deceived and his mind led completely astray. Even if we were to die ten thousand times for Christ, we would not yet have paid our debt, for the blood of God is one thing,

and the blood of the servant is something else, according to the nature of his flesh and not according to the Godhead. [?] Know, brothers, that if we were to judge and examine ourselves, we would find ourselves altogether
not having come near the footsteps of the early fathers, nor keeping the vow of monastic life well,

For until now, if we understand it rightly, we are still living within the passions of the world. The true monk is this: an eye of the soul that is not carried off this way and that, and an unshaken desire for God. The monk is he who rejoices at the onset of battles as a hunter rejoices at finding game, and who provokes them by pretending to flee, so that they will come against him. The monk is he
who all the days of his life is caught up in mind toward God, and always grieves over this life. The monk is he who longs for the virtues as much
as lovers of pleasure long for their lusts. The monk is he whose eye of the soul is unclouded [?] and bright. The monk is he

who has made his soul an abyss of humility, and in it every spirit of the passions is drowned and choked. Haughtiness brings forgetfulness of sins, for remembering them brings humility. Pride is the utter poverty of the soul,

for in dreams and in darkness it imagines itself rich, but when it wakes up and the light shines on it, then it learns that it does not even have bread. There are men who boast of wealth and have nothing, and there are others who humble themselves in the midst of great wealth. This foul one not only does not let a person make progress, but even casts him down from the height.
The proud man is a pomegranate, beautiful outside and rotten inside. For a proud monk no devil is needed;
For he himself is the enemy and adversary of his own self. As darkness is alien to light, so the proud monk is alien to all virtue. In the soul of the proud are born words of blasphemy,
but in the soul of the humble, visions of heaven. The thief hates the sun,

and the proud man hates meekness and humility. The proud have gone astray, I do not know how, and have counted themselves free of passion, and at the hour of death they discovered their own poverty. Whoever has fallen into the bondage of this chain, it befits such a one to make great supplication to God with weeping, that He may deliver him from that cave of darkness, for it is vain for men to help such a one unless the Lord helps him. I once found this headless one,
who was dwelling in my heart and was lifted up on the shoulders of his mother; I hunted him with the snare of obedience,

and I tormented them with the torment of humility, and I asked them to tell me how their entry into me comes about, by what kind of door. And when they were tormented, they answered and said to me: "We have no beginning
and no birth, for we are the beginnings and begetters of all the passions. But contrition of heart, born of obedience, fights against us not a little,
for we have learned obedience to no one. For this reason we were created as rulers in the heavens, and
we fell from there because of our disobedience. Therefore, to say it all at once, of all the deeds that stand against humility we are the begetters, for all those that assist it
stand against us. We caused turmoil even in the heavens, and you, where will you go to escape from our presence?
We have many times entered the heart even by way of dishonor, and of obedience, and of freedom from anger, and of not remembering wrongs, and of ascetic labor.
Our offspring are the falls of souls: anger and the remembrance of wrongs, wrath and blasphemy, loud shouting and duplicity, hatred and envy, contradiction and self-will, and disobedience.

There is only one thing that we are unable to overcome, and we will tell it to you: if you always accuse yourself before God in purity, know that you will see us melted before you like a spider's web. For as you see, the horse of pride is vainglory, but true humility and self-accusation will put both the horse and its rider to scorn, and they will sweetly sing the song of victory to the Lord, saying:
[?] and to the abyss of humility, whose is the glory, now and always and forever and ever.
Amen. Step twenty-three. Whoever ascends it, if only he is able to ascend, will become strong.
Discourse of the same, on those unspeakable thoughts of blasphemy. Chapter 23. From an evil root we have heard of an evil branch,
in the chapter spoken before this, for foul pride said

that its offspring is the unspeakable evil of blasphemy. Therefore it is necessary to bring this into the open as well, for its evil is not small but very great indeed, and worse than all the passions,
and it is so much worse that it is not even possible to speak of it easily, or to confess and expose it before a spiritual physician.
For this reason it has become the begetter of despair for many, for just as a worm does to wood,

In the same way the unclean one drains away all the power of their hope. This foul and wicked one often comes upon us at the time of the holy liturgy, and at the very moment of communion in the holy mysteries he wars against us, driving us to blaspheme the Lord and that holy offering. Because of this, let us understand all the more
that it is not our own soul that invents such incomprehensible and unspeakable evils,
but that those words belong to the God-hating devil, who fell down from heaven because he was a blasphemer of the Lord.
For if those foul words were ours, how could we receive those gifts with worship and thanksgiving? How is it possible to have both blessing and slander at once?

Many times this deceiver has driven many people completely out of their minds and made them demon-possessed, for no other thought is as hard to confess as this one, and for this reason it has even grown old with many people.

And nothing so strengthens the demons and the thoughts against us as concealing those demonic battles. Let no one think that the cause of those thoughts of blasphemy comes from himself, for the Lord is the knower of hearts and knows that not ours,
but our enemies' are those words that come upon us. Drunkenness is the cause of the stumbling of the feet,
and likewise pride is the cause of such evil thoughts. A man is blameless for the stumbling itself,
but for the drunkenness he becomes guilty and is punished. When we stand to pray, those unclean and unspeakable thoughts rise up against us,
and as soon as we have finished the prayer they depart at once, for those who do not fight against them,

nor do they [?] fight. This godless one not only blasphemes God and divine things, but also speaks certain foul and shameful things in our hearts, so that we might either abandon prayer or cut ourselves off from hope. He has hindered many from prayer,
and has turned many back from communion in the holy mysteries, and has wasted away the bodies of some with grief,
and others this evil, man-hating tyrant has weakened through fasting, and he has shown them no mercy at all.
And not only upon laypeople, but upon monks too

he has brought this. Then he cuts off their hope and tells them: "There is no longer any hope of your salvation; you have become worse than unbelievers and pagans." Whoever is tormented by the demon of blasphemy, let him understand that his own soul is not the cause of those thoughts,
but the unclean demon, who said to the Lord:
Therefore let us too disregard him, and let his words not be counted against us in any way, but let us say to him: "I worship and serve my own;

but this evil word of yours will turn back upon you, and your blasphemy too, both now and in the age to come. Whoever wishes to fight the demon of blasphemy without the word spoken above is like a man who wishes to catch lightning with his hand. For how will he catch
or how will he resist and answer the one who passes through the heart in an instant like wind,

And in the twinkling of an eye he sows that word and vanishes. All the other battles take their stand, fight, and linger, and give time to whoever wishes to fight them. But this one is not like that: as soon as it appears it vanishes, and as soon as the word is spoken it hides from us. Many times this demon has come to upright and innocent minds and troubled them,
those minds which are disturbed and stirred up the most. For this reason we say that it does not always arise from pride, but sometimes it also comes about from the envy of the demons.

Let us beware of judging our neighbor, and let us not be disturbed by the blasphemous words of the heart, for the first is the cause and root of the second. Just as someone who is shut up inside a house hears the words of those passing by outside, and answers them nothing,
so the soul shut up in the body hears the blasphemies of the demons, which they speak as they pass by that soul, and it becomes disturbed. Whoever despises this demon is freed from it;
but whoever wishes to fight it in any other way, it will remain in him forever,
for whoever wishes to seize an unclean spirit is like a man
who wishes to seize the winds. There was a certain zealous monk whom this demon fought for twenty years, and he wasted his flesh with fasting and vigils; and when he found no relief,
he wrote that passion down on a sheet of paper, brought it to a certain holy elder, and fell at his feet, and he could not look at him.
But when the elder had read it, he smiled, raised the brother up, and said to him: "Put your hand on my neck, my son."
And when the brother did this, the elder said to him: "Let this sin be on me, brother, however many years it has remained with you; only do not count it against yourself at all."

And that brother told me with full assurance: "I had not yet gone out of the elder's cell when that passion vanished." This [?] that brother made known to me, and great thanks be to God the most merciful, whose is the glory for ever and ever. Amen. Whoever has gained victory over this passion has cast out pride.
Discourse of the same author on meekness, simplicity and innocence,

which do not arise from nature but are acquired through diligence and labor; and on crookedness. Chapter 24. Light goes before the sun; the virtue of meekness goes before all humility. Therefore let us listen to that true Light, who sets them in order in this way, for he says it. Now therefore it is necessary
that we first be illumined by the light of the sun, and only afterwards look well upon the sun; for just as it is impossible to see the sun without light,

Likewise it is impossible to find humility without meekness. Meekness is an unchanging calm of the mind, which stays the same in honor and in dishonor. Meekness is this: when your neighbor reviles you and insults you, you, with all your soul,

pray for him with a purified heart. Meekness is a rock lying high above the sea of anger, which breaks all the waves that come from it and is itself not shaken at all. Meekness is the endurance of all trials with thanksgiving and joy.

Meekness is the firmness of patience and the door of love, or rather its mother, and it is the power of understanding, for it is said that: [?] It is the bringer of the forgiveness of sins and boldness in prayer; it is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit;
For the Holy Spirit says.

that: Meekness is a helper of obedience; it is a leader of the fear of God; a bridle on anger, a dissolver of wrath, an increaser of joy; it is a likeness of Christ, the character of angels [?], a fetter for demons, and a weapon against the passions. Upon the soul of the humble and meek the Lord will rest,
but the soul of the turbulent man is a throne of the devil. And the wrathful will be driven out of their land. The soul of the meek man
is a throne of simplicity, but the wrathful mind is a worker of wickedness and perversity. The meek soul will receive words of wisdom, for: [?]

and still more understanding. The simple soul is the consort of humility, but the perverse soul is the companion of pride. The souls of the meek will be filled with understanding, but the mind of the wrathful man with darkness and with [?] (the text reads "understanding"). The wrathful man and the scoffer [?]
have met with one another [?], and no word of simplicity was found in their thoughts.

If you open the heart of the first, you will find the remembrance of wrongs; and if you search the soul of the second, you will find cunning. Simplicity is a simple state of the soul, unmoved toward evil. Malice is a devilish art and their deformity, separated from truth. Duplicity is an evil state that darkens the soul and the mind, composed of every kind of crookedness. Simplicity is a guileless mind, an unfeigned face, and a true word, not contrived and not rehearsed beforehand. Innocence is a cheerful state of the soul, entirely separated from all cunning. Innocence is the nature of the Holy Spirit,
who are just as they were created, and who are kind, gentle, and untroubled toward everyone. Crookedness is a departure from simplicity, and a mind gone astray;
a word made up of lies, and false oaths; it is an abyss of scheming and of the remembrance of wrongs, a school of cunning, and lying by craft,
an enemy of judgment and obedience, a bringer of falls, an opponent of humility, confirmed pride, a making of a show of repentance,

a departure from mourning, an enemy of confession, a lover of self-will, an opponent of dispassion, a smiling at insults, a foolish sorrow, a contrived reverence, and a devilish life. The perverse man
is a companion and friend of the devil; therefore the Lord commands us concerning such a one
to say: Flee from the abyss, from wickedness, and from the cave of perversity, for it is written that: [?]
and: [?] for such as these are the pasture of the devil. As God is called Love,
so also is he called Simplicity; therefore that all-wise speaker of the Song of Songs says to that holy heart that [?] which is God; and again, the all-wise father of that wise man says that: [?]
and concerning the life of such as these he says that [?]; and again it is written that [?] of souls. Nothing at all is like Simplicity;
therefore, as long as Adam had it, he did not see the nakedness of his soul,
nor does it find its own flesh shameful. Good and blessed is that simplicity which is by nature, yet it is not of the same kind as that which has come from wickedness to simplicity by toil and sweat,

for the first is protected from wickedness and the passions, but the second is the bestower of great humility and meekness; and the reward of the first is not great, whereas that of the second is more exalted. All you who wish to gain the Lord sincerely and without guile,
approach him also with a simple and pure heart;
for since he is simple and not compounded, therefore he seeks simple

and innocent souls as well, for nowhere is simplicity and sincerity found separated from humility. A wicked and crafty man, a knower of hidden things, is a liar, for from words he speaks of the visions of the mind, and from outward appearances he boasts of knowing the thoughts of the heart. I have seen sincere people who learned craftiness and perversity from the crafty and perverse,

and I marveled at how a natural thing could be lost so suddenly. As quickly as the upright are turned to scheming, so hard is it for the scheming and crooked to come to simplicity. True exile from the world, and obedience,

and silence have been able to do many impossible things and have healed many who were incurable. If learning and knowledge puff many people up, then perhaps lack of learning often humbles some, for a man cannot be proud of his lack of learning. The pattern and true image of simplicity was the blessed Paul the Simple,
the disciple of the great Anthony,
for no one anywhere has seen such a person advance in so short a time,
nor will anyone see one. A simple monk is a rational sheep, and he lays his whole burden on the shoulders of his teacher. A sheep gives no answer to its shepherd;
nor does a simple soul answer its superior, but it follows that shepherd wherever he wishes, and it does not know how to answer back, even to the point of slaughter.

And with difficulty do those senseless ones, wise in perversity, draw near to meekness. Falls have often converted the perverse, and have brought them life and innocence against their will. Strive, brother,
to make yourself a fool, and to abandon that vain wisdom of yours, and so find life and simplicity;
through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and ever and unto ages of ages.
Amen. Whoever has gained the victory on this step, let him be bold; since he has become an imitator of Christ, he has attained salvation.

A discourse by the same on blessed humility, the destroyer [?] and ruiner [?] of the passions. Chapter 25. Whoever wishes to reveal by word to the ignorant and make known that true love of God in truth, and all-holy humility openly,
and that blessed purity and that radiance which comes from God, and his unfailing fear,
and that divine assurance which comes to be in the heart;
such a person is like a man who wishes by word and parable to show the sweetness of honey to those who have never at all experienced the taste of honey;

And this second one, who tries to convey the sweetness of honey in words, speaks much in vain. But the first either has no experience at all of the words and deeds he interprets, or is strongly reproached for vain arrogance. Once, in the assembly of the fathers, there was brought in for investigation a treasure stored in clay vessels, or rather in bodies of clay,
whose nature could not be known by word, and only the inscription of its name was known, which is: blessed Humility. And all who walked by the Spirit of God gathered at that spiritual tribunal,
and each brought tablets written by God, and with them tablets of wisdom and knowledge, and a great investigation took place to learn what is the nature of that blessed Humility.
And some said: Humility is the cautious forgetting of one's own good deeds. And others said: Humility is for a person to reckon himself the very last and the most sinful of all.
And others said: Humility is the good knowledge of one's own weakness. And others said: Humility is this, that a person should be the first to fall down before his neighbor in a time of anger.

And others said: Humility is the knowledge of the grace and mercy of God. And others said that Humility is the knowledge of the grace and mercy of God. And others said that Humility is the knowledge of a contrite soul and the renunciation of one's own will.
But when I heard all this and diligently examined within myself the nature of that blessed thing, I could not understand it from these words.
Therefore I, the last of all, like a dog, licked up the crumbs fallen from the table and from the mouths of those blessed ones; and I set this down and say concerning this matter:
Humility is an ineffable grace, known only to those who have acquired it. It is wealth, an unattainable naming and a gift of God,
for it says: not from an angel, nor from a man, nor from a book, but from the Creator of all; and in mind, from battles [?],
and relief from thoughts. One thing is the sight of this holy vine
in the winter of the passions, and it has another appearance in the field of the virtues, and yet another is its appearance in the summer and at the harvest of those good fruits;
although all its forms come together for joy
and gladness, and therefore according to its forms are its [?].
When the cluster of that all-praised one begins to blossom among us, then with labor we begin to hate all human glory and praise, and we cast out from ourselves all resentment and anger.
But when this queen of the virtues grows in the soul to that spiritual stature, then the good deeds we have done are reckoned by us as nothing, or rather as loathsome, and every day we think thus:

that we are adding to the burden of our sins, and that it is scattered from us without our knowing; and the graces that come upon us from God we look upon as an increase of our punishment because of our unworthiness. And then our mind is safe from robbery and stored away in the treasury of contrition;

and they hear only dreams and the sounds of thieves, and are harmed by none of them, for humility is an untouchable treasure. Behold, for the sake of the blossoming and small growth of this ever-delightful fruit I have dared to speak a little wisdom;

but as for what the full stature and fruitfulness of that priestly-beautiful [?] one of the Lord is, ask those servants of the Lord, and he will tell you, for I do not have the power to show it in words. Concerning the riches and height of this blessed one, telling is impossible.
