And a word about its nature is altogether inconceivable;
but about its forms we shall speak, according to the power of our understanding. Between true repentance and mourning cleansed
of every stain, and the all-holy humility of those newly come,
there is as much difference from one another as there is among flour, dough and bread; for the soul is crushed and ground by true repentance;

and it is joined, as it were, and, so to speak, kneaded together toward God with the water of those good tears; and then the fire of the Lord is kindled within it, and that blessed humility is baked and made firm,
unleavened and not puffed up. For this reason this blessed threefold chain becomes one power and is united, and even more so [like] the rainbow, and its works and powers are united,

and whatever you say of one of these three as belonging to it will be found to belong also to the second and the third; therefore I will show this briefly before you. The working of this good and glorious trinity of virtues:

the first is this: the acceptance and bearing of every insult and contempt with joy; when, with the outstretched hand of the soul, a person accepts and embraces as sweet every reproach and shame, as medicines that make the diseases of the soul vanish,

and that blot out great sins; the second form of that good three-powered virtue is the complete killing of anger, contrition of heart, and blaming oneself in everything; and the third good ladder is, regarding one's own virtues,
complete disregard and disbelief, and a constant desire for instruction, with faith. And of the prophets; and [?]
The end of all unclean passions is vainglory and pride, whose slayer is
this holy and blessed stag, and it protects its companion, with whom it dwells, untouched by every deadly venom; for where in it could the venom of double-mindedness and evil-speaking appear?
Where could the evil serpent hide in its heart, and not at once be exposed and killed?
Nor in union with it is there any sight of hatred, nor any form of disobedience and disputing, unless the word is for the sake of orthodoxy,

against unbelievers. Whoever is united with this blessed one becomes Sweet, Kind, Merciful, and Calm, and Radiant, Untroubled, Vigilant, Diligent, and why should I say many things? He becomes unharmed by every passion, for it is said that [?] and from passions and battles. A humble monk does not search into hidden and unspeakable matters;
but the proud one investigates the judgments of God. Demons appeared face to face to a certain spiritual monk and called him blessed, but that all-wise elder said:
If you cease praising me, I shall know from your departure that I am great; but if you do not cease praising me, then I shall know from your praise my lack of holiness;

So now, if you depart from me, I would myself have become great; but if you praise me, I shall gain humility through you. And they were astonished at his victory on both sides and at his wisdom, and they vanished.
Brother, let your soul not be a cistern of this living water, which at times wells up and at times dries up from the heat of vainglory and haughtiness,
but let it be a spring of dispassion, always sending up the water of contrition. Know, beloved, that the humble soul is a valley among the mountains of labor and virtues,
remaining unshaken and unexalted. I did not fast,
I neither awaken [?] nor cast down to the ground; but repentance raises up and exalts the soul,

And mourning knocks at the gate of heaven, and blessed humility opens it. As for me, I speak of and worship the threefoldness in one essence and the one essence in Trinity. The sun illumines everything that is visible,
and humility strengthens every work of virtue. If there is no light, everything is dark; and if there is no humility, all our labour is vain. One between [?],
which once saw the sun, and there is one thought, which many times begets humility. In one [?]
they rejoiced; and this is one virtue which the demons cannot claim for themselves. One thing is haughtiness, and another is not being haughty;
and another thing is humility, for the first judges others every day;
and the second judges no one, yet does not condemn himself either; but the third is uncondemned, and always condemns himself. Humility is one thing,
and striving toward humility is another; and the praise of the humble is another.
For the first belongs to the perfect; and the second to the truly obedient;
and the third to all believers. Whoever is humble within, such a one is not stolen away by his own lips, for what does not lie in the treasury

does not go out of the door [?]. Horses, as long as they run alone, think that they are swift; but when they enter the race-course, then they recognise their own weakness. When a man [?] of natural things, this is a sign that he knows healing [?]; but as long as he smells of that stench of the soul, he cannot smell the fragrance. All-holy humility said:
"that he should judge no one, nor contradict [anyone], nor love glory, nor cling to leadership — [this is] my lover, until he is joined to me,
for once he is joined to me, from then on for him [?]. A certain monk
who was eager to acquire this blessed thing, the demons came upon him and sowed praise from themselves in his heart; but the blessed one
employed a good means of overcoming them: he got up and wrote on the wall of his cell the names of great and lofty virtues,
such as perfect love, and angelic humility, and pure prayer, and inexpressible purity, and others like these.

When his thoughts began to praise him, he would say: Come, let us go to the reproof; and he would go and read those names, and say to himself: O wretched one, when you have acquired all of these, even then you are still far from God,

but since you have none of these as yet, how are you proud?" But what the power and essence of this cause [?] is, we are not able to say; yet from its deeds and habits, and from the sights of its image,
let us say a little also about its essence. Humility is a covering of God,

and the failure to see one's own virtues. Humility is an abyss of contrition, untouchable by all the thieves who steal the fruits of the soul. Humility is a strong tower, and all the more so when the thought of the heart has humbled them [?]. There are other signs in the soul of the one who possesses this blessed virtue,
apart from all those works mentioned earlier, by which he recognizes the wealth of his soul;
for all those that we mentioned earlier are visible to human eyes and are spoken of by people; but those signs

[the things] that come about in the soul of the humble are inexpressible. You will know that this blessed [humility] truly dwells in you when your heart is filled with the abundance of that inexpressible light, and there is in you an indescribable love for prayer; and before these, [when you have] a heart that judges no one for sins and errors. And the forerunner of this is hatred of all vain pride and of glory that comes from men. Everyone who has come to know his own weakness by true knowledge of the soul,
has sown his seed on good ground,

for if it is not sown thus, humility will not blossom there. He who has known his own weakness has arrived at the fear of the Lord, and walking in it he will reach the gates of love. Humility brings in there those who draw near to it; for I think that this is why the Lord said

that whoever comes to this door from this world [will go in] without fear and [find] pasture [?] in the paradise of delight. All who have come to monastic life by another way [?]. Let us examine ourselves well, we who are eager and desirous to find humility, and [see] whether we find that our soul, with all eagerness and with all its strength, wishes that its neighbour

should be better and more honored than ourselves in everything, then let us know that mercy is near. As fire is not found in snow, so neither is humility found among heretics. This virtue belongs to the orthodox,
and to those who have been holy and God-loving. Many of us call ourselves sinners,
and perhaps we even regard ourselves so; but insult from others tests the humility of the heart. Whoever is making for this harbor free of waves, let him not cease examining deeds and words,
and thoughts, and ways of acting, and places and modes of life that are lowly and humble, until, with the help of God, through such deeds, he is saved from that ever-surging sea of pride,
and brings the boat of his soul out from there; for whoever is saved from this evil alone will quickly find forgiveness for other sins,

like that publican. For some, the sins they committed earlier, even after they have been forgiven, are a constant reason for humility, and by them they crush the evil neck of pride. Others remember the sufferings of Christ, and by this they humble themselves and regard themselves as debtors. And others crush their hearts by the errors that come upon them day by day;
And others, through the trials and illnesses that befell them, have drawn to themselves that mother of the virtues. But there are some, and I do not know whether they still exist now,
who, however much they advance through the gifts of God, humble themselves
and consider themselves unworthy of such wealth, and they are as though day by day their debt

were being multiplied. This is humility, this is blessedness, this is that perfect measure. When you see someone, or hear of someone, who has attained lofty dispassion in a short time, do not suppose that he arrived there by any other way than by this blessed, short and unerring road. O what good spouses are humility and love,
for the first exalts people, and the second no longer allows the one exalted to fall, for love never falls. Contrition is one thing,
and self-knowledge is one thing, and humility is another. Contrition is the offspring of falls,

for he who falls is broken, and stands in prayer with trembling and with praiseworthy boldness, leaning upon the staff of hope like one who has grown weak, and with it he drives off the power of despair. Self-knowledge
is the unerring recognition of one's own measure,

and the constant remembering and searching out of one's sins, even in small detail. Humility is the invisible teaching of Christ, which dwells invisibly in the soul of the worthy and cannot be expressed in visible words. Whoever says that he catches even a slight scent of the fragrance of such an ointment,

and yet at the time of praise his heart is stirred even a little toward that praise, and he loves those words, let such a person not reproach [?] himself, but let him understand that he is entirely in error. I heard from a certain man, who said with the fervor of his soul, that [?]

For he knew that this nature of ours is unable by itself to keep itself free of passion. And again he said: That is, that in that age [?], for until I arrive there and hear the praise that comes from You, I have counted this praise of this world as nothing,
and rather as harmful. If this is the utmost limit of pride, that a person, for the sake of human glory, should lay claim to virtues that he does not have,
then surely it is a mark of great humility when we do not deny faults that we have not committed if someone accuses us of them, or when we even claim them of our own accord. So did

the one who took bread and cheese in his hand and sat at his gate astride a beam, and he displayed such humility; and likewise that other laborer of purity, who stripped off his garment and walked dispassionately through the city. Such people do not care about the offense taken by others,
for they have received through prayer the power invisibly to reassure everyone. Whoever is concerned about the first
signifies the deficiency of the second [?], for where God is ready to grant requests, there we are able to do all things. Let us choose this,

brothers, so that we may please God and not men; for God rejoices greatly when he sees us seeking dishonour from men, so that we may hem in and destroy that vain pride. True exile brings such goods as these,
for it comes upon one from one's own [?],
…is of very great dishonour and shame. Do not wonder at these words, beloved, for no one has ever climbed to the top of a ladder in a single step. We are [?], not when demons attack us,
but our [?]. Natural fruitlessness raises upward the branches of the tree called citron, but when they are bent downward they immediately become fruitful.

Whoever reads with understanding has grasped this saying. The ladder of this blessed virtue too has received from God ascents of thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold, and the last of these the perfect climb,
the middle one the zealous, and the first all are able to climb. Whoever knows his own measure will never go astray by undertaking a task beyond his strength,
and thus as one who has set his foot on this blessed path. Just as a hen is frightened by an eagle,

so too the humble person is frightened by answering back. Without prophecy, signs and wonders, many have entered the kingdom; but without humility no one will enter the bridal chamber. The second, humility, actively guards the first;
but the second has often been destroyed by the first in people of light mind. The Lord arranged this too for our humbling, for no one sees his own wounds as well

as another person does. For this reason we should not be our own teachers but be taught by a spiritual shepherd. When we are healed of our wounds, we should give thanks to God and to him. The humble person always regards his own will

as a deceiver, and so he loathes it and despises himself as ignorant. For this reason he humbly asks God for what is better, and with faith he learns what is good from Him. The humble person is always obedient and listens to better advice from others, because he never trusts himself but leaves his care to the Lord.
who opened even the mouth of the ass against Balaam. And even if he does and says everything in a godly way,
he still does not believe in his own understanding; for as asking others seems a burden to the proud, so does trusting himself seem to the humble. I think this:

that it belongs to angels alone not to be taken captive by sin, since even that great angel of the earth, Paul, said that [?]. For this reason we too must always hold judgment and blame against ourselves,
so that by voluntarily humbling ourselves we may escape those involuntary sins;
but if we do not do so, at the hour of death we will be grievously punished for them. Whoever asks a petition of God and holds himself unworthy of that petition,

he will receive more than it. A witness to this is that publican, who asked for forgiveness and found justification. The thief asked only to be remembered in the kingdom, and he inherited all of paradise.
On earth no fire is seen or found whose nature is small or great, for its nature is all one. Even though an ember is small, by nature it is equal to a great furnace.
In the same way, wherever true humility settles, it does not allow the matter of sin to exist there. As long as we sin willingly, humility is not found among us.
therefore the Lord, knowing that outward form brings the soul to humility, took a towel and showed us the means and the way of humility,
For the soul conforms itself to its deeds,

and as its deeds are, so it is shaped. Authority became for one of the angels a cause of pride, though that authority had not been given to him for this. The mind of one sitting on thrones is one thing;
and that of one lying fallen on dunghills is another. Was it not for this reason that the great and righteous Job sat on the dunghill outside the city?
For it was then that he acquired perfect humility, and he said with knowledge of the soul:
You will find Manasseh more sinful than all people. He defiled the temple of God

and all its worship with idols. Even if the whole world had fasted for him, it would not have been enough for his repentance; but humility was able to heal what was incurable. David says to God [?] the rod of fasting [?]; once the blessed one cried out [?]
to humility, because of adultery and murder, and immediately he heard that [?]. The blessed fathers called bodily labors the way of humility;
but I say also obedience and sincerity of heart,
which by nature stand opposed to haughtiness. If pride turned some of the angels into demons, surely humility is also able to make angels out of demons;
therefore let the fallen not despair. Let us hasten, brothers, and strive with all our strength to climb up onto the head of this desirable one;

and if we cannot reach her head, let us at least sit on her shoulders; and if we are too lame to climb even there, then at least let us not fall from her arms, for whoever falls down from there, I do not know whether he will meet with any divine grace. Her roots and ways, but not her images, are poverty and living as a stranger;
the concealing of wisdom, and the begging of alms; the hiding of noble birth; the banishing of boldness, and separation from much talking,
for nothing humbles the soul so much as the form and life of beggary and contempt,
for our love of God shows itself when it is in our power to be exalted,

and we flee from bodily exaltation without turning back. Whenever you arm yourself against some passion, take this good humility with you as a helper, for then it is as though you have made sin and despair vanish,
and have trampled down the devil and these dragons, the flesh, by the power of Christ.
Humility is a ladder that raises the soul up to heaven from the abyss of sins. Someone saw her beauty in his heart, and amazement seized him,
and he asked her to tell him the name of her parent. And she, with a radiant and joyful face, said to him:
Why do you ask the name of my parent, since he is wondrous and nameless? I will not tell you his name

until you have acquired God dwelling within you, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. The mother of water and of the spring is the abyss, and the mother of understanding and discernment is humility.

Discourse of the same blessed John on diacrisis, that is, the understanding and discernment of thoughts, passions and virtues. Chapter 26. Discernment and understanding for those newly come to the monastic life is this:
that they truly understand their own measure and their own conduct; and for those in the middle it is this:
that they acquire a rational perception that unerringly distinguishes the truly good from what is natural and from what is opposed to it;
But among the perfect it is a light of understanding that has come from the divine radiance, which
is planted by God in the mind, and by its own light is able to illuminate the darkness of others as well;
or else, this is discernment for all, for beginners, those in the middle, and the perfect: the unerring finding of the will of God, so that at every time and place and in every matter one may know
in what the will of God lies. This is found among those who are pure in heart, body, and mouth. Whoever has conquered the three has conquered the five as well,
but whoever has neglected the three will not prevail over even one of the five.

Discernment is an undefiled and holy intention and the knowledge of conscience. Conscience is the mind that understands good and evil, which God planted in man to expose evil. Let no one fall from foolishness into unbelief when he sees something
or hears of a deed beyond nature, for where a deed beyond nature dwells,

for where God, who is beyond nature, dwells, even greater deeds beyond nature take place there. More than anything else, every demonic attack against us arises from three sources: from negligence, from pride, or from the demons' envy.
The first is pitiable and the second is wretched, but the third is thrice-blessed. In everything, after God, let us use our conscience as our counsellor and rule.
so that we may know from which direction the breath of the wind is coming in,
and set our sails toward it. In every divine work of ours, the demons prepare three pits for us.
For first they fight us in order to corrupt us from doing good, and when they are defeated in this, they then strive that the work not be done in a godly way.
And when those enemies are defeated in this as well, they then come upon us secretly and call us blessed because we have accomplished the work in a godly way.
The enemy of the first is zeal and the remembrance of death; of the second, obedience and being despised; and of the third, constant reproach of oneself. Our [?],
our [?] the fire of God, for from then on there is no longer among us the warfare of former habits,
for [?] of all evil heat, and of darkness, and of the stirring of habits, inner and outer, visible and invisible. The demons continually strive to do the opposite of this thing spoken of before.
For when they have mastered the soul and darkened that light of the mind, from then on there is no longer in us wretched ones any vigilance of mind,
nor discernment, nor understanding, nor shame, but only mercilessness, senselessness, lack of discernment,
and blindness. This saying will be well understood by those who have turned back from fornication,

or have awakened from boldness, or have come to understanding from disorderliness: how, after their awakening from that blindness of mind and after the departure of that darkness, they are ashamed even of themselves in their mind over the words and deeds that they spoke and did
while they were in that darkness. If night does not first fall during the day of the soul, those thieves will not come in to steal,

They slaughter and destroy. [?] of the soul is the destruction of that natural good. Theft is when a person does what is evil and harmful as if it were good. Theft is the unperceived plundering of the soul. [?] of the soul is the death of the rational mind, through falling into evil deeds. [?] of the soul is the complete cutting off of hope after lawlessness.
Let no one plead weakness as an excuse regarding the fulfilment of the commandments of the Gospel, for there are many, brothers,

who have done even more than the commandment, and let this one convince us: he who loved his neighbor more than himself did not stop [?] at this, but did more than the commandment. Let them be comforted, and let them take courage, and let them take courage, those passion-ridden ones
who have humility alone, for even if they fall into all pits and are caught in all snares,
and grow weak with every disease, yet after their healing they will become luminaries and physicians and lamps and guides to all, and will teach the forms of that disease,

and from their own experience they will save those who are about to fall. If any are overpowered by their former habits and are able to teach by word alone, let them teach, and perhaps they may somehow be put to shame by their own words and begin to do good in deed as well; but let them not become leaders, but let them teach by word if they are able.
Let it not happen to them as I saw happen to some people. They had fallen into mire and were buried up to the neck, and they showed the way they had fallen in there
to everyone passing by, and begged them not to take that road,
and fall into the same pit. And because of the care they took for the life of others, the Almighty delivered them also from that clay.
But if those passion-ridden ones willingly give themselves over to desire, let them show their teaching of such things by silence, for it is written that whoever [?]
Truly we are crossing a harsh [?] and difficult sea, O monks, full of many gales and whirlwinds, and whirlpools and rocks and beasts and robbers,

…and with whirlpools and evil waves. Let us take the whirlpool of the soul to mean that sharp and sudden anger. Let us take the turning current [?] to mean despair, which wraps itself around the mind and hurries to drag it down into the abyss of perdition. Let us take the rock to mean insensibility, which relishes evil as if it were good. And let us take the beast to mean this heavy and wild flesh.
and let us take the robber to mean those evil demons of vainglory,
who carry off the cargo and the labor of our virtues.
And by the wave we mean the raging and glutted belly, which by its own violence delivers us to the mouth of the beast. And the waterspout is that plunging pride,
which lifts us up to heaven and brings us down into the abyss. All who study writings,
know which are the lessons of those newly come to learning, and which are those of teachers.
Let us take good care lest we spend a long time in learning and still be learning the alphabet, for this is a shame, when a person grown old in learning is still learning the alphabet.
The alphabet of monasticism is this: obedience, fasting, vigil, wearing sackcloth, sitting on ashes, weeping, confession, silence, humility, courage,

frost and cold, toil, hardship, being despised, contrition, not remembering wrongs, love of the brethren, meekness, simple and upright faith, freedom from worldly care, a sinless hatred of parents, flight from worldly affairs, innocence and voluntary poverty. The teaching of those in the middle, who have made progress in monastic life, is this: freedom from vainglory, freedom from anger, richness of hope, stillness, discernment, firm remembrance of judgment and death, and mercy.
Love of strangers, measured instruction, passionless prayer, hatred of material needs. This is the boundary and law of perfected souls:
With the fear of God, also a heart free from distraction, perfect love, a spring of humility, the passing of the mind over to God,
the entry of Christ into the soul, the illumination of undistracted prayer, an abundance of God's radiance, the desire for death,

hatred of this life, flight from the flesh; intercessor for the world, one who compels God to mercy, joined with the angels, an abyss of understanding, a temple of mysteries, a beholder of things unspeakable, a savior of men, a god to demons, a lord over passions;
master of the flesh, ruler of the mind, a stranger to sin, a house of dispassion, made like the Master, by the help of the Master himself.
The mind needs more than a little caution when the body is sick. For then, when the demons see us lying prostrate on our beds,

unable to fight them because of our sickness, they hurry to come at us with fierce assaults. When people who live in the world fall sick, the demon of anger attacks them, and often the demon of blasphemy too;
but those who are outside the world, if they have the necessities at hand, are attacked by the demon of gluttony and fornication;

but if they live in harsh and comfortless places, the tyrant of despondency and ingratitude torments them. I set my mind to examine the demon of fornication, and I saw that he added pains and aches to the sick, and amid those pains and aches he caused arousal of the flesh and discharge. The thing was astonishing: in the midst of severe pains and aches the flesh raged and held sway.
And I saw other sick people lying on their beds who were comforted by the power and compassion of God,
and they no longer suffered, but were as though no longer [under] the affliction of that disease, a deliverance [?];
and again I saw sick people

who through that sickness, as through some divine penance, were freed from spiritual sickness and evil passion, and I glorified Him who through the flesh made the flesh itself pure together with the soul. The rational mind has also been clothed with a rational perception,
which is within us and not within us; let us seek it unceasingly, for when it appears, these external stirrings will cease their work,
and this is why a certain wise man said: You have found divine perception.

Let the life of a monk be with understanding in every deed and word, in thought and in movement; for if it is not so, that life is not monastic, nor is it like that of the angels. Another is that of God,
And one thing is [?], and another is His [?], and another is His [?], and another is that which comes from [?]. And the first is over all created beings; and the second is for the faithful alone;
and the third is for the trustworthy and truly faithful; and the fourth is upon those who serve Him with zeal;
but the fifth is manifested upon those who love Him. Often a medicine that heals one person becomes deadly to another,

and often the very same medicine becomes beneficial to a person when he takes it at its proper time, and again, when taken not at its proper time, it becomes deadly to that same person. I saw a foolish physician
who afflicted a broken, sick man with reviling and with unseemly insults, and brought him nothing but despair; and I saw another, a skilled physician,
who with insult and reviling lanced a heart swollen with pride, and emptied out all its disease and stench. I saw the same sick man,
how at one time he drank the medicine of obedience, to purge the impurity of the passions, and went about and did not sleep,
and at another time the eyes of his soul grew weak, and he remained in stillness and did not converse. Some, I do not know how, for I have not

learned to inquire arrogantly into the gifts of God, but somehow, I do not know how, have by their very mind, so to speak, an inclination toward fasting, or love of stillness, or bodily purity, or lack of presumption, or gentleness, or compunction. And there are others
whose nature is opposed to these practices.
And they force themselves according to their strength,

and such people, even though they are at times defeated, yet, as those who do violence to nature, seem to me more pleasing than the former. Do not boast, O man, of wealth gained without labor, for the Giver of gifts knew beforehand your great [?] and weakness and defeat,

and by those free graces of His He gave you some small measure of salvation without your own labor. And even from childhood, upbringing and teachings and places either help us or oppose us with regard to virtue
and the monastic way of life. Angels are a light to monks, and true monks are a light to all people,

and for this reason we ought to strive in all things to be a pattern of doing good, in our word or in deed; for if the light becomes darkness, then how greatly will the darkness, that is, those of the world, be darkened! If you listen to me and obey me, it is better that we not scatter
our wretched selves in warfare of many kinds against the thousands, thousands upon thousands, and myriads upon myriads of our enemies, for we are not capable of searching out and finding their many
…those devices and schemes of theirs. Let us arm ourselves through the Holy Trinity against those three passions, and with [the weapons?] of the Holy Spirit,

otherwise we shall bring many toils on ourselves. Truly, if for us too there should come [?]… which our Israel too shall pass through, that is, the mind that sees God, without being drowned in that sea of the passions,
and may see those Egyptians, the passions, drowned in that water of tears,

but if he does not come to us [?], which is this flesh [?]. If God arises among us in deed, and if we hasten toward Him by beholding Him, then those of ours [?] will also become invisible. Let us hasten, brothers,
so that we may learn divine matters through labor and not by mere words, for it is not words that must be shown at the time of departure from this world,

but deeds. Those who hear of a hidden treasure hasten and take great labor upon themselves to find it, and when they find it they again take every labor upon themselves to guard it, for those who grow rich without labor will surely squander their wealth. It is difficult to do away entirely with the battle of former habits, and those who increase them and add to them have either cut off the hope of their own salvation, or have gained no benefit at all
from monastic life; although I know that all things are possible for God, and nothing is impossible for him. A question difficult to understand,
and beyond my comprehension, was put to me by certain people, one that I had found nowhere in the books I have read.

For they said that of the eight thoughts, [three?] are offspring of the five. In answer to their question I put forward a praiseworthy ignorance and begged them to teach me, and those blessed men taught me this:

The mother of fornication is gluttony, and the mother of despondency is conceit. Sorrow is the offspring of all three: of gluttony, of love of money, and of vainglory. Anger likewise is the offspring of the three. And the mother of pride is vainglory.
But I begged those blessed ones and said: Tell me this also: which are the offspring of those eight [?] thoughts? Or which one is the child of which?
And those dispassionate ones taught me gently, and said: There is no order or knowledge among the wicked, but only complete disorder and turmoil.
Those wise ones convinced me of this by extensive examples [?], a few of which we also write down here, so that from these few we may come to understand the others as well.
For they said: untimely and idle laughter is sometimes
born of fornication, and sometimes of vainglory, when someone inwardly takes wicked delight in himself; and sometimes of ease and comfort.
And excessive sleep is sometimes born of comfort; and sometimes of fasting, when the one who fasts grows haughty; and sometimes of despondency; and sometimes of nature.

And much talking sometimes arises from despondency and sometimes from vainglory; and despondency sometimes from comfort and sometimes from lack of the fear of God. And blasphemy is the offspring of pride, and many times it arises from judging a neighbor for that very thing; or it may also come from the envy of demons. Hardness of heart comes from satiety, and from pitilessness, and from idle love.
And idle love arises from fornication, or from love of money, or from gluttony;
or from vainglory, and from many other things. And perversity arises from loftiness and from anger; and duplicity from self-will and self-pleasing;
but the opposites of these are born of the parents opposite to those,

And so that I may not say much, for time would fail me if I wished to examine each one, let me say briefly that the true victory over all the passions mentioned earlier is humility; whoever acquires it has conquered everything. The parents of all evils are lust and wickedness, and these,

whoever has them shall not see the Lord; and we shall gain nothing from being rid of the first if we still have the second. Let us take rulers and wild beasts as our image of the fear of the Lord, and carnal passion as our image of the desire for him, for nothing prevents us
…and to take on the form of the virtues even from contrary things. This tribe is full of evil perversity, conceit and duplicity, for it displays bodily labours like those of the first fathers,
but it does not become worthy of their grace, although graces were never so needed by this nature as they are now. And this has justly happened to us, for not by labor,

but by simplicity and humility is God revealed in souls. Although the power of the Lord is revealed in weakness, the Lord will still not disregard a humble laborer. When we see one of the ascetic strugglers physically weakened, let us not seek out of malice to learn the judgment behind his weakness,
but rather, with good love, let us cherish him as our own limb, and let us receive him as a soldier wearied from battle and give him rest. Weakness often comes for the cleansing of sins;
and sometimes it comes for the humbling of the mind. When our good and sweet Lord and King sees someone slothful in ascetic struggle, he often humbles the flesh through weakness;
and sometimes, again, he cleanses the soul from passions and evil thoughts. Everything that comes upon us, whether visible
or the invisible, it can be received well, in a middling way, or badly. I saw three brothers who met with some hardship,
and one of them became angry, the second stayed untroubled, and the third was filled with joy.
I saw a field sown by many laborers, and each one had a different thought. One had this thought, to pay off his debt; a second, to gain wealth;
another, to win the favor of his lord with a gift; another, to show his work to those passing along the road and receive praise from them;
another, to stir his enemy to envy and trouble him; another, not to be reproached by people for idleness. These are the kinds of seed those laborers sow:
fasting, vigil, almsgiving, service and things like these,
But let the brothers quickly examine the thoughts of the heart, the ones I am speaking of. Just as, when we draw up water, we often draw up a frog along with it;
so too, when we practise the virtues, passions are often secretly woven in with them. Let us understand it this way: gluttony is woven in with hospitality;
with love, fornication; with discernment, cunning; with wisdom, perversity; with meekness, laxity, sloth and self-will; and with silence, arrogance.
and to joy, haughtiness; to hope, negligence; to stillness, despondency and sloth; to virginity, irritability; to humility, boldness;

and with all of these, as a marvel, vainglory is joined. Let us not be distressed, beloved, when we ask something from the Lord and for a time He does not hear us. For the Lord would wish that all people might attain dispassion in a single moment.
But all who ask something from God and do not obtain what they ask, by one of

these causes this befalls them: either they asked before the time, or they ask unworthily and with vanity, or, if what they asked had been given to them, they would have become exalted or would have fallen into negligence. All know this, that demons and passions depart from us for a time,
or even entirely; but in how many ways they depart from us, I think few know.
From some people the passions have departed, not only from believers but from unbelievers too, all except one. For they left that one with them as the leader of all evils,
and as the one that fills the place of all the other passions. Its wickedness is so great

that it was able to turn angels into demons. Again, the matter of the passions is consumed when it is burned by that divine fire and made to vanish from the soul. Again, demons leave a person of their own will so that they may lead him into carelessness,

and then suddenly fall upon him, seize him, and plunge him into the passions, so that from then on he becomes his own enemy. I know yet another departure of demons, when the soul has become used to the passions. Infants are an image of this saying,

for once they have grown used to sucking at the breast, even after they are weaned from the breast, they suck their own fingers. I know a fifth departure as well, of demons and passions from the soul,
which comes about from simplicity and great and good innocence; for true and just is the help given by God to such people, and He delivers

them mysteriously from evils, like little infants who are often stripped while they are unaware of what is happening. Evil passion by nature has not been created in our nature, for God is not the creator of the passions; rather, the virtues were created by Him in us. For mercy is natural in us;
for this reason even pagans show mercy to people. And love is natural, for even dumb animals become sorrowful at separation from one another.
And faith is natural, for all of us have received faith from ourselves,
and we give birth to it in our souls. And hope is natural; for this reason too we receive baptism in hope;

and again, in bodily matters, in hope of enrichment we sow and [?], and go to sea. And since this is so, and love, which is a marvel and the end of the law and the prophets, is natural with us, then the virtues are in no way far from our nature; and let all be ashamed who say that it is impossible to practice the virtues. Above nature is the complete purity of virginity,
and freedom from anger, and humility and prayer, and vigilance, and fasting, and perpetual weeping and mourning.
Of these things, then, for some people the teachers and givers are men, for some angels, and for some the Word of God himself. When two evils present themselves, the lesser must be chosen,
as when we are standing in prayer and some brother comes, and we are obliged to do one of two things: either to abandon prayer, or not to see that brother and so distress him. Then indeed let us

let us make [?] that love is higher and loftier than prayer. For prayer by itself is only one virtue, but love gathers together all the virtues. And again, once in my youth I came to a city. When I sat down at table, thoughts of gluttony and pride beset me,
but I was terrified of the offspring of gluttony, which is fornication, and so I was overcome instead by pride. Among lay people the root of all evils is love of money;
but among monks it is gluttony. Often God, by his providence, leaves some small passions in spiritual people,

so that they may blame themselves over those worthless things of no account, and may gain the wealth that cannot be stolen, that of blessed humility. Newcomers cannot acquire humility without obedience;
for everyone who has learned a craft by himself is certainly conceited about it. In two virtues all the work of virtue is gathered together, as the fathers say, of which

the one releases from desires, and the other preserves that release from the passions forever through humility. For this reason mourning is twofold, for it undoes sin and brings in humility. This is the task of those who fear God: to give to everyone who asks of them,
but for people to give even to those who do not ask belongs to the more exalted;
and for people not to demand back from those who plunder them, and all the more, if they were able [?], this
is the work of the wholly perfect. Let us examine ourselves regarding all the passions and virtues, as to what measure we are at: the beginning, or the middle,
or the end. All the battles of the demons against us arise from these three causes: from love of pleasure, or from pride, or from their envy,

and those of the last kind are blessed, those of the middle kind utterly wretched, and those of the first kind entirely useless. There is a certain thought and awareness that is called the guarantor of hardships, and if it settles in a person,
he will no longer be afraid, nor will he turn back from struggle and bodily affliction. By this blessed thought the souls of the martyrs were seized,
and they easily despised their tortures. [?] Another thing is the guarding of the mind; likewise this second is higher than the first, even though it is harder. One thing is prayer about a thought,
another is answering thoughts, and another is counting them as nothing,
and to the first another testifies, the one who said [?] and the like of this,
and to the second testifies the one who
said that the adversary [?]; and again he says that [?]; but to the third practice the saying testifies that: [?]

; and again he says this: of these, the middle one often helps the first kind, when the thoughts find them unprepared and they are unable to answer; but the first is not able to do the work of the second kind, so as to drive away the enemies by means of it,

and in the third case the demons disregard [him] completely. By nature it is impossible for the incorporeal to be confined within the limit of the body so that it can never pass outside that limit. But for one who has acquired God within himself, everything is possible through him. Just as those whose sense of smell is healthy can perceive
if someone is secretly carrying perfume among them, so too a pure soul [perceives] the fragrance that he has received from God,

and also the stench from which it has been set free, when it perceives them without the knowledge of those who have them. It is impossible for all to be free of passion, but it is possible for all to be saved and to be pleasing to God. Let those foreign offspring not have power over you,
who have wished, concerning the ineffable dispensations of God and his revelations, which he sends upon people,
the examination, and inwardly they suggest that God shows partiality. For they are entirely the offspring of arrogance. Sometimes the demon of love of money pretends to be humble;
and again, sometimes the demon of vainglory urges us to give alms; and the demon of love of pleasure does the same.
But if we become pure of these two in any way, let us not cease to give alms in every place. Some have said that there are demons opposed to demons;
but I have come to understand that all of them seek our destruction. The leader of every spiritual work, visible and invisible, is the thought and good desire, together with the help of God,
for if these do not go before, the virtues do not come into being. If there is [?], as the wise Solomon says,
and in all of it are also the works of this divine way of life of ours,

therefore let us understand this and seek each work in its own time, for certainly among those who struggle there is a time of freedom from passion, and a time of being subject to passion because of the immaturity of the strugglers. There is a time of tears, and a time of hardness of heart;

there is a time of obedience, and a time of leadership; there is a time of fasting, and a time of eating. There is a time of battle against those enemies of the flesh, and a time of the killing of that heat;
There is a time of spiritual winter, and a time of calm of mind; there is a time of sorrow of heart, and there is a time of spiritual joy; there is a time of teaching and a time of listening;
a time of defilement comes on account of pride, and a time of purity on account of humility.
There is a time of battle, and there is a time of rest;
there is a time of stillness, and a time of freedom from care, and of care, and of going out; there is a time of peaceful prayer, and there is a time of guileless service.
Let us not seek anything before its time out of arrogance. Let us not look for summer's work in winter, nor for the work of reaping at the time of sowing,
for there is a time for sowing labours,
and there is a time for reaping those inexpressible graces. But if we seek things before their time, we will not find them even in their proper time. For some, after labour,
And some, at the time of death, received from God gifts and the rewards of their labors, by an ineffable dispensation.
It is therefore to be asked which of them, among these three, is lower than the others. There is a despair that comes from the multitude of sins and from the burden of conscience,
and from great sorrow, when the soul is sunk in its wounds and, from their weight, falls into the abyss of despair.

And again, there is a despair that comes from arrogance and loftiness, when a person thinks, 'Why has this error come upon me? For I did not deserve this.' Whoever understands will find the difference between these two,
For the one gives himself over to disorder, and the other to ascetic struggle with despair, which cannot be reconciled [?],
But the first is healed by fasting and hope in God, and the second by humility and by judging no one. Let this serve you as a pattern and a rule in all ways of life
and in your deeds, whether you are under obedience or on your own, so that you may examine your every deed, visible or invisible, as to whether it is being done according to God.
-- And let us understand this as follows: we who have newly come, if we do some deed and humility is not added to us by it, more than what we had,
I do not think that deed was according to God, whether it be great or small. And this is the sign of God's will among us who are still infants;

and for those in the middle, the sign of God's will is the removal of faults; and for the perfect, the multiplying and increase of that divine light. Small errors are not small in the presence of the great;
but great ones, set beside the small, do not appear great. When the air is cleared of clouds, then the sun is seen purely;
and the soul, when it is made worthy of the forgiveness of its former sins, then sees that divine light well. Sin is one thing, negligence another, passion another, and a fall another;

let whoever is able search this out well with the Lord's help. Some bless wonder-working and prophecy above all spiritual gifts and graces, and do not know that there are many measures higher than these, which stand forever without falling.
He who has been completely purified sees his neighbor's soul and what it is like, even though he cannot see the very essence of the soul itself;

but he who has not yet been made perfect, and is still advancing through bodily works, understands the state of the soul as well [?]. A small fire often purifies [?] all matter, and a small hole often empties out all the labor. Often, while these enemies, the flesh, are at rest, the power of the mind stands still [?], and the fervor that has been lost does not rise again;
and again, often we have worn the flesh out with ascetic struggle, and evil stirrings are stirred up in us, so that we may not trust in ourselves,

but in him who invisibly puts to death these living enemies, the flesh. When we see certain people who love us for God's sake, let us be the more careful toward them, lest we become overly bold; for nothing so dissolves love and produces hatred as overboldness. It is beautiful and holy,

and the well-seeing eye of the soul; and after the goodness of the angels, it is higher than all nature. For this reason also the thoughts of those subject to passions, which are born in the hearts of others,

they are able to know through their love toward them, and especially when they are not defiled and submerged by these filthy bodies. If to him, like that material one [?], let whoever reads understand.
Those who also understand bodily trials as God's looking upon them;
but the perfect understand them through the coming of the Holy Spirit and the multiplication of graces. There are perfect ones who are strengthened by divine longing,

and with humility of heart they perform great virtues; and others undertake this work with pride and are put to shame. There is a demon who comes to us when we lie down on our beds, and hastens to wound us with evil and defiled thoughts;
and if we are negligent, and do not arm ourselves with prayer against him, and fall asleep amid those evil thoughts, we fall into foul dreams. There is also another demon,
who is called the forerunner and scout, who, when we wake up,

comes upon us and hastens to defile our first thoughts. Give the beginning of the day to the Lord, so that when it dawns, thoughts from him may settle in you, and not those from the devil, for whichever of them gets there first, to him that day will also belong. A praiseworthy saying was told to me by a good laborer of virtue:

that as soon as it dawns, I know how I am going to be that whole day. Many are the paths both of the service of God and of perdition; for this reason it often happens that what is contrary to one person comes well to another, and the deeds of both are pleasing before the Lord.
When some trial befalls us, then the demons fight against us, so that we might say something or do evil,
and when they cannot make us do this, then they approach us secretly and sow in us a thanksgiving full of pride. Some by that one part go up;
but those who think on earthly things go down, for of those who have been separated, no one remains in the middle. One has received existence together with another, and not alone,
and it is a wonder how, apart from that in which it received its existence,

it is able to be free of passion. Good daughters are borne by mothers, and the mothers by the Lord; and the opposing evil daughters are borne by their mothers, and their mothers by the devil. Fear, and still more God [?]; let not the last error
of the soul, it becomes worse than that first fall.
The light of all bodies is the perceiving eyes;
but the intellectual light of the divine virtues is discernment and understanding.

Of examination and of understanding of oneself, the second [?]. As the thirsting deer longs for the springs of water, so the soul of monks longs to know the will of God, which is good and acceptable and perfect, and along with this also the mixed will, and the opposing and evil will. About this our discourse is long and hard to interpret. It also concerns which deeds are needful, so that they may be done quickly and without delay, according to the saying: Woe to him who delays from one time to another.

Or there are deeds that must be done calmly and with much deliberation, as the speaker teaches us who says: [?] and again says: [?]. For not everyone is able to understand these hard-to-understand things easily, since even that God-clothed one, who had the Holy Spirit within him, often prayed about such matters. At one time he said: [?] and again at another time

he said: [?] and again: [?] from all the cares and passions of this world, and I lifted up [?]. Those who wish to know the will of God must put themselves to death, and they must pray with faith and with a simple and innocent heart. They must ask fathers or spiritual brothers and accept the counsel given by them as if from the mouth of God, even if that word is contrary to the word of their own heart;

— even if the people they ask are not very spiritual or discerning. For the Lord does not disregard the souls who, in faith and innocence, have entrusted themselves to the counsel of the fathers, even if those they ask are ignorant. Rather, the one who speaks to them is the Lord, the All-wise and Good. Those who practise the aforementioned work with joy and without doubting are full of great humility. For if someone used to utter parables through a musical instrument [?], how much higher than that soulless instrument are a rational mind and an intelligent soul! Those who did not wish to do the aforementioned work, but strove by themselves to know the will of the Lord, used many different kinds and forms of means. They told us about these, and we shall now mention some of them. Some, when they had two choices before them and wished to know which was the will of God, separated their minds completely from all carnal affection and restrained their minds, so that neither

...were inclining toward one of the two. Then, with their mind stripped of their own will, they presented it to God in fervent prayer for appointed days, and so came to know His will. Either the invisible Mind spoke invisibly to their mind and told them which was better, or one of the thoughts vanished entirely from their soul. Others again came to know that a matter was from God because of the trouble of disturbance that came upon them in it, like the one who said: [?]. And others again took the opposite as their sign: from the afflictions and trials that came upon them in a matter, they knew that God's will was in it.

And others again knew from prosperity and success that God willed it, as it is said that God grants success to everyone who does good. When a person has God within himself as his illuminator, his mind is itself enlightened by God. He becomes fully assured about each matter, whether it ought to be done quickly or later. For when a person is double-minded about matters and cannot become fully assured, it is clear that his soul is still unenlightened and loves glory. There is no injustice with God, that He should shut the door on those who knock in humility and make entreaty. In everything we do, let us look at our thought and see what it is inclined toward. For every deed that we do for God, pure of every carnal deed and thought,

will have a good end, even if it does not appear good. But if a carnal thought is in it, I do not know whether it will turn out for the better, for that is a fearful thing. The judgments of the Lord cannot be put into words. Many times, by His providence, He hides His will from us. He knows that even if we came to know it, we would not mean to do it. So He does not reveal it to us at all, so that a greater punishment may not come upon us for failing to do it. An upright heart is kept clear of the crookedness of affairs, and it sails without sinking in the boat of innocence. There are brave souls who, out of love for divine things and humility of heart, undertake struggles beyond their strength. And again there are proud hearts that do the same.

For many times the demons make us eager to undertake deeds beyond our strength. They do this so that we lose heart because of it, fall away even from what we had the strength to do, and become a laughingstock to our enemies. I have also seen weak souls and bodies that, because of the multitude of their sins, undertook struggles beyond their strength and could not bear them. I taught them and told them that God, the Creator of all, accepts repentance according to the measure of humility and not according to the measure of labors. Sometimes the place where one is brought up becomes the teacher of many evils, and sometimes the company of evil people does. But more often the wickedness of the soul
and the perversity of the mind become the cause of ruin. Whoever is separated from these two is also separated from the third. But whoever has the third is untried in every place.

For there is no place that can keep a person from sin if he does not guard himself. If unbelievers, or people who believe wrongly, argue with us out of ill will, let us withdraw from them after we have instructed them once or twice;

but if someone sincerely wants to know the truth, let us not stop speaking what is good until the end. In both cases, though, let us act according to our firmness and the measure of our souls. It is great folly for someone to hear of the saints' deeds that are beyond nature and then lose hope about his own life. For if he is willing, he can gain two benefits:

either he takes up a courageous zeal to imitate the good, or he comes to know himself and rightly understands his own weakness, through that blessed humility which brings good things. There are defiled demons, more wicked than other demons, who fight us not only to lead us into sin but also to make us draw others into the same evil, so that we may be handed over to a heavier punishment. I saw a man who had learned an evil habit from another man. The one who had taught him that practice came to his senses, stopped doing evil, and turned to repentance. But because of that disciple's sin, his repentance became weak and difficult. Truly very, very great is the wickedness

of those evil spirits, and few people recognise it, and I think that even the few do not recognise all of it. For sometimes, when we were living in comfort and were well fed, we stayed properly awake; but when we fasted and struggled, we sank pitifully into sleep. When we lived in solitude, our hearts grew hard; and when we mixed with people, we were moved to compunction. When we were hungry, we saw evil dreams, and when we were full, we saw nothing. In the time of our ascetic struggle we were darkened;

and when we drank wine, we were moved to compunction and became cheerful. Concerning all this, let whoever is able, through the Lord, enlighten those who are unenlightened; for we are unenlightened and cannot understand such matters;

but we do say this: such a change does not always come from the devil. Sometimes it comes from the makeup of the nature I was given, from this wretched, coarse and rebellious flesh. When any of the things mentioned above happens to us, let us pray to the Lord fervently and humbly. If after that prayer we still find things the same for a long time, let us recognise that it does not come from the workers [?],
but the matter comes from nature,
or else it is some dispensation of God, and through contrary things he wills our benefit, so that in every way our pride

humbled [?]. It is hard and difficult to search out the abyss of God's judgments, for those who search into such things are sailing in the ship of pride. A brother once asked an elder, one of those who see hidden things, and said to him: "Why did God know beforehand that certain people would fall, and yet he adorned them

…them with gifts and miracles? And he answered: First, so that other souls also might be made cautious; second, so that he might show that human beings have free will; and third, so that at the judgment to come he might leave those fallen ones without excuse. The Old Law, as being weak, said: [?]; but the Lord, as being mighty, commanded us even to turn our brother back, and said: [?] and what follows. If your gladness is holy and your learning humble, act on the word of the Lord, and especially with those who accept it. But if you are not of that measure, then act on the same word of the Law, and guard yourself. Do not be surprised if even those you love become your enemies, for some are vessels of the devil, especially against his enemies. I marvel, beloved!

…at one thing among our affairs: how, for the virtues, we have help from God, who is able to do all things, and from his angels and his saints; but for evil things the demons alone are our helpers, and yet we are more eager for evil things and passions,

and for this reason I am not able to say much, nor do I wish to. If all created beings remain in the same nature in which they were created (as I am the image of God and am mingled with this clay, as the great Gregory the Theologian says), [they are at rest?]. But if any created being is outside the nature in which it was created, it undoubtedly longs insatiably for its own proper state.

Let a man use every means and strive with all eagerness to lift up this clay and seat it on the throne of God. Let no one make excuses about that ascent, for the way and the door are open. Hearing about the spiritual virtues of the fathers awakens a person's mind and soul to imitate their zeal. Hearing their teaching in turn stirs up a desire for them and leads him to become like those who have godly zeal. Reading is a lamp in darkness, a guide for those who have gone astray, and an enlightener of the blind. Reading is a means of finding health, and it dissolves pains and makes them disappear. Those who marvel at the small deeds of others do so for one of two reasons:

either from great lack of understanding, or from great humility they magnify and exalt the deeds of their neighbor. Let us strive not only to fight the demons but also to defeat them. Whoever is fighting sometimes wins and sometimes is defeated; but whoever has won completely always wins. Whoever has become victorious over the passions wounds and crushes the demons. He appears to them in form and appearance as though he still has passion, and so he deceives the enemies and is left by them without warfare and without temptation. Once a certain brother was insulted with abuse by another. He was not at all stirred to agitation in his heart, but prayed in his mind. Then he began to cry out at the top of his voice, with a feigned voice of passion, and made it appear that the abuse had hurt him, and

In this way he hid his freedom from passion. Another brother, on the other hand, completely hated sitting in the first place. Yet he put on an appearance and acted as though it pained him and he wanted to sit first. How shall I tell you and explain the purity of the one who went into a brothel? He made it look as if he were going in for evil, but he drew even that harlot to purity. Someone brought another solitary a bunch of grapes at dawn, for [?] him. As soon as the one who had brought them left, the elder fell on the grapes quickly and ate them without desire, to make himself look like a glutton to the demons. Another man, adorned with virtue, suffered slightly from [?]. Every day he acted as though he were grieving over that [?], but he did not care about it at all. People like these need great watchfulness and caution.

They must not, then, be mocked by the demon while they mean to mock the demons. For these are the ones of whom the blessed apostle Paul said, "as [?] and yet true." Whoever wishes to present a pure body and heart before Christ, let him keep freedom from anger and fasting. Without these, all our labour is in vain. The light of the eyes varies: some see sharply and some poorly. In the same way, the perceptible comings of the triple Sun into the soul of man take many different forms. One kind comes through bodily tears:
joy in the soul. Another kind comes through spiritual tears, and another through the bodily eyes;
and another through the spiritual ones;
another comes from hearing words, and another arises in the soul by itself;

another comes from obedience, and another from stillness. Distinct from all of these is another, which through the rapture of the mind presents the soul before the light of Christ in a way that cannot be told or spoken. There are virtues, and there are mothers of virtues;

so whoever is wise is more eager to acquire the mothers. The Lord alone, by his own power, teaches the mothers, but many others can also teach the offspring. Let us beware, then, that when we fast by going short of food, we do not spend the time in sleep;

for this is what fools do, just as it is folly, again, to eat a great deal at the time of vigil. I have seen labourers in virtue who, because of some affliction [?], had relaxed a little in the matter of food. At once these vigorous and brave men tormented their belly with whole nights of standing, and taught it to flee gladly from fullness. The demon of love of money fights fiercely against those who own nothing. When he cannot defeat them, he brings in the poor as a pretext instead,

and in this way he forces those who are free of possessions to become attached to material things. When the spirit of despair fights against us, let us remember the commandment that the Lord gave Peter, how he commanded him to forgive. For he who commanded another would not He [? text breaks off]

[?] did he himself do more? But when we grow proud, let us then remember the saying that the spiritual [?] over one passion, which is haughtiness [?]. There are wicked spirits and envious demons who deliberately withdraw from the saints, so that they will not be defeated by them, and so they rob them of being crowned. No one disputes this. But I saw someone who created enmity between two people, and I called him blessed. There were two people who had a love of fornication for one another. But a certain wise and experienced elder created hatred between them, for he told one of them about the other: "He always speaks ill of you and says evil things about you," and he said the same to the other one. And that wise man was able to undo the wickedness of the demons by human means, and created a hatred that broke up the fornication. There are people who, for the sake of one commandment, break another commandment;

for I saw young men who loved one another in a godly way with a pure heart, and for the sake of the passion and conscience of others they made each other aggrieved [?], and for some time they separated from one another, so that no one would meet with a stumbling block. Just as the wedding day and the day of being carried to the grave are opposed to each other, so here pride and despair are opposed to each other; and often, through the disorderly work of the demons,

these incompatible passions are found in the soul at one and the same time, which is a marvel. There are some unclean demons who teach us the interpretation of the Scriptures, and they do this especially in the hearts of the vainly proud, and especially in those who are learned in the teachings of the philosophers. At first they begin by suggesting true things, so that little by little they may lead them astray and cast them into heresy and blasphemies. When we see turmoil, restlessness and disorderly joy at the time of such understanding, let us recognize from this that the theology of the demons is fighting against God and is not theology. Each created thing has received from the Creator an order and a beginning, and some also an end. But the limit and end of virtue is unattainable, for the Psalmist says that [?] and endless [?]. If I went in strength [?],
that is, from the strength of action to the strength of contemplation,
and love never comes to an end, and of fear [?], of love, whose end is endless; and if we advance in it, we shall never come to rest, neither in this world nor in the age to come.

…upon light, to receive yet another light and good understanding. Even if this saying seems strange to some, I say, O blessed one, that just as I said above that virtue has no end, so now I also say that not even the incorporeal natures of the angels are without progress, always remaining at one point. Rather, they always rise from glory to glory, and they keep adding understanding to understanding. Do not be surprised if the demons put some good thing into our minds and then themselves oppose the thoughts of our heart. They do this to convince us that they know the thoughts of our heart. But far from it: they know nothing else except what they themselves have put into our minds [?]. Do not be a bitter judge and a harsh critic when you see some who are lofty and great in word, teachers and enlighteners of souls,

but not quick to struggle in deed. Often the benefit of their word makes up for what their deeds lack. Not all of us have everything in equal measure: in some, word surpasses deed, and in others, deed surpasses words. God has neither created nor made anything evil. For this reason some have erred who said that certain passions are natural to the soul. They did not understand that we have turned into passions the things that were created good in our nature and for the benefit of our nature. By nature there is seed in us for the sake of children, but we have turned it into fornication. By nature there is anger

in us against the demons, but we use it against our neighbour. There is also zeal in us by nature, so that we may be zealous in doing good, but we use it for evil. By nature there is desire in us, but for the Kingdom, and we have turned it toward sin. We also have loftiness by nature, but against the demons, and we have applied it where it is not fitting.

He also gave us joy by nature, but for the Lord and over our neighbour's good, and we have directed it toward evil. By nature we also have the remembrance of wrongs, but against the enemies of the soul, and we have turned it against our brothers. The soul of the zealous stirs up the demons to anger against it, but when battles multiply, crowns multiply too. [?] …he who will not be crowned either. But whoever does not fall into despair over the falls that befall him, and does not give up the battle, will be glorified by the angels as a brave soldier. He who

…within, he lives forever. And whoever proves victorious at the three times will no longer be defeated, nor will he die forever [?]. If, by providence and for our instruction, after the rising among us of the one who is known [?], again from us [?], then among us the wild beasts that had first gone out from us [?], and all the beasts of the forest, the thorny things of the passions [?] of our hope [?], also ask for passions, or deeds, or thoughts [?]. When humility spreads among us, again, the souls that love pleasure [?], and the demons are no longer with us, so that we too may again say [?]… but you have been pitifully put to flight [?]. What [?] is a soul raised above every earthly desire, what [?] is a heart formerly darkened by passions, idols,
…and the evil words of the heart of this mind. If our Lord Jesus Christ fled from Herod in the flesh, he who was all-

powerful, let the proud learn not to hand themselves over willingly to temptations. For it says that loftiness is entwined with courage, as [?] is entwined with the cypress, which is called "zmilaki" [?]. Let us examine ourselves with a good examination, to see whether there is any true good in us; and thus we shall find ourselves lacking in every true good. Search out the forms of the passions unceasingly, and you will find that there are many among us which we do not see, because we are weak in mind. But if the eyes of the soul are enlightened, then we shall see them clearly; for as long as they rule in us, we are not able to see them. God judges the intention, but requires deeds according to our strength, and all with love for mankind. Great is the man who does not fail to do the deeds that are within his power,

but greater than him is the one who with humility undertakes even deeds beyond his power. Often the demons turn us away from very small deeds, from which our benefit would come, and urge us to do heavy deeds beyond our power. I find concerning Joseph that he was called blessed for turning away from sin, and not for dispassion. We must ask for which sins, and for how many, turning away earns a crown; for it is one thing

to flee from darkness, but greater is to flee to the sun. Darkness brings stumbling, and stumbling [?] brings falling, and falling brings death. Those darkened and fallen through wine have often been washed with water, but those fallen through the passions have been washed with tears. Disturbance of the mind is one thing, agitation is another, and darkening is another. Fasting heals the first, stillness the second, and obedience and the Lord Jesus Christ the third, who [?]. Nothing prevents us from taking, as an image of the purification of the soul, those who clean material garments. For the fuller and the dye clean and adorn those garments, and the spiritual fullery is the community of the monastery, which cleanses the soul of its filth, grossness and sins. When the soul in that community strips off all the grossness of anger and of remembering wrongs, then stillness becomes for it a beautiful, richly coloured dye. Some say that falling back into one's first sins comes from a lack of repentance for those first falls. But we must ask whether everyone who does not fall back into his first sins has repented worthily and fully. Some have fallen back into their first sins

because they plunged the former ones into the abyss of forgetfulness and did not remember the torments coming to them for those sins; or because, through love of pleasure, they reckoned God to be loving toward mankind beyond measure; or because they had cut off hope of their own salvation. But let no one blame me if not

I would say this: perhaps it comes from the fact that these enemies could not bind the flesh, which held sway over them by the power of habit. It must be asked how it is that, since the soul is incorporeal and immaterial, it does not see the incorporeal beings who come to it as they really are. Perhaps this is because of its union with the body, which He alone knows who joined them together. A certain spiritual and learned brother asked me about a matter that I wished to learn. He said to me: "Tell me, which sins humble the mind, and which exalt it?" And I admitted my ignorance.

Then he said to me: "I will put a little leaven of teaching in you, and afterwards you examine it well. Fornication, gluttony, anger, despondency and sleep cannot raise up the horn of the mind. But love of money, love of power, much talking, judging others and many other things add evil upon evil and exalt the mind." Suppose someone has gone to laypeople, or has received them in his cell, and after they leave an arrow of sorrow strikes him, and he does not instead become joyful that he has escaped snare and stumbling. The demon either of vainglory or of fornication is making sport of such a person. First we ought to see from which direction the winds are rising, so that when we raise the sail it does not become a hindrance to our course. With love, comfort the laboring elders who have worn themselves down with the labor of fasting, and give them a little rest. Compel to fasting the young men who have broken

their souls with sin, and remind them of the eternal torments. As we said above, it is impossible that as soon as we leave the world we should at once be completely cleansed of gluttony and vainglory. But let us not fight vainglory with gluttony. Rather, let us entreat the Lord with fasting to deliver us from it. For the time is coming, and for those who desire it, it already is, when the Lord will subject that too under our feet. Young men and old men who come to the monastic life do not have the same battles, for their maladies are not the same. Therefore blessed humility is truly blessed, for it becomes an unerring repentance for both young and old. Do not be amazed at the saying I am about to speak. There are few such souls, but there are souls that are simple, innocent, and ignorant of cunning and perversity, for whom living among people is entirely harmful. In stillness, by living with their spiritual father alone, they are able to climb to heaven as if by a ladder, remaining untouched and unharmed by the disturbances and tumults of monasteries. Lovers of fornication are healed by men;

the wicked are healed by angels; but the proud are healed by the Lord alone. This is also often a form of love: when our neighbor comes to us, let us leave matters to his will, whatever he wishes, and in everything let us show him a cheerful face. Let us examine

When repentance becomes a dissolver of good things, just as it is a dissolver of evil ones. Let us examine and understand well when, or in what matter, or for how long it is fitting for us to stand and fight against the matter of the passions; for sometimes the choice of flight is right because of our weakness, so that we do not die. Let us see and understand which demons exalt the mind and which humble it; which make it hard and which falsely claim to bring light; which make us slack and which make us hasty; and which lead us into gloom and which into joy. Do not be surprised if, when we come to be monks, we see ourselves at the beginning as more free from passions [?] than when we were in the world;

for the matter of the passions must first be stirred up and driven out, and only then does health come. Or else those beasts were hidden among us before and we did not see them, but now we have seen them. When something happens and those who are close to perfection are defeated by the demons in some small matter, they strive by every means and repay the matter a hundredfold. Just as the winds sometimes stir the surface of the sea, when they are not violent, and at other times again

churn it up from the abyss, so it is with the passions. In those who are subject to passions, they disturb them from the depths of the heart, but in the perfect they disturb only the surface of the mind. That is why the perfect quickly regain their own usual mindfulness [?]. This is the work of the perfect: always to recognize in their own soul which thought comes from the conscience, which comes from God, and which comes from the demons. The demons do not suggest everything as evil from the outset, and that is why this is hard to discern. The body is given light by the two bodily eyes, but the discernment of thoughts and of outward actions gives light to the eyes of the heart.

Among the other virtues: firm faith is the mother of ascetic struggle, and its opposite is plain. Good hope makes us hate the world, and its opposite is plain. Love of God is the cause of exile from home, and its opposite is plain. Obedience is born of self-blame, of eager desire, and of [love of] dishonor. Fasting is the mother of soundness [?] and a reminder of death. The remembrance of death and meditation on the sufferings of Christ are helpers of purity.
