Stillness makes the heat of the flesh disappear. Vigil and fasting crush evil and foul thoughts and calm the warfare. Faith and exile from home kill the love of money, while mercy and love lead people to give up even their own bodies. Constant prayer destroys despondency, and the remembrance of judgment increases zeal. The medicine for anger is love of insult and shame, while psalmody, mercy and poverty put out sorrow. Hatred of visible things makes us love invisible things;
and silence and stillness fight against vainglory; but if you live among people, love dishonor. Visible pride is healed by a broken and abased [?] way of life;

But the invisible by the invisible one, the one born before the ages. Of all visible reptiles, the deer is the killer; and of all invisible beasts, humility is the killer. There is one among the things of nature that teaches us about all invisible matters. As with the old skin: unless [the snake] goes into a narrow hole, [it is not stripped off]. In the same way, we cannot strip off our former habits and the filth of the soul, or the garment of the old man, unless we pass along the narrow and hard way of fasting and of being despised. A heavily fattened quail cannot fly up to the height of the sky, and neither can one who fattens his own flesh. Pigs cannot rest on dried-up dung, and demons cannot rest on flesh that has been dried up by toil. A great deal of smoke often puts out a fire, and in the same way excessive grief darkens the soul and dries up tears. A blind archer cannot hit the mark, and in the same way a contentious disciple will perish. Good iron sharpens soft iron, and in the same way a zealous brother often saves a slothful one. As an egg that is hidden in dung
brings forth chicks, so the thoughts of the heart that are not revealed are carried out in deed. As horses in a race, which compete with one another,

so is a community of good brothers. As a cloud covers the brightness of the sun, so evil thoughts darken the mind. When a sentence of death is passed on someone, he no longer asks about, or says anything about, jesting [?] and singing. In the same way, a true mourner will not fill his belly. When the poor see the treasures of kings, they recognize their own poverty all the more. In the same way, the mind of a soul that reads about the lofty virtues of the fathers and the martyrs is humbled all the more. Iron obeys the magnet even against its will, and in the same way those who have become habituated to a passion are dragged along by it by force. Oil calms the sea, and in the same way fasting quenches the burning heat of the flesh. Water rises upward when it is confined. In the same way, a soul confined by battles and temptations rises toward God through repentance and escapes from its oppressors. One who carries fragrant ointment becomes known by its fragrance, even if he does not wish it. In the same way, one with whom the Spirit of the Lord is becomes known to everyone by his speech and his humility. As winds stir up the sea, so ...

Anger disturbs the mind more than all the other passions. As a thing the eye has never seen is not greatly desired, so those who are virgins in body are lighter in the warfare than those who have experienced evil. As thieves do not much dare to approach the treasuries of a king that are surrounded by guards, so he who has established prayer in his heart is not much plundered by those invisible robbers. As fire does not come out of snow, so he who seeks the honour of this world cannot attain the honour of heaven. As a single coal often burns up a great deal of material, so a single good deed may be found that wipes out a multitude of sins. As it is impossible to kill wild beasts without weapons, so neither can anger be killed without humility. As human nature cannot exist without food, so it is not fitting for a person to be negligent even for one moment, right up to death. As the light of the sun, when it enters a house through a hole, lights up everything, so that even the smallest dust can be seen, so when the fear of God enters a person's heart, he sees all his sins, both open and hidden. As the crab sometimes walks forward and sometimes backward and makes no progress, so the soul that sometimes laughs, sometimes weeps and sometimes indulges itself gains nothing. As stealing something from a sleeping person is easy,

so those who stay close to the world are easily stripped of good works. As one who fights a lion is killed if he is careless even for one moment, so one who fights his own flesh will be defeated by it if he gives it rest. As harm comes to one who climbs a broken ladder, so all human honour and glory are opposed to humility. As it is impossible for a hungry man not to think of bread, so life is impossible without remembering death and judgment. As water wipes out writing, so tears wipe out sins. As some writings are not wiped out by water, and we erase them by some other means, so souls that have no tears have their sins wiped out by sighing, mourning and great grief. As dung breeds worms, so a great deal of food breeds falls and evil, defiled thoughts. As one whose feet are bound cannot walk, so one who gathers money cannot rise to heaven. As a fresh wound heals more easily, so old wounds of the soul are hard to heal, and if they heal at all, it is only with hard work. As it is impossible for a dead man to walk,

Likewise it is impossible [?] for one who cuts off hope of his life. As one who says, "I have the true faith," and commits sin is like a face that has no eyes, so one who does not have the true faith and performs ascetic labour is like a man who draws up water and pours it into a pierced jar. As a ship that has a good pilot enters the harbour in peace, so the soul that has a good shepherd ascends to heaven in peace, with the help of God, if it is obedient, even though it has committed many sins. As one who walks on an unknown road without a guide easily goes astray, even if he is intelligent, so one who walks in the monastic life by his own authority and according to his own will easily perishes from the very beginning, even if he has the wisdom of the whole world. If someone is weak in body and has committed many sins, let him walk the way of humility and its works, for he will not find life any other way. As it is impossible for one who has been sick for a long time to return in a single moment to his former strength and health, so it is impossible for a man subject to the passions to destroy his passions completely in an instant. Learn the measure of every passion and virtue that you have, and always watch when it grows and when it diminishes; in this way you will know its progress and its measure.

As those who exchange gold for clay suffer great loss, so do those who reveal their spiritual virtues for the sake of bodily honour. Many have received forgiveness of sins quickly, but no one has quickly acquired freedom from the passions; for this requires God's help, length of time, and much labour. Let us take note which beasts or birds fight against our field at the time of sowing, which at the time of sprouting, and which at the time of harvest, so that we may set up traps and lay snares for them fittingly. As it is improper for someone who has a fever [?] (literally "head-neck") to kill himself, so it is evil to despair, right up to death. As it is shameful for someone to bury his father and, on returning from the burial, immediately hold a wedding, so it is unfitting for those who mourn for their sins to seek honour, or rest, or glory from men in this passing world. As the dwelling of rulers is one thing and that of the condemned another, so those who have sinned must take up a changed way of life and a harsh dwelling,

and not one like that of the sinless. Just as a king does not disregard a soldier whose face has been wounded in battle, but gives him gifts and honor, so the eternal King Christ will crown with the crown of joy the monk who is beset by many afflictions and trials in the battle with the demons.

Wisdom is in the soul by nature, but sin destroys that wisdom. Knowledge of evil gives rise to ceasing from it, and knowledge comes from conscience, which is the mind that knows good and evil. God gave us conscience to accuse us of our evils and to guard us, and baptism strengthens it within us. The more it is purified, the better it can accuse us, and the more it is trampled down, the weaker it becomes. That is why it accuses the unbaptized of evil only weakly, not strongly. But it makes the baptized who listen to it stop doing evil. Ceasing from evil gives rise to hatred of evil, and hatred of evil is the beginning of repentance. The beginning of repentance is the beginning of life and purifies the mind. Purification of the mind gives rise to ascetic struggle. Ascetic struggle is the beginning of the virtues, and the beginning of the virtues is the flower of the soul. Fear gives rise to keeping the commandments. Keeping the commandments is the image of love. The beginning of love is the growth of humility, and abundant humility is the mother of dispassion. To acquire dispassion is to perfect love. The perfection of love is the indwelling of God, through dispassion, among the pure in heart. To Him be glory and might, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

A discourse of our holy father John, on the stillness of body and soul. Chapter 27.

We have become slaves of those impure passions and have obeyed them. Because of this we have come to know a little of their wiles, their devices and their works, by which the evil spirits have taken control of this wretched soul of ours. But there are others who know the evil spirits' tricks through the power of the Holy Spirit and because they have been completely freed from them. One kind of person learns from the pains and sufferings of illness how restful health is. Another kind learns from the joy of health what the misery of sickness is, and can describe it. So now, being weak, we are afraid to speak words of wisdom to you about that harbor of stillness. For I know this: a dog stands by the table, watching for a chance to snatch the bread and eat it by itself. In the same way the devil stands by the good community of obedient brothers. He is eager to snatch a soul away from there, using stillness as the excuse, to find it alone without a helper, and to devour it. That is why I have not, until now, thought it right to speak about peace and quiet to those who are in the battle, the soldiers of the heavenly King. I did not want this discourse of ours to give the devil a foothold, or to give an excuse to those who are looking for one.

But this alone we say: for those who fight well, a crown of peace and stillness is prepared. And now, if you wish, let us say a little by way of understanding, so that no one may be grieved if we leave this subject wholly unexamined. Stillness of the body is the ordering and calming of habits and senses; stillness of the soul is the understanding of the thoughts of the heart, and a mind that is not stolen away. A brave and manly thought is the friend of stillness; it stands at the doors of the heart unceasingly and sleeplessly, and of the enemies who come, some it kills and some it drives away. Whoever has become still with understanding of heart knows what is said here; but whoever is still an infant does not know this and has not tasted it. A hesychast who has understanding has no need of words, for he is enlightened by deeds rather than by words of his own. The beginning of stillness is to flee from the voices and tumults of the people, since they disturb the mind; its end is no longer to fear that the tumults and voices of the people will disturb one's calm, but to remain wholly unharmed in the midst of them. Whoever becomes still with understanding will be instructed and will become a house of love, and he will be wholly gentle and unmoved by contradiction and anger;
but whoever does not sit in stillness with understanding becomes, as it were, a slave of anger and pride.

The hesychast is one who shuts up his incorporeal and immaterial mind within his material cell, a wonderful and great thing. The pearl-seeker seeks [?] the pearl; but the mind of the hesychast seeks the invisible pearl. Do not despise the parable told above; otherwise you have not yet come to know stillness. Not [?] with a monk, for one who is alone needs great caution and a mind that is not stolen away. A neighbor often helps one who lives with others, but an angel helps one who lives alone. The spiritual powers of the angels help and dwell with the spiritual hesychast; but the opposite of this I will keep silent about and not speak of. The abyss of divine things is deep, and the mind of the hesychast dwells in it. Swimming in one's clothes is not without danger, and theology is not peace for one with passions. The cell of the hesychast is a wall for the body, and the body of the hesychast is a wall for the mind, and within it the mind has the house of understanding. Whoever has passions and spiritual sickness and takes up stillness is like a man who throws himself from a ship into the heart of the sea, holding a small plank in his hands, and wishes to reach land without toil.

Those who are fighting against this clay, this flesh, may do well to enter stillness at the proper time, provided they also have a guide, because complete solitude requires the strength of an angel. What I say here is for true solitaries, who are in stillness in both soul and body. A solitary overcome by despondency would tell lies and use some pretext [literally "by a parable"] to call people to him, so that it might draw him out of stillness. When he leaves his cell, he blames the demons and does not realize that he has become a demon to himself. I have seen solitaries whose blazing, fire-like longing for God they fulfilled insatiably through stillness, and they produced fire from fire, love from love, and desire from desire. The solitary is the true image of an angel on earth. With the charter of desire for God, written in the letters of zeal, he has set his prayer free from all sloth and despondency. The solitary is the one who cries out in truth: "Always…" [?]. The solitary is the one who said: "Shut the door of the cell to the body, beloved, and shut the door of the tongue to speech, and shut the door of the heart to the evil spirits." The calm of the sea and the heat of the sun test a sailor's patience, and a lack of necessities shows a solitary's patience.

The sailor grows despondent when he has to swim in the waters, and the solitary loses heart when he mixes with the crowd. Do not be afraid of apparitions and sounds, because one who mourns knows no empty fear and is not terrified by apparitions. Whoever's mind has learned true prayer speaks with the Lord face to face, like a man who talks privately with a king. Whoever prays only in words, in a bodily way, is like a man who falls down before the king in front of all the princes. And those who live among lay people are like people pleading with him in the uproar of a whole crowd. If you have learned this art well, you will understand what has been said. Sit as a guard over the words of your heart, if you only know how to keep watch. Look carefully, and then you will learn how, when, from where, and how many come into your vineyard to steal. When you grow tired of watching and keeping guard, get up and pray, and then sit down to your work again with courage. Someone very experienced in this wanted to speak about this subject in detail, but he was afraid. He feared that it might make even the worker slack, and that those who wanted to enter into this life might be turned back by the terror of his words. The demons rage against anyone who speaks about stillness in detail and with understanding, because no one exposes their foulness as he does. Whoever has attained the perfection of stillness, [the passage breaks off here]

knows the depth of the mysteries; but he does not arrive there unless he first endures the tumults of the waves, and the fierceness of the winds and their assaults. The apostle Paul confirms this saying, for if he had not been caught up to paradise through stillness, he would not have heard the unutterable words. The ears of stillness will hear wondrous things from God, for in Job too this all-wise stillness spoke. The solitary is he who flees from people, without hatred, in the same way that the faint-hearted and slothful person flees to people, but who flees for this reason: that the sweetness of God may not be ruined within him. Go, for selling requires time, but scatter it also to the monks, so that by prayer they may help you toward stillness, burdened as you are by obedience; and bear mightily the weight of the slaying of the passions, and [?] to blessed stillness, and I will teach you visibly the work and way of life of the invisible powers. Those heavenly ones are not sated forever and ever with praising the Creator, nor will those who have been in that heaven of stillness be sated with glorifying the Maker. Those bodiless ones have no care at all for what is bodily; nor do those bodily bodiless ones care for necessities. The former have no desire for

…toward [?]; nor the latter toward any human need, or for the sake of bodily rest. The heavenly ones do not care about possessions; nor do these care about wickedness and the warfare of the demons. The heavenly ones have no desire for created, visible things; nor do these have lust for persons. The heavenly ones never cease advancing in the love of God; nor do these cease imitating them. The riches of their progress are not unknown to the former; nor to these the longing to ascend to heaven. The heavenly ones do not cease until they reach the Seraphim; nor do these until they become angels. Blessed is the one who has the hope of attaining this measure; thrice blessed is the one who has drawn near to it; and an angel is the one who has attained it.

Concerning the various kinds of solitude

This too is known to all: in all works and arts there are differences of will, of intention and of measure. For not all have the perfect measure; some have the perfect one and others a lesser one, either because of their weakness or because of their sloth. For this reason there are differences in this work as well. For some enter this harbour, or rather this abyss, because of the weakness of their bodies and of their mouths and because of the tyranny of their habits, so that they may cut these off. And others do so because they were irascible, and

the wretched ones could not overcome their anger while among people. Others wished to enter this sea because of their self-will and arrogance. Others entered into it because, while living among material things, they could not separate themselves from material things. Others did so in order to acquire diligence through solitude. Others chose it so that they might torment themselves in secret for their sins. And others entered into it so that they might win glory for themselves from people. But there are others (if only the Son of Man, when he comes upon the earth, should find such ones) who joined themselves to this blessed state out of desire and thirst for the love of God. Before entering into it, they gave a bill of divorce to every thought of despondency, for to dwell with despondency is to be separated from the former.

According to this small wisdom that was given to me, I have hewn out a ladder like an unskilled architect. Now let each one see on which rung of this ladder of the solitaries he stands. The first rung is for the sake of self-will; the second for the sake of human glory; the third because of weakness of the tongue; the fourth for the sake of flight from material things; the fifth because of the tyranny of anger; the sixth so that they may torment themselves; the seventh so that they may acquire diligence; the eighth so that they may add fire to fire. The seven rungs are the works of this seven-day age, some good and some harsh, but the eighth foreshadows the age to come.

Watch, O monk who lives alone, at the time when the beasts come; otherwise you will not be able to set the snare well.

If the one who received the written bill of separation by hand has gone away, the handiwork is superfluous; but if he has not yet been separated, I do not know how I should remain in stillness [?]. Why did not as many luminaries appear from the holy Tabennesiots as appeared from the Sketiotes? Let him who understands understand, for I am not able to say it, and still less do I wish to. Some by struggle against and resistance to the passions; and some by chanting and by spending the greater part of the time in psalmody; and some by standing in prayer; and others by being in contemplation — they pass their times according to these ways. Examine also what was said above, and let him who understands by the Lord understand. There are lazy souls who, when they entered the community of a monastery and found food in abundance as a help to their dissoluteness, came to utter perdition; and there are others who stripped off their own dissoluteness by living together with others. And this has often happened in the same way not only to the lazy but also to the zealous. By the same rule we also say concerning solitude that it has received many who were tested and made them untested, and through self-will revealed their love of pleasure; and it has taken others and, through fear and concern about bearing their own judgment, made them zealous and fervent. Let no one who is overcome by anger and pride, by hypocrisy and by remembrance of wrongs, seek to see even the trace of solitude, lest his mind acquire nothing but error. But whoever is pure of these

he himself will know what is better, and I think that not even he will know all of it. Those who practice stillness as is fitting, these are their signs: a sleepless mind, a pure heart, rapture toward God, keeping judgment before the eyes, remembrance of death, insatiability in prayer, a watchfulness that cannot be stolen, the mortification of fornication, ignorance of vainglory, death to the world, hatred of gluttony; a source of speaking about God,

a spring of understanding, perpetual tears, the destruction of much talking, and other things like these, whose multitude resists [?]. But for those who do not carry it out as is fitting, this is the mark of their poverty: the growth of anger, the hoarding of remembrance of wrongs, the dissolving of love, the increase of pride — and I will pass over the rest in silence. Since the discourse has come to such a point, it is good that we should also speak about the truly obedient: what their characteristics and signs are, for the discourse is directed chiefly to them. Those who have been in obedience lawfully, well and fittingly have these signs, according to the word of the holy Fathers: daily growth in that humility of the new ones [?], the weakening of anger, the disappearance of gloom, deliverance from the passions, freedom from hatred, the effacing of desire in the face of reproofs and shames [?], ignorance of despondency, the increase of zeal, the love of mercy, estrangement from arrogance, which all these

[?] … is to be sought by [?], and it is found by few. When there is no water in a spring, its name is empty; and the wise will understand what follows from this. The soul that does not keep the vow it made to the Lord defiles itself, and these works of defilement follow it: forgetfulness of death, gluttony of the belly, failure to restrain the eyes, the pursuit of vainglory, endless sleep, hardness of heart, mercilessness, a store of evil thoughts in the heart, the multiplication of passions, captivity of the heart, great turmoil, disobedience, quarrelsomeness, vain attachments, unbelief, unseemliness, too much talking, and insolence, which is the most evil of all. And worst of all is hardness of heart, which is followed by fearlessness toward God, for this is the mother of all falls and passions. For solitaries, and for those who live in obedience, three [?]. A solitary who is overpowered by despondency will be in great distress, for in his struggle with it he will lose his hours of prayer and contemplation. Once I grew weary of staying in my cell and lost heart, so that I wanted to leave it. As I was about to go out, some men came and called me blessed as a solitary. At once the thought of despondency was driven away by vainglory, and I marveled at how that demon of vainglory, like a bull's head, overcomes all the other demons.

Set your mind at every hour to examining your scales: from which side they tilt, at the time of turning back, and again at the time of tilting and of leveling, and see to what point and from what direction the tilt and the victory are greater. But whoever has acquired stillness through the Holy Spirit knows this saying. The first work of stillness above all is freedom from care about affairs, both proper and improper, for whoever opens the door to the former will undoubtedly be seized by the latter. The second work of stillness is prayer removed from all negligence; the third is the unrobbed contemplation of the heart. Just as it is impossible for one who has not learned to join letters together to read books as well, so it is impossible for those who have not acquired the first to perform properly these two that follow. I was [?]

I reached [?], and they illumined the thirsty one, and behold, I was among them. But what its former visible color was, I could not learn, for the ruler did not wish it. Yet I asked to know how it is now, and he told me that it is in its own [state]. But I only said, "What is the upright standing and the sitting of that ailment [?]?" And he said that it is impossible to speak of this to the ears. Then I asked about what I longed for, and he said that the time has not yet come to hear about such a deficiency [?] of that fire of incorruption. Whether this was with this earth I do not know, or whether without it, I am altogether ignorant.

It is hard to drive away [?] by sleep at that midday hour, especially in the days of summer, and only then is handiwork good. I saw the demon of despondency, how it outruns and runs ahead of the demon of fornication, in order to loosen the flesh and sink it in sleep, and in this way bring defilements upon solitaries. If you resist them, they will fight you powerfully and fiercely, so that you may say, "It profits me nothing," and thus cease from ascetic struggle,

But be courageous; for nothing so reveals the defeat of the demons as their battles against us. When the time comes to go out from your cell, guard firmly what has been gathered within the cell; for when the door is opened, those confined birds quickly fly away, and the benefit of stillness vanishes. A small hair troubles the eye, and a small care ruins stillness; for stillness is the gathering in of the mind and the putting away even of proper cares and concerns. Whoever has acquired true stillness does not care even for his own body, for He who promised is unfailing. Whoever wishes to present his mind pure before the Lord yet multiplies his cares is like a man who binds his feet tightly and wishes to run swiftly. Some say that it is difficult to learn all philosophical teaching, and that few are found who do; but I say that it is far more difficult, and that few are found who know that wisdom of stillness.

Whoever has not come to know God as he should is wholly inexperienced in stillness, and many waves will break over him. Stillness is hard for the inexperienced. Because they have never seen the taste of God's sweetness, they spend their hours in despondency, distraction and every kind of thought. Whom [?] from the crowd, like a wild ass [?]. For what else has healed that wild ass gone savage, except prayer? A person whose passions have gained the mastery is trained by them in the desert. A holy elder told me this. I mean George of Arsilaia, whom your Honour also knows. He taught this poor soul of mine about stillness and said: "I set my mind to watch, and I saw that the demons of vainglory and lust come at dawn. At midday come the demons of despondency, sorrow and anger. And in the evening come those dung-loving demons of gluttony." A poor disciple is better than a solitary who is caught up in worldly cares. If someone lives as a solitary and does not see that he is making progress day by day, know that either he is not doing the works of stillness or he has been taken captive by pride. Stillness is to stand before God without ceasing and to serve him.

Let the remembrance of the Lord Jesus stay with you as your breath does, and then you will know the benefit of stillness. The fall of a disciple is his own will, and the fall of a solitary is the ruin of prayer. If you rejoice at the arrival of guests, know that you are joined to despondency and not to God. As an image of prayer, take that widow who was afflicted by her adversary; and the image of stillness is the great solitary Arsenius, the equal of the angels. Remember, O you who live alone, the conduct of this angelic solitary, and see how many times he turned away even those who had come to him, so as not to lose what was greater. I saw demons who, as was fitting [?], sent wandering and negligent monks to solitaries, so that by this means they might hinder those workers of virtue at least a little. Learn to recognize such people, O true solitary, and do not shrink from distressing them with the fear of God; perhaps they will be ashamed and cease from their wandering about. Beware lest, on account of this example mentioned above, you distress in vain a soul that comes to you thirsting to draw up water; but in all things the lamp of discernment is needful for you. Let the life of solitaries, and still more of all monks, be lived with understanding and the witness of conscience. He who lives according to the rule, all his deeds and words and the thoughts of his heart
and impulses he should do according to the will of the Lord, and for the Lord, with understanding of soul and with beholding the face of the Lord; but if he goes astray,

he is not living according to the rule at all. The prophet says something, but I say: I will tell my will to the Lord in prayer, and from him I will receive full assurance. Faith is the wing of prayer,
for if prayer does not have it, it will return again to our bosom [?]. Faith is the standing of the soul without doubting,
so that it may not be shaken by any opposing wind. A believer is not the one who believes that God can do this,
but the one who believes, 'My request will surely be given to me.' Faith obtains [?] things beyond hope, and the thief showed this. The mother of faith is diligence and a sincere heart,
for the one makes a person free of doubt, and the other fulfills the request in deed. The mother of solitaries is faith,
for if he does not believe, how could he live well in stillness? Those who are bound in prison tremble for fear of the judge,
but he who lives in stillness in a cell wastes away for fear of the Lord. The first does not so fear the court
as the second fears the judgment of Christ. Acquire the fear of the Lord mightily in stillness, O beloved,
for nothing drives out despondency as it does. The condemned man in prison watches for when

[?] the judge will come, but the true solitary [considers] when death will come. The former is bound by sorrow, and the latter by a fountain of tears. If you have acquired the staff of patience, the powers of despondency will depart from you. Patience is the sinew and strength of the soul, which does not fall because of afflictions and battles. The patient person is a worker who does not fall, and if he does fall, he conquers even by falling. Patience is the daily expectation of trials. Patience is the destroyer of excuses and the guarding of oneself. As this nature of ours necessarily needs food, so the solitary needs patience. The latter is a cause of being crowned, while the former often becomes a cause of passions. The monk is dead before burial, and his tomb is his cell. Patience is born of hope and mourning, for whoever is apart from these two is a slave of despondency. The soldier of Christ ought to know from which enemies he must flee at a distance, and which he must let come near and fight hand to hand. Sometimes battle plaits a crown, and sometimes withdrawal from battle leaves a person untested. These rules cannot be taught by words, for we are not all at one level, nor do we have equal battles. One [?]

It wars against you without ceasing, in standing and in walking, in sitting and in lying down, in prayer and in sleep. Not only with a single word of the heart do they remember [?]. For some have this as their exercise: "[?]"; and others have this: "[?]"; and others practise this: "[?]"; and others meditate on this: "[?]"; and others meditate on "[?]"; and others practise "[?]"; and others meditate on the saying "[?] without labour [?] a crown." He who is advancing well toward perfection does his own work not only when he is awake but even in his sleep; for this reason some fight the demons even in their sleep and overcome them. Do not expect visitors, and do not prepare in advance for their arrival, for the rule of the solitary is simple and straightforward. No one can build the tower of stillness unless he first sits down and reckons whether he has the materials to build it;

otherwise, after he has laid the foundation, he may become a laughing-stock to his enemies and a stumbling-block to the other workers who do good. Examine carefully the sweetness that comes to you in the time of stillness, in case it comes from bitter physicians, or rather from murderous enemies. At night give the greater part of your time to prayer and a small part to psalmody; and again by day manage things according to your strength. The reading of books does much to collect and enlighten the mind, for they are the words of the Holy Spirit and they strengthen those who read them. Read books that speak about the virtues and the passions, and everything that teaches you how to live, so that your mind may be well collected. Seek to find the words of life through labours rather than through books. Do not read the thoughts of those who have gone astray before you reach great perfection, for they are words of darkness and they darken the weak. By a single sip the taste of wine is known, and by a single word the whole inner work of a solitary becomes known to experienced teachers. Fight with all your strength against pride, for nothing robs the mind more grievously than it. Guard your tongue when you go out of your cell, for it quickly scatters many labours. Acquire a simple life, for [?] defiles [?]

…in stillness, crookedness [?]. Those who come to you, provide them with whatever is fitting, whether bodily or spiritual. If they are wiser than we are, let us show wisdom by silence; but if they are our equals in measure, let us open the door in moderation. Yet it is good for us to reckon all of them as higher than ourselves. The strength of a king is a multitude of people and treasures, and the strength of solitaries is abundant prayer. Just as, in words, the confession of the holy, uncreated and worshipful Trinity stands in contrast to the confession of the incarnate dispensation of the One of that same holy Trinity — for what is spoken of there as divided is spoken of here as one, and what is spoken of there as one is spoken of here as divided; for there we speak of three persons and one nature, and here of one person and two natures — so likewise the works of stillness are one thing and the works of obedience another. The holy prophet and the holy apostle say that [?]; but I say: who has truly known the mind of a man who is solitary in body and soul by the power of the Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. The strength of a king consists of wealth and many subjects; and likewise the strength of the solitary consists of abundance of prayer.

Discourse of the same, on all-holy prayer, the mother of the virtues, and on standing well in it with both body and mind. Chapter 28. Prayer, by its nature, is the union of God and man; and in its working it is the stability of the world and reconciliation with God; the mother of tears and again their child; the remitter of sins; a bridge over temptations and a dividing wall against afflictions; the crusher of battles; the work of angels and the food of the bodiless powers; the joy of the age to come; an unending work and a fountain of virtues; the leader to graces; invisible progress; the food of the soul; the light of the mind; the slayer of despair and the cause of hope; the deliverer from sorrow; the wealth of monks and the treasure of solitaries; the dispeller of anger; the mirror of perfection; the revealer of one's measure; the image of right order; the foreshadower of the age to come; and the sign of courage. For one who truly prays, prayer is a court of judgment and a judgment seat before that great judgment. Arise, let us listen to this blessed queen of the virtues, to the voice with which she cries out to us, saying with a loud voice: [?] and refreshment

of your wounds, and physician of the great diseases of sin. All of us who go to meet God and our King, let us not make that journey unprepared, lest he see us from afar unarmed and naked of royal adornment, and command his servants to drive us far from his face, bound, and our written petitions be returned torn to our very faces. When you go to stand before the Lord, let the garment of your soul be woven with the [?] ("heel-piece"; perhaps "thread") of not remembering wrongs; otherwise you will gain nothing from prayer. Let all your asking be made with a humble mind, for the publican and the prodigal became pleasing to God by a single word. Standing before God in prayer has one form, but many divisions,

and each of its kinds is distinct. Some speak as to a friend and King, interceding for others and no longer for themselves; others ask for glory and spiritual riches and greater boldness; others implore to be delivered from their adversary; others seek to receive honor; others pray for complete release from their debt; others fall down in supplication for release from prison, and others for forgiveness of sins. Before everything else, on the chart of our petition let us set thanksgiving, and second, confession and contrition of heart with understanding, and only then let us make our request known to the King; for this is the good form of prayer, as was made known to a certain brother

by an angel. If you have ever stood before a visible judge, you will need no other model for how to stand in your prayer. But if you have neither stood there yourself nor seen others standing, then take this model at least from the sick person, how he implores the physician when he is about to cut or burn him. Do not speak with philosophical wisdom in prayer, for many times tender young children, by simple words, have made their Father in heaven merciful toward them. Do not seek much speaking, so that your mind may not be scattered in searching for words;

for one word of the publican made God merciful, and one word of faith saved the thief. Much speaking has many times scattered the mind, but saying even one word fervently gathers it together. When you are moved to compunction at some word in prayer, stay on it and say it many times, for our guardian prays near us and with us. Do not show boldness in prayer, even if you have great purity, but rather approach with great humility, and you will become all the more bold. Even if you have climbed the whole ladder of virtues, still pray for forgiveness of sins; for you hear what Paul, that great apostle, says about sinners, that [?]. Oil and salt are the seasoners of food, and what gives wings to prayer is purity and

...tears. If you clothe yourself wholly in meekness and freedom from anger, you will not have to labor much to free your mind from captivity. Until we acquire pure and proper prayer, know that we are like small children who are able to see well [?]. Strive to lift up your mind and to confine it within the words of your prayer; and if it grows weak because of its immaturity and sinks low, raise it up again. Instability is proper to the mind, but he is able to restrain it,

who can do all things: God. O beloved, if you struggle well, he will come upon you too who hedges in the sea of the mind, and he will say [?]. It is impossible to bind a spirit, but where the Creator of the spirit is, all things obey him. If you have seen the sun, you can speak about it; but what you have not seen, how can you speak of it without falsehood? The beginning of prayer is that thoughts come only in small measure and are easily driven away; the middle is that the mind be only in the words; and its perfection is the love of God. One thing is the joy of prayer that occurs among the obedient, and another is that which occurs among solitaries; for in the first there may perhaps arise even the illusion of arrogance, while the second is full of humility.

If you always teach your mind not to depart from you, even at table, it will be with you when you lie down. But if you accustom it to wander about unchecked, it will never come to you. The great worker of true prayer, Paul, says that in the church [he would rather speak a few words with his mind]. But this is far from those who are infants in mind. For along with the gathering of our mind, we also need a quantity of prayer, and the second is what brings about [?] the first, as Scripture says that he will grant [it], and holy [?] with labor and hardship, to the one who supplicates him. The defilement of prayer is one thing, its corruption is another, its theft is another, and its blemish is another. Defilement is when a person stands before the Lord and dwells on evil thoughts. Corruption is when, at the time of prayer, a person is carried off captive to useless cares. Theft is when the mind wanders about without our noticing. Blemish is any idle thought that comes to us at that time. If we are not alone at the time of prayer, let us form the manner of supplication inwardly. But if those servants of praise [?] are not with us, then let us also make our supplication with outward posture. For in many ways the mind is conformed to the body in those who are not yet perfect. All who approach the King need a contrite heart, but above all those who ask for remission of debts and forgiveness of sins. If we are still in prison,

let us listen to him who says to Peter: Arise, wrap about you the garment of obedience, strip off your own will, and, naked of it, look to the Lord in your prayer, and call upon his will alone; and then you will find God holding the rudders of your soul, and he will steer your life without its sinking. Arise from love of the world and love of pleasure.

Cast away cares, deny your flesh, and strip off the thoughts of the heart, for prayer is nothing other than the renunciation of the world, both visible and invisible, as that speaker says: [?] "but only this, that I may always be nailed to you." To some, wealth seems good, to others glory, and to others honor; of dispassion [?]. Faith gives prayer wings, for without it prayer cannot ascend to heaven. Although that judge does not fear God, for he himself is God, yet because of the trouble caused him by the soul widowed from the good through falling into sins, he will give her justice against her adversaries, the flesh, and against the demons who fight her. Let us who are subject to the passions not cease entreating the Lord, for all the dispassionate have attained dispassion from a state of passion. Our good Lord draws grateful and good souls to his love by granting their requests quickly, but the ungrateful

and to those who are not mindful he does not give quickly, so that through hunger and thirst for what they ask he may make them persevere in prayer, always supplicating him. For when a dog receives bread, it goes away from the one who gave it; and when a foolish and senseless soul receives what it asked for, it no longer falls down before God in supplication. Do not say, 'I have spent much time in prayer and have made no progress.' For see, you have already made progress, in that you stand before the Lord and converse with him. For what higher good could there be than standing before the Lord and being united with him through prayer? A condemned man does not fear the sentence of his punishment as much as the ascetic fears prayer, lest perhaps it harm him. Therefore, if he is wise and prudent, through that concern he will remove from himself all malice, worry, quarreling, sorrow and overeating. Prepare your soul with prayer beforehand, before the time of prayer and of your supplication to God, and you will soon make good progress. I have seen men who shone in obedience and who, as far as was possible, did not neglect the remembrance of God in their minds. As soon as they stood up to pray, they quickly took control of their minds, and streams of tears flowed like rivers, because they had been prepared beforehand through obedience. Psalmody with many people brings distraction of the mind, while solitary psalmody does not bring so much distraction of the mind. But again, despondency fights against the one who prays alone, and with many people, zeal of heart

[?] helps. The love of a soldier for his king is shown by battle on his behalf, and the love of a monk for God is shown by the time of prayer. Your prayer will reveal your measure and your deeds to you, for the holy fathers have named it the mirror of the monk. Whoever is occupied with some task at the time of prayer, the demons make sport of him, for this is the will of those demons: to steal away from us one hour after another. Do not disregard someone who begs you, "Pray for me," even if you do not have perfect prayer; rather, pray for him with a contrite heart, for the faith of the one who asks many times with contrition has saved the one praying as well. Take care not to become proud when you pray for others and the Lord hears your prayer; rather, know that it was because of their faith that the Lord granted that grace. Every teacher demands from a child each day the recitation of what he has learned, and the Lord will demand from every mind, day by day in prayer, the power it has received from God. When you pray well,

then the battles of the enemies will rise up against you, for this is always their custom. Every virtue, and prayer above all, should be practiced with understanding and with fervor of heart. The soul prays fervently when it has overcome anger. Every thing gained by much asking and labor

and by time is firm. Whoever has gained the Lord within himself has no need to be taught prayer by word, for then the Holy Spirit himself is his intercessor with his own self. Do not accept any visible fantasy or vision in prayer, lest madness come upon you and your mind be led astray. The assurance of every request appears in prayer. Assurance is freedom from all doubt. Assurance is unwavering knowledge of unknown things. Be [?] of holy prayer, for by it monks [?] but the latter with the latter. When the fire of fervor is kindled in the soul, then prayer rises up and ascends, and when prayer rises up and is lifted to heaven, there comes a descent of that divine light into the upper chamber of the soul. Some say that prayer is higher than the remembrance of death, but I glorify one person with two natures. A good horse, when it goes on and warms up, adds all the more to its running; and by running I understand

the singing of prayer, and by the horse the courageous mind. Such a one perceives the spirit of battle from afar, and having prepared in advance he stands unconquered forever. It is harsh for a thirsty man to have water snatched from his mouth, and how much harsher it is for a zealous monk who is praying with compunction if someone should interrupt that longed-for prayer before its completion. Do not [?] until you see the fire and the water turned back to you again, for you may perhaps not find another such time for the forgiveness of your sins in all your days. Whoever has seen the taste of prayer defiles his mind by saying a single word, many times over; and when he goes to prayer, he does not find that longed-for sweetness as he usually does. It is another thing to have oversight of the heart by the mind, the ruler and chief priest who offers those rational sacrifices to Christ.

Upon some who approach it, that holy fire of heaven burns them, as one of the theologians says; it burns them because of their deficiency in purity. And others it illumines, because of their measure of perfection, for the same is called both burning fire and purifying light. For this reason some come out from prayer as from a furnace, purified of the matter of sins; and others come out from it as those illumined by light and clothed with the heavenly [?] of humility and joys.

But those who come out of prayer without either of these two states have prayed as though bodily and not spiritually. If bodies that touch another's body have the appearance and condition of their nature changed, then how shall he not be changed who touches the body of God with innocent hands? Something like the ways of the kings of the earth is seen also with that good King of ours: for sometimes he himself, sometimes through his friend, sometimes through a servant, and sometimes in an entirely hidden way, he bestows his gifts on his soldiers; but he multiplies his graces toward us according to our humility. Just as it is abhorrent to an earthly king if someone stands before him and turns his face away and converses with the king's enemies, so also it is abhorrent

[?] is before the Lord, whoever stands in prayer and entertains impure thoughts. When that dog that takes the mind captive comes upon you, drive it away with the weapon of prayer; and however many times it grows fierce, do not let up, and do not give it room. Ask with mourning, seek with obedience, and knock with patience. For he who [does] thus [?]. Be on your guard, and do not pray much for a woman in your prayer, lest you be taken captive from the right side. Do not begin to confess your bodily sins in prayer just as you committed them, lest you become your own murderer. Do not make the time of prayer a time for examining and studying spiritual matters, unless [?] the higher need presses upon you. Whoever holds the staff of prayer without ceasing will not stumble; and even if something happens and he stumbles, he will not fall completely. For prayer is a wondrous, divine and sweet thing, which does not let a man turn toward evil. From this we learn its great benefit: nowhere do the enemies fight against us as they do in prayer. But we shall learn its fruit when our enemies are utterly defeated, for by this we shall know that in the time of battle [?]. The psalmist says [?], that is, with the mouth, and with the soul and with the mind. For in whatever prayer the soul and the mind come together

soul and mind together, [?]. Neither bodily conditions nor spiritual ones are the same for everyone. For some, quicker psalmody in prayer is suited, and for others, slower psalmody. The former struggle against the captivity of the mind, and the latter against ignorance. If you entreat the King without ceasing against your enemies, be bold when they approach you. You will not have to labor much; they will flee from you of their own accord. For when those impure ones see you, they do not want you to receive a crown through their warfare. Instead, scourged by prayer, they flee as from fire. Acquire good courage, and in this way you will gain God as your teacher of prayer. The sight of the eyes is not taught by words, for it is natural. In the same way, the beauty of prayer is not taught by someone else's words, for it has God as its teacher. It is not words that you might hear and learn, nor the excellence of a craft that you might receive from someone else. God is its teacher, who teaches men knowledge, grants the requests of those who pray to him, and blesses the years of the righteous. For his is the glory, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

Discourse on dispassion and perfection, and on the resurrection of the soul before the general resurrection. Chapter 29. Behold, we too, lying in the deep pit of ignorance, in the darkness of the passions and in these shadows of the death of the flesh, boldly begin to speak about this high firmament, which is dispassion. The visible firmament of heaven has the stars as its adornment, and dispassion has the virtues. For I understand dispassion as nothing other than a heaven of the heart and mind, which counts all the assaults of the devil as a mere breath of wind. The truly dispassionate man is the one who has made his flesh free of passion and wholly incorrupt, has raised his mind above created things, has subjected all his senses to it, has presented his soul before the face of the Lord, and continually goes toward Him even beyond his own strength. Again, some say that dispassion is the resurrection of the soul before the resurrection of the body. Others say that dispassion is [?] of God equal to that of the angels, or only a little short of theirs.

That perfect and unending perfection of the perfect, when it comes to a person, so sanctifies the mind and lifts it away from the material things of the world, as someone who had tasted it told me, that its companion [?], caught up out of the world, spends most of the time of his life in the harbor of heavenly contemplation. Concerning this, the one who had tasted it said: Such was that Egyptian, who did not dare to lift up his hands to heaven for long when he prayed with others, for otherwise he would forget where he was, and he would not come back from there for a long time. There is the dispassionate man, and there is another more dispassionate than the dispassionate. For the one strongly hates evil, while the other is always very rich in virtues. Purity of virginity is also called dispassion, and rightly so, for it is the forerunner of the general resurrection and of the incorruption of corruptible natures. He who said, "I have the mind of the Lord," showed dispassion. The Egyptian who said, "I do not fear the Lord," showed dispassion. He who prayed that [?] might return showed dispassion [the text breaks off here].

Who in this transitory life, before the age to come, has gained such dispassion and perfection as that Syrian did? For David, the renowned and great one among the prophets, said to the Lord, [?]; but this great struggler of the Lord said: "Restrain, O Lord, the waves of your grace." That soul has dispassion which is as fervent for the virtues as the passionate are for their lusts. If this is the limit of gluttony, that a person forces himself to eat even when he does not want to, then this is indeed the limit of fasting: that he does not give food to his hungry nature even when it would be blameless. If this is the unnatural limit of the love of fornication, that a person is aroused even by animals and lifeless objects, then this is indeed the limit of perfect purity: that he looks on everyone, as far as passion goes, as though they were lifeless. If this is the end of the love of money, that a person never ceases gathering and is never satisfied by it, then this is indeed the perfection of poverty: that he does not spare even his own body. If this is the extent of despondency, that a person has no patience even when at rest, then this is indeed patience: that he counts affliction as patience. If this is the depth of anger, that a man grows angry even when he is alone, then this is indeed the work of long-suffering: that he looks on the one who troubles him as a friend. If this is the height of vainglory, that even if no one is present to praise him, he

still performs deeds for show, then this is indeed the form of humility: that even among people the mind does not slip away into showing off. If this is the form of pride, that a person is exalted over worthless deeds, then this is indeed the excellence of humility: that he counts his own lofty virtues as nothing. If this is passionateness, that a person follows all the thoughts sown by the demons, then this is indeed the sign of that blessed dispassion: that a man can truly say, "I do not know how it came, or why, nor how it went away; but I am entirely ignorant of evil things, and I am, and shall be, wholly united with God always." Whoever is made worthy of such a measure in this very world has God as his own teacher, who dwells within him, and inwardly he hears His voice brightly, by that divine light, higher than every visible voice: "For I can no longer bear the intensity of that desire, but I seek that goodness which he granted me before this clay." Why should anyone speak at length about dispassion? For he no longer lives, as says the one who fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the true faith. Just as a king's crown is not made from a single precious stone, so dispassion is not

[?] comes about, if even one virtue is neglected. Understand dispassion in this way: as if it were the palace of the great King, and there are many mansions in it, and its wall is the forgiveness of sins. Let us run, my brothers, I beseech you, let us run and hasten to enter that palace of the great King and that bridal chamber of joy. But if, because of the weight of sins and evil habits, we cannot enter that bridal chamber (alas for this trial!), then let us at least hasten to reach one of its mansions. And if we cannot enter even there, let us not remain outside the wall, but let us hasten by every possible means to get inside that wall. For whoever does not enter within that wall before the end will wander astray outside in the deserts and be devoured by wild beasts.

For this reason the prophet prayed, saying [?], and another prophet says, as from the mouth of God, that [?]. Let us cut through, O beloved, the middle partition of that wall, which we wickedly built through disobedience, and let us obtain here the forgiveness of debts, for there is no consolation or repentance in hell. Let us be still and understand, for we have no excuse: neither the multitude of sins, nor the weight of the burden, nor the adversity [?] of the times, nor anything else. For those who received the Lord through that washing of the second birth [?], and he said: I AM GOD, and I am dispassion

and holiness. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen. Blessed dispassion raises the mind of the poor from the dunghill of the passions and lifts it from earth to heaven, and all-praised love seats it with the princes of the angels, with the princes of the people of the Lord.

Work of the same holy father of ours, John, abbot of Sinai, on the triad, concerning the three virtues: faith, hope and love. Chapter 30. And after all these things said before, it confirms and holds fast that which is marvelous above all: of all [?], for it is called God. And I see the first as a ray, the second as light, and the third as the disc of the sun.
And all three together as one radiance and splendor. For the first is able to do all things;

and the mercy of God surrounds the second; and the third does not fall, nor does it ever cease from running, and it no longer allows the heart wounded by it to rest from that divine longing. Whoever wishes to speak about love has undertaken to speak about God, and speaking about God in words is a stumbling block for the incautious. The word of love is known only to the angels, and to them only according to the measure of their radiance. And whoever wishes to state its definition is a blind man in the abyss, counting the sand. Love by nature is likeness to God,

[?] as far as is possible and attainable for human beings; in action it is the good drunkenness of the soul, and in its character it is a fountain of faith, an abyss of long-suffering, and a sea of humility. True love is the removal of every contrary thought. Love, dispassion, and adoption as sons differ in name only, but their power is one, as with fire, flame, and light. As far as love diminishes, fear increases, for whoever has no fear is either filled with love or dead in soul. Is there anything to prevent us from adopting images of the fear of God, of diligence, of good zeal, of service, and of the love of God? Blessed is he who has acquired such a love of God as an evil lover has for his beloved. Blessed is the man who fears the Lord as those condemned by a judge fear him. Blessed is he who longs for the Lord as a hungry man longs for bread. Blessed is he who is as eager to serve the Lord as faithful servants are toward their master. Blessed is he who has such zeal for the virtues as men who love the glory of the world have for royal honors. Blessed is he who stands in prayer

[?] within, before the Lord, as soldiers stand in fear before the king. Blessed is he who strives to win the favor of the Lord, as friends do with one another. A nursing infant does not long for its mother as much as a son of love longs for the Lord. Whoever has firm love and passion for someone always pictures the face of his beloved and delights in it with an inward sweetness. Even in sleep his longing does not fade; he still sees that person. This is how it is with bodily loves, and also with bodiless ones. Someone who was wounded by this spoke marvelously, saying that because of the nature of the flesh [?] … because of the abundance of love. Know this, O blessed one: when the hart, which is the courageous soul, destroys those evil reptiles, then [?] toward the Lord. For they are burned up by the fire of love as if by a burning drug. The work of hunger is hidden and unseen, but that of thirst is fierce, plain and known to all. Therefore the one who longed for God said: “If the sight of a friend makes us glad, what would the sight of the face of God not do, when it comes invisibly to a pure heart?” When the fear of God is joined to fervor of soul, it consumes and wipes out defilement, for

it says that [?]. But holy love devours some, as that speaker says that [?], and again it makes others radiant and glad, for it says that [?]. When a person is wholly mingled with the love of God, then outwardly too, as in a mirror, he displays that inner radiance of the soul, for thus was Moses, the seer of God, glorified;

And those who attain to such an angelic measure as this often forget even the food of the body. And what is surprising in this, since even evil desire has often made people forget food? So I think that the bodies of those who attain to this incorruptible measure do not fall into sicknesses in the usual way either,
for the causes of disease have perished from them,

just as the flame of fever has been quenched; nor does the food they take give them pleasure any longer, for water nourishes the root of trees, but that fire of heaven nourishes their soul. The growth of the fear of God is the beginning of love, and the end of love is the beginning of theology. He who has wholly united his senses to God has learned the mysteries of his words; for if it is not so, it is difficult to speak about God. The essential Word makes purity perfect, and his coming puts death to death; and when death has been put to death, then that disciple is enlightened

in theology. The word of the Lord abides forever and ever, but he who does not understand the Lord God as is fitting speaks by conjecture. Purity and love made that beloved disciple a theologian, who by his words confirmed the faith in the all-holy Trinity. He who loves the Lord has first come to love his brother, for the sign of the first is this second. He who loves his neighbor will never listen to slander, but will flee from it as from fire. He who says, "I love the Lord," and hates his brother is like a man who runs in his sleep. The strength of love is hope,

for through it we await the reward of love. Hope is the wealth of unknown wealth. Hope is the undoubting treasure before the treasure. Hope is rest in labors; it is the door of love; it is the crusher of despair; and it is the image of that age to come. The lack of hope is the disappearance of love, for on it depend ascetic struggles, on it hang labors, and around it stands mercy. The monk who is a worker of hope is a slayer of despondency, for he slays it with the sword of hope. The tasting of the Lord's gifts gives birth to hope, but those who have not tasted them cannot

[?] to them, so that suspicion may not arise in you. Anger destroys hope, for hope is never put to shame, but anger is a thing of shame, according to the word of Solomon. Love is the head of prophecy. Love is the giver of miracles. Love is an abyss of radiance. Love is a spring of fire: the more it wells up, the more it burns the one who thirsts. Love is the firmness of angels. Love is the progress of eternity. Tell us, O fairest among the virtues, and make known to us [?]. Enlighten us, give us to drink, lead us on, and bring me up, for we long to ascend to you, since you rule over all. And now you have set my soul on fire, and I can no longer bear that flame of yours. Therefore I will sing your praise forever. The proud thoughts of the heart [?] … and you have kept those who love you free from warfare. But how did Jacob see you at the top of the ladder? I want to learn. Tell me, for I long to know: what is the form of the ascent of that ladder? Or what is the arrangement and order of its rungs, which your lover [?]? Tell me. Or what is their number? I thirst to know. Or what is the time of the ascent there? For I know that the guides are angels, as your lover Jacob taught us.

Finally, after all this, the sovereign of the virtues looked down from heaven and spoke in the ears of my soul: "O my lover, unless you are freed from the grossness of this transitory world, you will not be able to see my beauty as it ought to be seen. But if you would inquire about that ladder, its steps and structures, behold and learn the spiritual arrangement of the virtues. And I sit at the top of them all, as the great Paul, the minister of my mystery, says, that [?]" A brief exhortation, which contains within itself all that has been said at length in this book. But now let us ascend, brothers, let us ascend, for you hear the one who speaks, who says: "[?] to victory with his song [?]." Run, all of you, I beseech you, with him who says: "Let us hasten [?]" He who, at thirty years of the visible age of his flesh, was baptized, and is seated upon this thirtieth step of our spiritual ladder; for love is God, to whom belongs the song [?], to whom [?]
belongs steadfastness, to whom belongs power, to whom belongs every cause of good things, who was and will be, now and forever, and unto those endless good and radiant ages. Amen.
